title: Home
content:
The Purpose of the Path

Beyond Worldly Bondage
Towards the Deathless

The world is governed by the universal law of aging and death, decay and dissolution. However refined and elevated our worldly existence may become, the central question remains: how can the mind-heart (Citta) be released from the bondage that ties it to the world?

Gautama's liberation teaching points towards a goal beyond worldly ascension: Arahantship and Tathāgata, having set out to go to Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm beyond the world.

Arahanism is dedicated to preserving Gautama's true dhamma of liberation and restoring the central purpose of renunciation: the attainment of Arahantship and complete liberation from worldly bondage.

WHAT IS ARAHANISM?

A Calling to Preserve the Original Liberation Teaching

Arahanism is a renunciant path devoted to the liberation teaching of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Rooted in the Theravāda monastic tradition, Arahanism seeks to preserve Gautama's true Dhamma of liberation teaching that remain within Theravāda while critically examining later doctrinal and practical developments that have obscured the original teaching.

Its mission is to restore the centrality of the liberation path, cultivate sensory restraint, a disciplined life of purification practice, and guide dedicated practitioners towards Arahantship. Through the progressive training of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, practitioners learn to withdraw from worldly entanglements, overcome the bondage of rāga (Worldly craving and attachment), dosa (fear, anger, aversion, violence and hatred), and moha (ignorance and delusion, not knowing the path of liberation from the world), and progress towards disenchantment with the world (nibbidā), fading of worldly passion (virāga), and liberation from the world (vimutti).

Sīla → Samādhi → Paññā → Nibbidā → Virāga → Vimutti

Know more about Arahanism

Brahmacariya

The Way of Renunciation

Worldly renunciation is the practical foundation of Gautama’s ancient path of liberation. Through the progressive training of Sīla, practitioners gradually withdraw from worldly entanglements and prepare for the higher trainings of Samādhi and Paññā.

The training begins with the Five Precepts, the ethical foundation of lay life. Then by undertaking the Eight Precepts on Uposatha days, lay practitioners act as part-time practitioners, taking their first steps toward renunciation. Celibacy becomes a defining discipline, while abstaining from entertainment and luxurious comforts reduces dependence on worldly sources of pleasure. Wearing white clothing and undertaking Eight Precepts full-timely, Upāsakas and Upāsikās progress from part-time lay practitioners to become full-time lay practitioners.

The next stage is Pabbajjā, or novice professional practitioner in robes, undertaken through the Ten Precepts as a Sāmaṇera or Sāmaṇerī. This marks a deeper withdrawal from the world, in which the practitioner leaves household life and dedicates themselves to spiritual cultivation. A defining discipline is renouncing personal possessions and involvement in worldly economy: refraining from handling money, buying and selling, and participating in economic transactions. Through celibacy, simplicity, voluntary poverty, and detachment from worldly entanglement, the novice begins to loosen the bonds of worldly life and prepare for full renunciation.

This leads toward Upasampadā—full ordination as a bhikkhu or bhikkhunī—undertaking the Pāṭimokkha (literally meaning "towards liberation") and the wider discipline of the Vinaya. Full ordination marks a complete commitment to renounce worldly entanglement, dedicated entirely to the ultimate goal of Arahantship. The relinquishment of possessions and complete sense control paves the foundation for the rigorous purification of the citta from rāga, dosa, and moha. Through celibacy, sense restraint, and sustained training of Samādhi and Paññā, the bhikkhu or bhikkhunī walks the ancient path toward complete liberation from worldly bondage.

Each stage deepens one's commitment to the ancient renunciant path of liberation, laying the foundation for Samādhi, Paññā, and the ultimate goal: Arahantship and the realization of the Deathless.

know more about our training

A Canadian Theravāda Lineage

The Arahanist Order of Canada

The Arahanist Order of Canada is a Canadian Theravāda lineage dedicated to preserving and transmitting Arahanism—the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Grounded in the Theravāda Vinaya as preserved in the Pāli Canon, the Order establishes its distinct institutional identity around the systematic cultivation of worldly renunciation, ethical discipline, sense restraint, meditation, liberating wisdom, and the pursuit of Arahantship.

Arahanism places the renunciant path at the centre of spiritual life. The Order seeks to establish a living monastic community in which the Dhamma can be studied, practised, and transmitted across generations of dedicated renunciants. Its work includes supporting the formation of Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs, cultivating disciplined contemplative communities, and establishing the conditions necessary for sincere practitioners to devote themselves to the complete liberation of the mind from worldly bondage.

The Order's institutional identity is distinctly Arahanist, while its monastic discipline is grounded in the Theravāda canonical tradition. As a Canadian Theravāda lineage, it seeks to establish a sustainable monastic institution that upholds the discipline of renunciation, draws upon established traditions of monastic training, and remains open to respectful dialogue with other Theravāda lineages.

The Order's purpose extends beyond religious affiliation, ritual ceremonies, or institutional expansion. It exists to sustain the living practice of the Liberation Path, cultivate a community devoted to renunciation, and transmit its training to future generations. At the heart of this undertaking lies the ultimate objective of the renunciant path: Arahantship and the realization of the Deathless.

Know more about our lineage

Teachings & Publications

Explore the teachings, books, and writings of Arahanism on Gautama’s Liberation Path, renunciation, meditation, and the realization of the Deathless. Through scriptural study, practical training, and comparative spiritual inquiry, these works invite readers to examine the path towards Arahantship.

Meet the Ācariya

Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera
Founder and Spiritual Head of the Arahanist Order of Canada · Founding Ācariya of Arahanism

Bhante Mudita is a Canadian Theravāda monk, meditation teacher, and founding Ācariya of Arahanism—the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant. Following his ordination at Pa Auk Forest Monastery in Myanmar and years of meditation retreats in Myanmar and Thailand forest, he dedicates himself to the study, practice, and teaching of the Dhamma of Arahanism.

His mission is to preserve Gautama’s original liberation teaching, restore renunciation and Arahantship to the centre of spiritual practice, and guide practitioners through the progressive training of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā towards complete liberation from worldly bondage.

Through Arahanism, publication, teaching, and meditation retreat, he leads a dedicated Arahanist community committed to the Liberation Path and the realization of the Deathless.

title: Training
content:
The Path: Arahanist Training for Liberation

Arahanism is the direct, original path of Gautama the Supreme Arahant — a complete system of training that leads to arahantship: full purification of citta, independence from the world (anissito), and entry into Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm.

“The path is not a philosophy or cultural practice. It is a lived, verifiable training leading to full liberation.”

Core Structure of Arahanist Training

Sequential Path:

Sīla → Samādhi → Paññā → Nibbidā → Virāga → Vimutti

Each stage builds upon the previous, forming a rigorous, experiential trajectory toward the Deathless.

1. Sīla — Ethical Withdrawal from the World

  • Foundation of all practice: Brahmacariya and sense restraint redirect citta away from sensual craving and survival instincts.
  • Purpose: Purifies conduct, eliminates remorse, and establishes inner safety.
  • Outcome: Prepares the mind for deeper meditative work and insight.

Without Sīla, citta remains scattered and bound.

2. Samādhi — Lifting the Mind Beyond Physical Reality

  • Concentration gathers and unifies citta, transcending sensory-dominated perception.
  • Stabilizes attention, dissolves fragmentation, and elevates the mind to higher-dimensional realities aligned with Brahma qualities (brahmavihāra).
  • Provides clarity, luminous stillness, rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and the stability to penetrate reality without collapse.

Samādhi bridges worldly reactivity to divine stability.

3. Paññā — Direct Realization Through Higher Seeing

  • Vipassanā across layered fields — body in body, feeling in feelings, citta in citta, dhammā in dhammā — reveals the conditioned nature of all worldly phenomena.
  • Penetrates impermanent and unsatisfactory nature of the world, not a safe base for true self (ATTA-DIPA) or refuge (ATTA-SARANA).
  • Uproots rāga (WORLDLY attachment AND CRAVING), dosa (SURVIVAL INSTINCTS OF FEAR AND ANGER), and moha (ignorance AND DELUSION OF NOT KNOWING THE LIBERATION PATH).
  • Dismantles the false self, perceiving the world as a constructed field with no lasting support.

Paññā establishes unshakeable insight into the NATURE OF MULTI-DIMENSIONAL HUMAN EXISTENCE AND WORLD COSMOLOGY.

4. Nibbidā — Disenchantment from the World

  • Mature recognition of the futility of all WORLDLY conditioned existence.
  • The mind no longer clings to WORLDLY pleasure, power, identity, or even refined meditative states.
  • Naturally arises from Paññā — citta sees that nothing in the world fulfills the deep human wish for eternal life, peace AND JOY.

5. Virāga — Fading of Worldly Attachment

  • Worldly craving and clinging weaken naturally.
  • Citta no longer leans toward worldly phenomena.
  • Attachment dissolves; survival instincts and ignorance no longer bind the mind.

6. Vimutti — Liberation from the World

  • Citta stands fully independent (anissito) from the world.
  • False self constructed from worldly attachments is seen through and DISMANTLED.
  • The luminous citta ABIDES IN Nibbāna-dhātu — the Deathless realm of Amata (Deathless), Ajara (Ageless), Dhuva (Stable), Sukha (Blissful), Suddha (Pure), Santi (Peaceful).

No MORE worldly becoming arises; liberation FROM THE WORLD is complete.

The Two Streams of Practice

Arahanism unites two inseparable streams:

  1. Satipaṭṭhāna — Foundational Mindfulness Training
    • Penetrates layered fields of experience to dissolve worldly clinging and the derived false self.
    • dwells independent (anissito ca viharati), and does not cling to anything in the world (na ca kiñci loke upādiyati).
  2. Anussati — Higher Mindfulness Training
    • Ten advanced mindfulness practices
    • Keeps citta oriented toward liberating references: Gautama the Supreme Arahant, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, precepts, generosity, devas and Brahmas, death, Kāyagatāsati, Ānāpānasati, and the ultimate peace of Nibbāna-dhātu.
    • Strengthens resolve, purifies intention, and aligns citta with the Deathless REALM.

Integration: Satipaṭṭhāna provides AWAKENINGinsight; Anussati ACHIEVES orientation & resolve AND ATAINMENT OF liberation.

The Path is Open

  • The method is clear.
  • The realization is attainable.
  • The luminous citta awaits purification.
  • The Deathless REALM awaits departure.

Walk the path. The true home is Nibbāna-dhātu.

title: About
content:
About the Center for Liberation Studies

The Center for Liberation Studies is a research and educational organization dedicated to exploring structured pathways to human liberation through contemplative training systems. the Center aims to bridge traditional wisdom with contemporary inquiry, offering programs and research that integrate ethical, attentional, and cognitive disciplines for personal transformation.

Our work is grounded in the Arahanism contemplative framework, a rigorous system of practice developed within the Theravāda tradition by the Supreme Arahant, Gautama. This framework emphasizes the sequential cultivation of Sīla (ethical withdrawal), Samādhi (lifting concentration), and Paññā (penetrative wisdom) as the foundational methodology for awakening and entering the Deathless realm (Nibbāna-dhātu)—the complete liberation from the world.

The Center serves multiple strategic functions:

  1. Education and Training – We offer structured programs ranging from foundational practices, such as Kāyagatāsati (Mindfulness Directed to the Body), to advanced samādhi-intensive training. Programs are designed to be academically accessible while preserving doctrinal integrity, allowing participants to experience the transformational processes that lead to liberation.
  2. Research and Contemplative Science – Our research division translates contemplative insights into the language of contemporary science, collecting empirical data, conducting pilot studies, and presenting findings at conferences. This work supports evidence-based understanding of consciousness, ethical regulation, and cognitive transformation.
  3. Outreach and Partnerships – The Center collaborates with universities, interfaith organizations, and mental health institutions to facilitate experiential learning, workshops, and lectures. We engage with institutions, promoting dialogue on human potential, ethical cultivation, and the phenomenology of advanced states of mind.
  4. Communications and Media – Through digital platforms, public lectures, and media content, the Center disseminates knowledge on liberation practices and contemplative science, making these teachings accessible to a wider audience without compromising depth or precision.

While the Center for Liberation Studies functions as the public and academic interface, it embeds the Arahanism framework internally as a deeper system of doctrinal and meditative training. This dual-layer model allows us to integrate seamlessly with institutions while preserving the transformative depth of traditional practices.

Our mission is to advance understanding and practice of liberation through rigorous, experiential, and scientifically-informed contemplative training—supporting individuals in realizing freedom from worldly attachments and the full potential of human consciousness.

The Arahanist Path

7 Day Meditation Retreat


Sīla • Samādhi • Paññā

Enter the direct training established by Gautama Buddha, the Supreme Arahant, for those seeking full liberation from the world.

A precise and demanding path to dismantle the forces that bind the mind to worldly existence—initiating a transformation that transcends human limits and to become more than human.

The Liberation Triad:
• Disenchanted from the World (Nibbidā)
• Fading off Worldly Passion (Virāga)
• Liberated from the World (Vimutti)

A retreat grounded in disciplined practice, deep inquiry, and open doctrinal clarification. Questions are encouraged. Doubt is examined and resolved.

From mud to sun — the lotus rises.
From the world to liberation — the mind ascends.

More information...

The Arahanist Path

Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā: A Progressive Curriculum for Walking the Ancient Path to Liberation

True liberation is not found through meditation alone, but through a life aligned with the original teachings of Gautama. Join us at the Wutai Shan Buddhist Garden for a program dedicated to the threefold training of the Arahanist Path.

Through the cultivation of Sīla (Virtue), Concentration (Samādhi), and Paññā (Wisdom), we train the Citta to disenchant from the world (loka). This integrated practice is the only way to achieve the complete eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha, leading to the true freedom of the Brahmacariya life.

  • When: Friday – Monday | 2:00 PM – 4:00 PM
  • Where: Wutai Shan Buddhist Garden
  • Requirements: No reservation needed. Please bring your own sitting cushion.

Walk the path that leads to the Deathless realm.

Programs

This Foundational course is rooted in the training of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, integrating study, meditation, and daily-life application. it brings the ancient wisdom of Gautama Buddha into direct dialogue with the psychological and existential challenges of modern life.

Many people today experience stress, anxiety, emotional turbulence, and mental fragmentation caused by the fast pace of modern life. this program is designed to address these conditions at their root by stabilizing, refining, and gradually liberating the mind to cultivate a healthier inner life.

An 8-week transformative Dhamma-based healing program, guiding the mind toward inner healing, clarity, and awakening-oriented stability.

More information

This one-day meditation retreat offers an introduction to the authentic teachings of the Buddha as preserved in the Theravāda tradition. Through meditation, Dhamma talks, guided contemplation, and open discussion, participants will explore the path of ethical purification, wisdom, and inner freedom while reflecting on life's fundamental questions, including the nature of suffering, the purpose of human life, and the possibility of genuine liberation.

more information

Temporary ordination creates a rare space to step outside the usual patterns of life and enter a completely different mode of being. Without the usual distractions, the mind begins to settle. What was previously hidden becomes visible. Patterns of attachment, habit, and restlessness reveal themselves clearly.

As the mind stabilizes, There is less pressure to react, less need to hold onto things, and a growing sense of inner space. For some, this becomes a reset. For others, it marks the beginning of a much deeper journey. it is a rare opportunity to encounter the mind directly and to take a meaningful step on the path of liberation.

title: Mindfulness Directed to the Body
content:
Mindfulness Directed to the Body (Kāyagatāsati)

An 8-Week training Program for Mental Clarity, Inner Stability, and Awakening-orientation of the mind

This Foundational course is rooted in the training of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, integrating study, meditation, and daily-life application. it brings the ancient wisdom of Gautama Buddha into direct dialogue with the psychological and existential challenges of modern life.

Many people today experience stress, anxiety, emotional turbulence, and mental fragmentation caused by the fast pace of modern life. this program is designed to address these conditions at their root by stabilizing, refining, and gradually liberating the mind to cultivate a healthier inner life.

Over the course of 8 weeks, this transformative Dhamma-based training provides practical and structured tools to:

  • establish ethical grounding (Sīla) that reduces inner conflict
  • develop meditative stability (Samādhi) that lifts the mind beyond sensory turbulence
  • cultivate insight (Paññā) that clarifies the nature of experience and loosens attachment

The aim is not only temporary relief, but a progressive reorientation of the mind—from fragmentation toward coherence, from agitation toward stillness, and from confusion toward clarity aligned with the path of awakening.

dhamma foundation of the Program

This program follows the classical path structure, guiding participants through three complementary phases:

1. Sīla — Stabilizing Life

  • Practical ethical alignment through the Five Precepts
  • Lifestyle refinement to support mental stability
  • healthy Body, energy, and daily mindfulness practices

2. Samādhi — Stabilizing the Mind

  • Mindfulness directed to the body (Kāyagatāsati)
  • Deep abdominal breathing and energy awareness
  • Techniques to calm agitation and unify attention

3. Paññā — Discernment & Inner Freedom

  • Recognizing wholesome vs. unwholesome states of mind
  • Releasing mental patterns that cause instability
  • Cultivating an independent, stable mind (Anissito)

Progressing through these phases, participants develop both inner stability and transformative insight, supporting well-being, clarity, and the mind’s independence from external conditions.

Core Principle: Body in Body vipassana

The central practice of this program, Mindfulness Directed to the Body (Kāyagatāsati), is grounded in the authentic teachings of the Buddha. Rather than merely observing the body from the outside, this practice trains awareness to enter and abide within the field of the body itself.

Through this Multi-layered immersive practice:

  • Attention stabilizes and lifts
  • Mental agitation diminishes
  • Awareness begins to stand independently, no longer dependent on external conditions for clarity, calm, or happiness

This is the healing dimension of the training, which naturally supports inner transformation and freedom of mind.

Complementing this, participants practice Mettā (Loving-Kindness Meditation), cultivating warmth, goodwill, and emotional resilience. Together, these practices form a balanced system for both inner stabilization and deeper awakening.

This program is rooted in the authentic teachings of Gautama Buddha, the Supreme Arahant. In pali canon, he described himself as a physician, a surgeon, and a healer—one who understands suffering, removes its causes, and guides the mind toward freedom.

Following that same principle, this training is not merely for relaxation or stress management, but a systematic method for inner healing, mental clarity, and transformation, aligning with the original intent of the Dhamma.

Program Structure

  • Duration: 8 weeks, 8 guided sessions
  • Session Components:
    • Short teaching connecting meditation to modern life
    • Guided meditation practice
    • Practical instructions for daily practice
    • Time for reflection and questions

Participants will learn to:

  • Stabilize attention through body-centered mindfulness
  • Calm mental agitation and improve focus
  • Cultivate kindness and emotional balance
  • Develop a deeper sense of inner grounding and autonomy
  • Build a sustainable meditation habit

Expected Benefits

  • Reduced stress and mental tension
  • Improved emotional stability and resilience
  • Greater clarity, focus, and inner calm
  • Increased sense of goodwill and compassion
  • Growing independence of the mind from external conditions

Who This Program Is For

This program is suitable for:

  • Beginners seeking mental clarity and emotional well-being
  • Practitioners wishing to deepen their meditation
  • Anyone interested in a practice that combines healing, inner stability, and authentic awakening-oriented training

No prior knowledge of Buddhism is required. The practices are presented in a practical and accessible way, while remaining fully aligned with the authentic Dhamma.

title: Ordination
content:
Theravāda Temporary Ordination Program

A Seven-Day Entry into the Ancient Path of Renunciation

From the earliest teachings of Gautama the Supreme Arahant, the life of renunciation (Pabbajjā) is presented as a decisive turning point in the path toward liberation.

“The household life is crowded and dusty; the life of renunciation is open and spacious.”
“Sambādho gharāvāso, rajāpatho; abbhokāso pabbajjā.”

This program offers a rare opportunity to step beyond the structures of ordinary life and enter, even temporarily, into this open and spacious field of training.

The Meaning of Temporary Ordination

Temporary ordination is not a symbolic retreat. It is a direct participation in the renunciant path.

For seven days, participants leave behind the habitual patterns of worldly life and adopt the discipline of a renunciant:

  • Living simply under ethical training
  • Withdrawing from external distractions
  • Cultivating meditation and inner stillness
  • Engaging in structured Dhamma study

This shift is not merely external—it is a reorientation of consciousness.

In ordinary life, energy flows outward into responsibilities, ambitions, and attachments. In renunciation, that movement is reversed. Attention turns inward. The mind begins to observe itself. The structures of worldly attachment and craving, survival instincts of fear and anger, and ignorance and delusion of not knowing the liberation path (Raga, Moha, and Dosa) become visible.

Rooted in the Great Renunciation

This training follows the archetypal path established by Prince Siddhattha, who, upon encountering aging, suffering, and death, recognized the limitations of worldly existence and chose a path beyond.

His renunciation marked the beginning of a path that led to complete liberation—the realization of Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm beyond the world.

This program is grounded in that same lineage of practice:
not the pursuit of worldly comfort or identity, but the purification of citta (mind-heart) and the realization of freedom beyond worldly conditions.

The Training: Sīla, Samādhi, Paññā

Participants are guided through the threefold training established by Gautama the Supreme Arahant:

  • Sīla (ethical withdrawal)
    Stabilizing conduct and gradually withdrawing from worldly entanglement
  • Samādhi (lifting concentration)
    Lifting the mind beyond the sensory field into higher states of clarity
  • Paññā (penetrating wisdom)
    Seeing clearly the nature of existence and the path of liberation

Together, these form a complete system of inner transformation, supported by the structure of renunciant life.

A Structured Seven-Day Immersion

The program provides a disciplined and supportive environment in which these trainings can unfold continuously.

Participants will engage in:

  • Pāli chanting
  • Daily meditation practice
  • Dhamma teachings and guided reflection
  • Observance of renunciant precepts
  • Periods of silence and contemplation

This is not a casual retreat. It is a focused immersion into the conditions that support liberation.

The Role of the Companion Text

This program is supported by a structured study guide, which serves as a companion text throughout the seven days.

The text provides:

  • Daily thematic teachings
  • Guided reflections
  • Doctrinal clarification of the path

Together with direct practice, it forms a complete training framework, integrating study and realization.

Who This Program Is For

This training is offered to individuals who feel a genuine call to:

  • Step back from the momentum of worldly life
  • Examine the mind directly
  • Experience the discipline of renunciation
  • Explore the path toward liberation

No prior monastic experience is required. What is essential is sincerity, discipline, and openness to transformation.

An Invitation

At certain moments in life, a deeper question emerges:

What lies beyond the cycle of striving, gaining, and losing?

The path of renunciation begins when that question is taken seriously.

This seven-day ordination offers a direct way to enter that inquiry—not through theory, but through lived experience.

Even a brief period of renunciation can open a profound shift in understanding. For some, it becomes a turning point.

Join the Waiting List

Due to the structured and initiatory nature of this program, participation is limited.

If you feel the call to undertake this training, you are invited to apply for the upcoming session:

title: Our Founder
content:
Founder and Spiritual Head of the Arahanist Order of Canada

Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera

Founding Ācariya of Arahanism — The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant

Academic Director, Buddhist College of Canada, Wutai Shan Buddhist Garden

Head of Theravāda Division, Buddhist Association of Canada

Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera is a Canadian Theravāda monk, meditation teacher, religious scholar, and author. His life and work are dedicated to preserving and transmitting Gautama's original liberation teaching, restoring renunciation and Arahantship to the centre of religious life, and establishing Arahanism as a living Theravāda lineage. Through monastic practice, doctrinal research, meditation instruction, publications, and the founding of the Arahanist Order of Canada, he seeks to make the complete Liberation Path accessible to those sincerely seeking freedom from worldly bondage.

Arahanism.org is the official website and research archive of Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera, documenting his religious work, doctrinal studies, teachings, publications, and the development of Arahanism. It also serves as the principal online platform for the Arahanist Order of Canada and its educational and spiritual activities.

1. A Calling to Gautama's Liberation Teaching

Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera is a Canadian Theravāda monk, meditation teacher, religious scholar, and author. He is the Founder and Spiritual Head of the Arahanist Order of Canada and the Founding Ācariya of Arahanism—the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant. His wider religious and educational work also includes serving as Academic Director of the Buddhist College of Canada at Wutai Shan Buddhist Garden and Head of the Theravāda Division of the Buddhist Association of Canada.

His religious life is guided by a commitment to preserving, examining, and transmitting Gautama's liberation teaching, with particular emphasis on restoring renunciation and Arahantship to their central place in the religious life. He regards the complete eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha, culminating in liberation from worldly bondage, as the supreme purpose of the path taught by Gautama.

Through his monastic practice, canonical studies, meditation training, doctrinal research, and teaching, Bhante Mudita has undertaken the development of Arahanism as a systematic presentation of this Liberation Path. Rooted in the Theravāda monastic tradition, Arahanism seeks to preserve the teachings it identifies as belonging to Gautama's original dispensation, while critically examining subsequent interpretations and developments in religious doctrine and practice.

His work extends beyond the study and explanation of Buddhist teachings. It encompasses the translation and publication of religious literature, comparative studies of ancient spiritual traditions, the development of structured renunciant training, and the establishment of an institutional community dedicated to the cultivation and transmission of the Dhamma.

The founding of the Arahanist Order of Canada represents the institutional expression of this undertaking. Through the Order, Bhante Mudita seeks to establish a living Theravāda lineage in which canonical study, monastic discipline, sense restraint, meditation, renunciation, and the pursuit of Arahantship remain integrated within a coherent religious tradition.

At the heart of his work is a conviction that Gautama's Liberation Path must remain a living practice: studied carefully, cultivated through disciplined effort, and transmitted to future generations for the benefit of those who sincerely seek the Deathless.

2. Monastic Formation and Spiritual Practice

Bhante Mudita's religious formation began with his ordination in 2013 at Pa-Auk Forest Monastery and Meditation Center in Myanmar, where he undertook intensive training within the Theravāda monastic tradition. His formation included the systematic cultivation of Samatha–Vipassanā meditation, study of the Pāḷi Canon, and observance of monastic discipline. This period established the foundations of his approach to the Dhamma, bringing together scriptural learning, ethical restraint, concentration, and contemplative practice.

Following this training, he spent a further five years practising within the Thai forest tradition. The simplicity and solitude of forest monastic life provided an environment for deepening renunciation, strengthening meditative discipline, and giving sustained attention to the practical dimensions of the path. This experience further shaped his understanding of the relationship between worldly relinquishment, mental cultivation, and the pursuit of liberation.

His years of monastic training in Myanmar and Thailand continue to inform his approach to religious education. He places particular importance on the integration of canonical understanding and direct contemplative cultivation. Scriptural study provides the framework for understanding the teaching, monastic discipline establishes the conditions for its practice, and meditation develops the concentration and wisdom necessary for progress along the path.

In November 2024, Bhante Mudita returned to Canada to dedicate himself to the systematic teaching and development of Arahanism. This marked a new phase of his religious work: bringing together his monastic formation, meditation experience, and canonical studies in the establishment of a structured teaching tradition and a developing renunciant community.

His teaching draws upon the disciplines cultivated through his years of practice, including ethical discipline, sense restraint, Samatha, Vipassanā, and the progressive development of wisdom. He emphasizes that the religious life requires sustained commitment to training and relinquishment, with Arahantship as its supreme objective.

The forest tradition remains an important influence on his understanding of renunciation, simplicity, and contemplative life. His present work seeks to carry these foundations into a Canadian institutional setting, creating opportunities for serious Dhamma study, meditation training, and the gradual development of a living monastic community.

3. The Doctrinal Foundation of Arahanism

A central undertaking of Bhante Mudita's work is the examination and systematic presentation of Gautama's liberation teaching through Arahanism. His approach begins with the Pāḷi Canon, giving primary authority to the Sutta and Vinaya traditions as the foundations for understanding Gautama's teaching, the renunciant life, and the discipline leading towards Arahantship.

Within this framework, Arahanism distinguishes the early canonical foundations from subsequent doctrinal developments. In particular, it regards the Abhidhamma as a later systematization of Buddhist thought rather than an original foundation of Gautama's teaching, and therefore does not adopt it as an authoritative basis for its doctrinal framework. Commentarial literature and later interpretations are likewise examined critically, with attention to their historical development, textual foundations, and relationship to the teachings preserved in the Suttas and Vinaya.

Bhante Mudita's work seeks to examine the meaning, context, and practical purpose of individual teachings, giving particular attention to the relationship between renunciation, mental cultivation, wisdom, and final liberation. This includes reconsidering inherited interpretations of fundamental concepts and examining whether they remain consistent with the path and purpose presented in the early canonical teachings.

Among the subjects receiving particular attention are the nature and cultivation of citta; the meaning and scope of attā and anattā; the relationship between the individual, the aggregates, and worldly existence; the nature of worldly attachment and bondage; and the destination of one who completes the liberation path. Arahanism develops its own doctrinal explanations of these subjects through its interpretation of the canonical material, while recognizing the importance of careful textual examination and precise terminology.

A defining feature of this work is the restoration of Arahantship as the supreme objective of the renunciant life. Bhante Mudita emphasizes that the teaching of Gautama must be understood in relation to its ultimate purpose: the complete overcoming of rāga, dosa, and moha and the realization of Vimutti. Ethical conduct, meditation, concentration, and wisdom are therefore understood within the larger progression towards liberation from worldly bondage.

This understanding is expressed through the systematic sequence:

Sīla → Samādhi → Paññā → Nibbidā → Virāga → Vimutti

Sīla establishes the foundation of disciplined conduct and renunciation. Samādhi develops the collected and concentrated mind. Paññā provides the wisdom necessary to understand and see directly the worldly bondage. Through Nibbidā, disenchantment with conditioned worldly existence develops; through Virāga, worldly passion and attachment fade; and through Vimutti, complete liberation from worldly bondage is realized.

Through Arahanism, Bhante Mudita seeks to bring these teachings into a coherent doctrinal and practical framework, connecting canonical study with monastic discipline, meditation, and the progressive cultivation of the renunciant life. His intention is to preserve what he understands as Gautama's original liberation teaching, distinguish it from later developments, and make its principles accessible for serious study and practice.

This doctrinal undertaking provides the foundation for his wider work as a teacher, author, researcher, and founder of the Arahanist Order of Canada.

4. The Liberation Path and Spiritual Training

A central dimension of Bhante Mudita's work is the systematic teaching of Gautama's Liberation Path as a progressive course of spiritual training directed towards Arahantship. Within Arahanism, the path is understood not simply as the acquisition of religious knowledge or the cultivation of temporary mental well-being, but as a comprehensive transformation of the practitioner's life, conduct, and citta, culminating in complete liberation from worldly bondage.

His teaching is organized around the fundamental training sequence of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, which develops progressively towards Nibbidā, Virāga, and Vimutti.

Sīla — Ethical Discipline and Renunciation

Bhante Mudita emphasizes that ethical discipline provides the essential foundation for spiritual cultivation. Through the observance of precepts, restraint of the senses, simplicity, and progressive relinquishment of worldly pursuits, practitioners establish the conditions necessary for deeper meditation and wisdom.

Renunciation occupies a particularly important place in this training. He teaches that the movement towards Arahantship requires more than an improvement in ordinary conduct or a reduction of worldly attachment. It involves a fundamental reorientation of life away from household concerns and sensual pursuits towards the disciplined cultivation of liberation.

Samādhi — Concentration and Meditative Cultivation

Drawing upon his training in the Pa-Auk and Thai forest traditions, Bhante Mudita teaches the importance of systematic meditation, particularly Samatha and Vipassanā.

Samatha develops mental stability, collectedness, and concentration, while Vipassanā cultivates penetrative understanding through contemplative investigation. Together, these practices support the development of a mind capable of sustained examination and deeper insight.

His approach gives importance to disciplined meditation training rather than treating meditation as an isolated relaxation technique. Concentration and insight are cultivated within the larger framework of ethical withdrawal, sense restraint, renunciation, and the pursuit of liberation from worldly bondage.

Paññā — Wisdom and Understanding of Worldly Bondage

Wisdom provides the understanding necessary to recognize the conditions that sustain worldly attachment and continued bondage. Bhante Mudita emphasizes the importance of examining experience, understanding the limitations of conditioned worldly existence, and distinguishing genuine liberation from temporary states of tranquility or extraordinary meditative experience.

Within his teaching, Paññā must ultimately contribute to the weakening and eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha—the fundamental defilements that sustain worldly bondage.

Nibbidā, Virāga, and Vimutti — The Fulfilment of the Path

The development of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā leads towards a deeper transformation expressed through three further stages.

Nibbidā is disenchantment with worldly existence, arising through a profound understanding of its limitations. Virāga is the fading and cessation of worldly passion and attachment. Vimutti is complete liberation from worldly bondage, the culmination of the training.

Bhante Mudita presents these stages as integral to understanding the ultimate purpose of Gautama's teaching. Within Arahanism, Arahantship represents the complete eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha and the liberation of citta from worldly bondage, culminating in the realization of Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm.

Progressive Training and the Renunciant Vocation

His teaching also encompasses a structured approach to progressive renunciation. Beginning with the Five Precepts, practitioners may undertake the Eight Uposatha Precepts and more committed forms of lay training before proceeding towards Pabbajjā as a Sāmaṇera or Sāmaṇerī and, where appropriately qualified, Upasampadā as a Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī.

Within the Arahanist framework, committed resident Upāsakas and Upāsikās may also undertake a more systematic form of lay preparation for renunciation. This is an institutional training arrangement rather than a separate category of Vinaya ordination.

Bhante Mudita regards the fully renunciant life as the necessary vocation for completing the path to Arahantship. The monastic life provides the comprehensive framework of discipline, celibacy, sense restraint, simplicity, and sustained cultivation through which the highest objective of the path is pursued.

Through these teachings, he seeks to establish a coherent relationship between canonical understanding, ethical discipline, sense restraint, meditation, and monastic training. His ultimate concern is that practitioners understand not only the principles of the Liberation Path but also the practical commitments required to undertake it.

5. Scholarship, Comparative Studies, and Publications

Alongside his monastic practice and teaching, Bhante Mudita has devoted considerable effort to religious scholarship, textual examination, translation, and publication. His writing seeks to make the teachings preserved in the Pāḷi Canon accessible through systematic explanation while examining their relationship to the wider history of religious and philosophical thought.

His publications encompass several interconnected areas: Gautama's liberation teaching, early renunciant literature, meditation and spiritual cultivation, canonical interpretation, and comparative studies of ancient religious traditions.

Arahanism and Gautama's Liberation Teaching

A major focus of his writing is the systematic presentation of Arahanism as the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Through works such as The Arahanism Suttas: Handbook for Walking the Path of Complete Liberation, he seeks to articulate the doctrinal foundations, spiritual objectives, and practical training of Arahanism. These writings examine renunciation, Arahantship, the purification of citta, and the progression towards Nibbāna.

His broader work on original Buddhism and Gautama's teaching similarly examines the relationship between canonical sources, later interpretations, and the practical purpose of the liberation path.

Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and Early Renunciant Literature

Another important area of his scholarship concerns the verses of the early elders bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs preserved in the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā.

Through his Voices of Liberation: Theragāthā & Therīgāthā series, Bhante Mudita presents the spiritual experiences, reflections, and renunciant aspirations expressed by those early elder Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs.

The project combines translation and commentary, seeking to communicate the significance of these verses within the wider context of monastic life, renunciation, meditation, and the pursuit of liberation.

This work also gives attention to the voices of early female renunciants, whose verses preserve important accounts of the spiritual vocation and contemplative accomplishments of Bhikkhunīs.

Meditation, Samādhi, and Contemplative Training

Bhante Mudita's publications also explore the practical dimensions of mental cultivation and contemplative discipline.

His writings on Satipaṭṭhāna, Anussati, mindfulness, and Samādhi examine the relationship between systematic meditation and the development of liberating wisdom.

Works such as Body in Body: The Art of Inner Seeing and The Complete Mindfulness Training Toward Liberation explore contemplative methods within a broader framework of spiritual development.

He is also interested in examining the relationship between traditional meditation training and contemporary approaches to sound-assisted contemplative practice, including research and writing concerning Samādhi and related methods.

Comparative Religious and Philosophical Studies

A distinctive feature of his scholarship is the examination of other ancient religious traditions through the perspective of Theravāda canonical teachings and renunciant spirituality.

His studies include the Bhagavad-Gītā, Vedic and Indian spiritual traditions, and early Christianity.

In his writings on St Paul, including The Life and Teachings of St. Paul: Renunciant Spirituality in Early Christianity and its related studies, he examines questions of renunciation, ascetic discipline, spiritual vocation, and the relationship between early Christian religious life and the broader history of renunciant traditions.

His Bhagavad-Gītā: A Theravāda Buddhist Reading project similarly approaches an important Indian religious text through comparative textual and doctrinal examination.

These studies reflect his interest in understanding the similarities, differences, and historical relationships among religious traditions, particularly concerning the ideals of renunciation, spiritual discipline, liberation, and the ultimate purpose of religious life.

A Continuing Body of Research and Publication

Bhante Mudita regards publication as an extension of his responsibility to preserve, examine, and transmit religious knowledge. His books are intended not only for general readers but also for serious students, practitioners, and researchers interested in canonical studies, renunciant spirituality, meditation, and comparative religion.

His publications are released on Amazon under the name Ven. Mudita Bhikkhu Thera, and his catalogue continues to develop through new books, revised editions, translations, and ongoing research projects.

Through this body of work, he seeks to contribute to the preservation of early religious literature, the systematic understanding of Gautama's liberation teaching, and the wider study of humanity's search for spiritual freedom.

title: Our Lineage
content:
Our Lineage: Arahanist Order of Canada

Arahanism is the renunciant path of arahantship — the direct training established by Gautama the Supreme Arahant for complete liberation from the world.

“The purpose of the Arahanist Order is singular: to maintain the integrity of the path and ensure that the training remains verifiable, experiential, and oriented toward the Deathless realm.”

Our lineage preserves and transmits the original training system of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā without doctrinal dilution, sectarian reinterpretation, and worldly reduction.
Our goal is not identity, belief, or affiliation — it is liberation itself.

Jurisdictional Structure

The Arahanist Order is organized for doctrinal clarity, structural discipline, and logistical support:

1. Grand Council (Central Body)

  • Functions as the Grand Vihara, holding the Charter for all viharas
  • Ensures the Brahmacariya standard is maintained
  • Safeguards the teachings of Arahanism

2. Provincial Secretariat

  • Regional administrative hubs (e.g., Ontario Secretariat)
  • Handles legal matters, land-use, and coordination for local viharas

3. Local Vihara

  • Small-scale meditation centers with kutis for solitary practice
  • Named to reflect Arahanist spiritual bond + local location
  • Governance includes:
    • Presiding Bhikkhu/Bhikkhuni: Spiritual guide
    • Warden of the Gate: Maintains Sīla and visitor conduct
    • Steward of the Kutis: Oversees dwellings

Arahanist Viharas as Ethical-Renunciant Cells Within Canadian Society

One of the most historically significant yet often overlooked aspects of early Christianity is that many Pauline communities functioned as proto-monastic ethical cells embedded within urban society. Long before formal monasteries emerged in the deserts of Egypt and Syria, the early Christian movement had already begun cultivating:

• disciplined communal life,
• moral regulation,
• sexual restraint,
• mutual aid,
• renunciant values,
• and networks of compassion operating inside the cities of the Roman Empire.

Today, Arahanist Viharas communities in Canada function as proto-monastic ethical cells embedded within urban society, dedicated to preserving the Path of Liberation by cultivating:

• disciplined communal life,
• moral regulation,
• sexual restraint,
• mutual aid,
• renunciant values,
• and networks of compassion operating inside the Canadian cities.

Arahanist Viharas do not require large centralized monasteries or vast institutions. They may remain:

• decentralized,
• small-scale,
• residential vihara-based,
• meditation-oriented,
• and socially integrated within broader Canadian society.

Yet structurally, many of the features anticipate the rebuilding of a genuine liberation-oriented civilization. This is crucial for understanding Arahanism not merely as a doctrine, philosophy, or belief system, but as a transformative ethical civilization oriented toward the Deathless realm.

Communities Within Modern Canada

Modern Canada produces unprecedented levels of material comfort, mobility, education, and technological connectivity, yet also widespread:

• loneliness,
• social fragmentation,
• family breakdown,
• addiction,
• psychological instability,
• moral confusion,
• and existential insecurity.

Urban life in cities such as Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary, and Ottawa is often characterized by:

• isolation despite population density,
• economic pressure,
• status competition,
• consumerism,
• sensual stimulation,
• and weakening communal bonds.

Arahanist Viharas emerge within this environment as alternative ethical societies.

They provide:

• belonging,
• ethical orientation,
• spiritual training,
• mutual support,
• disciplined living,
• and a direct path toward liberation from worldly suffering.

These communities function as islands of moral containment within the larger social system.

Shared Resources and Economic Solidarity

One of the most distinctive features of future Arahanist communities is the practice of shared support and economic solidarity.

Members assist one another through:

• dāna,
• volunteer service,
• food support,
• transportation assistance,
• hospitality,
• care for elderly practitioners,
• support for monastics,
• and maintenance of meditation facilities.

This represents more than charity alone.

The community increasingly functions as an extended spiritual family.

Material wealth becomes relativized in comparison to:

• compassion,
• service,
• ethical responsibility,
• preservation of the Dhamma,
• and collective spiritual development.

As Arahanist Viharas multiply, networks of support naturally emerge between distant communities across Canada.

Such developments are historically significant.

In a society structured heavily around:

• individualism,
• economic competition,
• consumer identity,
• and institutional dependence,

Arahanist communities seek to cultivate more ethical and spiritually grounded forms of association.

Moral Codes and Ethical Discipline

Arahanist Viharas also maintain strong moral expectations.

Arahanism is not merely intellectual agreement, philosophical discussion, or ritual participation.

It involves disciplined transformation of life.

The training system remains rooted in:

• Sīla,
• Samādhi,
• and Paññā.

Practitioners are encouraged to cultivate:

• restraint,
• honesty,
• humility,
• compassion,
• generosity,
• mindfulness,
• self-control,
• and simplicity.

They are expected to gradually abandon:

• exploitative behavior,
• uncontrolled sensuality,
• addiction,
• violence,
• greed,
• dishonesty,
• and destructive conduct.

The vihara itself becomes a training ground for transformation of consciousness.

This ethical rigor reflects the ancient renunciant principle that liberation requires:

• containment of lower impulses,
• regulation of conduct,
• inward vigilance,
• concentration of mind,
• and purification of consciousness.

The Arahanist Vihara therefore functions not merely as a meditation center, but as a complete ethical formation system.

Brahmacariya and Renunciant Training

One of the strongest dimensions of Arahanist training is its emphasis on Brahmacariya.

Modern society normalizes many forms of sensual indulgence through:

• entertainment culture,
• consumerism,
• pornography,
• casual sexuality,
• endless stimulation,
• and attachment to pleasure.

Against this background, Arahanist training increasingly advocates:

• restraint,
• simplicity,
• contentment,
• celibacy for monastics,
• disciplined conduct,
• and reduction of sensual craving.

Sensual restraint becomes linked directly to spiritual development.

The purpose is not repression, but liberation from dependency.

Practitioners gradually redirect energy toward:

• meditation,
• contemplation,
• wisdom,
• compassion,
• and realization of the Deathless realm.

This reflects the core principles of Brahmacariya:

• containment of sensuality,
• disciplined redirection of life-energy,
• simplification of existence,
• and orientation toward higher spiritual realization.

Mutual Care and Spiritual Community

Arahanist communities also cultivate strong interpersonal bonds.

Members increasingly relate to one another as:

• kalyāṇa-mittas,
• fellow practitioners,
• spiritual companions,
• supporters of the Dhamma,
• and members of a shared training community.

The community provides:

• emotional support,
• practical assistance,
• encouragement in practice,
• companionship in renunciation,
• and stability during personal difficulties.

Practitioners are encouraged to develop:

• patience,
• gentleness,
• compassion,
• forgiveness,
• endurance,
• and willingness to support one another.

These values gradually create networks of care extending throughout Canada and eventually beyond it.

Compassion Networks Across Canada

Perhaps most important is the development of organized compassion beyond ordinary social boundaries.

In modern society, concern often remains strongest within:

• family,
• ethnicity,
• political affiliation,
• economic class,
• or cultural identity.

Arahanist training increasingly universalizes compassion itself.

Care extends toward:

• practitioners,
• visitors,
• the poor,
• the elderly,
• the isolated,
• the suffering,
• and all beings seeking freedom from suffering.

The spiritual community becomes trans-ethnic, trans-cultural, and trans-regional.

Compassion itself becomes portable across geography.

A practitioner visiting an Arahanist Vihara anywhere in Canada should encounter the same spirit of ethical discipline, mutual support, and commitment to liberation.

Small Viharas Before Large Institutions

The growth of the Arahanist movement should not be understood primarily as the construction of large monasteries or institutional structures.

Its foundations lie first in small local viharas.

The later development of a larger network will emerge from principles already present within these communities:

• Brahmacariya,
• simplicity,
• ethical rigor,
• meditation practice,
• mutual aid,
• compassion networks,
• inward purification,
• and gradual withdrawal from worldly conditioning.

The difference between a small vihara and a future larger organization lies mainly in scale and administrative form.

The essential training remains unchanged.

Ethical-Renunciant Cells Within Canadian Civilization

Arahanist Viharas may therefore be understood as ethical-renunciant cells operating inside Canadian civilization.

They do not seek transformation through political power, ideological conflict, or cultural confrontation.

Instead, they cultivate:

• alternative values,
• transformed consciousness,
• moral discipline,
• compassion,
• restraint,
• Brahmacariya,
• and liberation-oriented training.

This gradual ethical transformation possesses long-term historical power.

The Arahanist movement will spread not primarily through wealth, advertising, or institutional influence, but through:

• communities of care,
• disciplined conduct,
• authentic meditation training,
• mutual support,
• renunciant values,
• and direct experiential transformation.

In this sense, the Arahanist Vihara becomes an alternative ethical civilization operating within Canadian society itself, preserving the ancient training of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā while opening a practical path toward the Deathless realm.

Membership & Degrees of Insight

Procedures:

  • Chartering: New viharas must be consigned by an existing vihara and approved by the Grand Council
  • Voting: Anonymous ballots for residency and leadership
  • Tiled Meetings: Closed administrative meetings maintain meditative focus

Sequential Training Path

Sīla → Samādhi → Paññā → Nibbidā → Virāga → Vimutti

  • Sīla: Ethical withdrawal from the world
  • Samādhi: Mind lifted beyond sensory reality
  • Paññā: Direct realization through Higher Seeing
  • Nibbidā: Disenchantment from worldly phenomena
  • Virāga: Fading of attachment
  • Vimutti: Liberation from the world and its jurisdiction

The endpoint is not religious identity, but the Deathless realm (Nibbāna-Dhātu).

Who We Are

We are renunciants and lay practitioners committed to:

  • Rigorous training in renunciation and meditation
  • Deep meditative cultivation to purify the mind
  • Direct insight into the impermanence and unsatisfactoriness nature of the world, and a strong determination to leave the world
  • Know-Yourself: find the true self (Atta-Dipa), attaining full independence (anissito) and liberation (vimutti) from the world

Orientation: Practical, verifiable, realization-based

What We Are Not

Arahanism is not:

  • A new sect or reform movement
  • A cultural or philosophical reinterpretation
  • An abstract philosophical system

It is the restoration of the radical renunciant path leading to arahantship.

Our Commitment

We maintain:

  • Doctrinal clarity
  • Renunciant integrity
  • Structural discipline
  • Liberation as the sole objective

Lineage continues through realization, not ceremony or title.

Goal: Arahantship — complete liberation from the world’s jurisdiction.

Practitioner Portal

The Practitioner Portal is a restricted platform for members engaged in sustained training within the Arahanism contemplative framework. It provides access to advanced teachings, reflective Journals, practice materials, and doctrinal resources that extend beyond the Center’s public programs.

Access is granted to members who have completed foundational training and demonstrate readiness for deeper engagement, ensuring alignment with commitment and disciplined practice.

Within the Center’s dual-structure model, the Practitioner Portal serves as the inner training environment, complementing the Center for Liberation Studies as the public, academic interface.

👉 Access the Practitioner Portal (Login Required for Authorized members only)

title: Our Mission
content:
The Arahanist Order of Canada

A Canadian Theravāda Lineage

OUR MISSION

Preserving and Transmitting Gautama’s Liberation Path

Arahanism — The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

The Arahanist Order of Canada is dedicated to upholding and transmitting Arahanism—the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant—within the Theravāda tradition. Its supreme spiritual purpose is the restoration of renunciation and Arahantship as the fulfilment of the religious life: the complete liberation of citta from worldly bondage termed as rāga, dosa, and moha, culminating in the realization of Nibbāna-dhātu, the deathless realm.

To fulfil this purpose, the Order is committed to preserving Gautama's original liberation teaching and the Pāḷi Canon, training renunciants in the complete path to Arahantship, teaching and publishing the Dhamma, sharing knowledge openly for the benefit of humanity, and establishing sustainable monastic communities in Canada. Through these interconnected responsibilities, the Order seeks to preserve a living Theravāda lineage in which the Dhamma is studied, practised, and transmitted for the welfare of future generations.

1. Restoring Renunciation and Arahantship as the Supreme Spiritual Purpose

Worldly renunciation is the foundation of Gautama's Liberation Path. It is not merely a change of lifestyle, an outward expression of religious devotion, or a temporary withdrawal from ordinary responsibilities. It is a progressive relinquishment of worldly attachments and the conditions that bind citta to worldly existence.

Arahanism holds that the ultimate purpose of spiritual life is complete liberation from worldly bondage through the eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha. These three fundamental defilements sustain worldly yoke: rāga encompasses worldly craving, passion, and attachment; dosa encompasses worldly survival instincts of fear, aversion, anger, hatred and hostility; and moha encompasses ignorance and delusion concerning the nature of worldly existence and the path to liberation from worldly bondage.

The renunciant undertaking is directed towards the complete overcoming of these defilements of the mind-heart citta. Through the progressive cultivation of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, practitioners develop ethical withdrawal, sense restraint, inner purification, meditative concentration, and liberating wisdom. This training leads towards Nibbidā, disenchantment with worldly conditioned existence; Virāga, the fading of worldly passion and attachment; and ultimately Vimutti, liberation from worldly bondage.

Arahanism therefore places Arahantship at the centre of its spiritual purpose. Arahantship represents the fulfilment of the Liberation Path through the complete eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha. It is not simply an elevated spiritual attainment or an ideal to be contemplated, but the supreme objective towards which the full renunciant life is directed.

For those undertaking the complete renunciant vocation, this means dedicating their lives to Brahmacariya, monastic discipline, celibacy, sense restraint, meditation, scriptural study, and the progressive relinquishment of worldly attachments. Spiritual training must remain directed towards the purification of citta and the realization of Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm beyond the universe.

The Arahanist Order of Canada seeks to establish the communal and institutional conditions necessary for this undertaking. Through progressive lay preparation, novice training, and full monastic ordination, it aims to support practitioners who sincerely aspire to dedicate their lives to the Liberation Path.

Worldly renunciation is therefore not simply the outward abandonment of worldly life. Its ultimate purpose is the complete liberation of citta from the bonds that perpetuate worldly existence.

2. Upholding Gautama's Original Liberation Teaching

Arahanism is dedicated to upholding the original liberation teaching of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant, the Sammāsambuddha. Its doctrinal foundation is the understanding that the ultimate purpose of spiritual cultivation is not the improvement, refinement, or continuation of worldly existence, but liberation from worldly bondage and the realization of Nibbāna-dhātu.

We understand Gautama's original teaching as a complete path of spiritual cultivation in which Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā work together towards the purification of citta and the eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha. The fulfilment of this training is expressed through the progression from Nibbidā to Virāga and ultimately Vimutti.

Arahanism maintains that the Liberation Path must be understood in its entirety, including its purpose, its renunciant orientation, its discipline, its contemplative development, and its final destination. Individual teachings and practices must therefore be examined in relation to their contribution to the complete liberation of the practitioner.

Grounded in the Theravāda canonical inheritance, Arahanism maintains its own distinct doctrinal and institutional identity. It draws upon the Pāḷi Canon as its primary textual foundation while undertaking a critical examination of inherited interpretations and subsequent religious developments.

This examination includes fundamental questions concerning worldly renunciation, the nature of worldly bondage, the relationship between citta and the world, the interpretation of attā and anattā, and the destination of the liberated individual. Arahanism maintains its own doctrinal positions on these matters and seeks to articulate them through careful textual study, philosophical examination, and contemplative practice.

Upholding Gautama's original teaching requires more than the preservation of religious terminology or the repetition of inherited explanations. It requires a sustained commitment to understanding the purpose and coherence of the Liberation Path and ensuring that its central objective is not obscured by interpretations or practices that direct attention towards worldly attainment.

Arahanism therefore seeks neither to establish a new path independent of Gautama nor merely to reproduce later institutional forms. Its aspiration is to recover, preserve, articulate, and transmit what it understands as Gautama's True Dhamma (satdhamma): the teaching leading towards complete liberation from worldly bondage.

Through the Arahanist Order of Canada, this doctrinal commitment is given practical expression through canonical study, monastic education, disciplined spiritual cultivation, and the establishment of a living renunciant tradition.

3. Preserving the Pāḷi Canon and Theravāda Textual Heritage

The preservation and study of the Pāḷi Canon constitute an essential responsibility of the Arahanist Order of Canada. The canonical teachings provide the primary textual foundation through which we examine, understand, and transmit Gautama's Liberation Path.

We regard the preservation of the Theravāda textual inheritance as more than the safeguarding of historical manuscripts or religious literature. It is the preservation of a substantial body of teachings concerning ethical discipline, sense restraint, meditative cultivation, wisdom, renunciation, and liberation.

The Pāḷi Canon provides the primary textual foundation for Arahanism through the Sutta and Vinaya Piṭakas, which preserve Gautama's teachings and the discipline governing the renunciant life. Arahanism does not adopt the Abhidhamma Piṭaka as part of its authoritative doctrinal foundation, regarding it as a later development beyond the original body of teachings. Even within the Sutta Piṭaka, Arahanism applies careful textual, historical, and doctrinal discernment, examining the language, terminology, context, consistency, and practical purpose of individual teachings. Particular attention is given to suttas that appear to preserve earlier layers of Gautama's doctrine and contemplative practices, allowing the original framework of the liberation path towards Arahantship to be studied and understood with greater clarity.

Accordingly, Arahanism places particular importance on studying particular  canonical sources in Pāḷi while making their contents accessible through translation, explanation, and systematic examination. Pāḷi terminology is retained wherever necessary to preserve doctrinal precision, especially when familiar translations may not adequately communicate the original meaning.

Our approach also involves critically examining inherited interpretations, commentarial explanations, and subsequent developments within the broader Buddhist tradition. Such examination is undertaken to distinguish canonical teachings from later interpretations and to investigate whether particular explanations remain consistent with the fundamental purpose of Gautama's Liberation Path.

We recognize that the transmission of religious texts across centuries involves complex questions of textual history, interpretation, and preservation. Therefore, careful scholarship, comparison of sources, and responsible translation are indispensable to our work.

The Arahanist Order seeks to contribute to this preservation through publications, translations, commentaries, textual research, and digital archival initiatives. By making our research and written materials accessible through scholarly repositories and open digital platforms, we also seek to support future generations of practitioners and researchers.

Our commitment is to preserve the textual foundations of the Liberation Path while ensuring that their meaning and practical significance remain available for serious study and spiritual cultivation.

The Pāḷi Canon is not preserved merely as an inheritance from the past. It is studied and transmitted as a foundation for understanding and undertaking the path towards liberation from worldly bondage.

4. Training Renunciants in the Complete Path to Arahantship

The Arahanist Order of Canada is dedicated to establishing a systematic framework for renunciant training directed towards the complete liberation of citta from worldly bondage and the attainment of Arahantship.

We regard renunciation as a progressive undertaking that requires more than formal religious affiliation or ordination. It involves a gradual transformation of one's way of life through ethical discipline, sense restraint, celibacy, meditation, wisdom, and the relinquishment of worldly attachments.

Accordingly, the Order seeks to provide progressive stages of preparation and training through which sincere practitioners may undertake increasingly complete forms of renunciation.

Progressive Preparation for Renunciant Life

For lay practitioners, the Five Precepts provide the initial ethical foundation. Those wishing to undertake more substantial renunciant discipline may observe the Eight Precepts on Uposatha days, cultivating temporary restraint, simplicity, and greater freedom from ordinary worldly entanglement.

The Order also provides a framework for resident lay practitioners undertaking a more committed religious life as Upāsakas and Upāsikās. Through guidance, ethical discipline, celibacy, and participation in the communal life of the Order, they may prepare themselves for formal novice ordination.

Novice Ordination and Monastic Formation

The next stage is Pabbajjā, the going forth into novice renunciant life as a Sāmaṇera or Sāmaṇerī, undertaken through the acceptance of the Ten Precepts.

Novice training introduces a more comprehensive form of renunciation, including monastic discipline, celibacy, simplicity, meditation, scriptural study, and the cultivation of proper conduct. It provides the foundation for developing the discipline and understanding necessary for full monastic ordination.

Full Monastic Ordination

The culmination of this progressive training is Upasampadā, full ordination as a Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī under the Theravāda Vinaya and the disciplinary framework of the Pāṭimokkha.

Full monastic life represents a complete commitment to the renunciant vocation. It requires sustained dedication to ethical discipline, sense restraint, meditation, wisdom, communal responsibilities, and the continuous relinquishment of worldly attachments.

The Order recognizes the importance of preserving the traditional monastic standards and disciplinary requirements governing full ordination. It also seeks to establish appropriate conditions for the training and support of both male and female renunciants, including the future development of a Bhikkhunī training and ordination framework in accordance with the relevant Vinaya requirements.

The Complete Path of Spiritual Cultivation

Throughout these stages, the central objective remains the progressive cultivation of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, leading towards Nibbidā, Virāga, and Vimutti.

Training is therefore not measured merely by the number of years spent in religious life, the acquisition of formal titles, or the completion of institutional requirements. Its deeper purpose is the transformation of citta through the progressive eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha.

The Order seeks to provide an environment conducive to this undertaking through monastic residence, meditation facilities, Dhamma instruction, canonical education, spiritual guidance, and a disciplined communal way of life.

Ultimately, the purpose of renunciant training is not simply to produce ordained members or maintain a religious institution. It is to cultivate practitioners who sincerely dedicate their lives to the complete Liberation Path and aspire towards the realization of Nibbāna-dhātu.

The Arahanist Order therefore regards the establishment of a living renunciant training tradition as one of its most important responsibilities.
