title: 10 Marks
content:
TEN MARKS OF ARAHANISM

1. The Soul-Spirit (Attā / Ātman) and the Five Aggregates: The True Self, Worldly Manifestation, and Liberation

1). The Fundamental Question: Who Am I?

One of the most difficult questions in the spiritual life is also one of the simplest: Who am I?

Most people answer this question without hesitation. They identify themselves with their bodies, their thoughts, their feelings, their memories, their personalities, their social relationships, and the stories they have constructed about their lives. When they say “I,” they ordinarily mean the familiar individual who inhabits a particular body, possesses a particular name, remembers a particular past, and anticipates a particular future. This identity feels so immediate and natural that few people think to examine it.

Yet the spiritual inquiry begins precisely when this apparently obvious identity is questioned.

The body changes from childhood to adulthood and from adulthood to old age. Feelings arise and disappear. Perceptions change, memories fade, thoughts contradict one another, and personalities develop in response to circumstances. Even the sense of being a particular person is influenced by the condition of the body, the activity of the mind, the surrounding environment, and the experiences that shape one's life. What we ordinarily call “myself” is therefore not a single, unchanging worldly condition. It is a continually changing configuration of physical and mental processes.

The question is whether this changing configuration constitutes the entirety of our being.

Arahanism answers that it does not. Beneath the temporary identity through which we participate in worldly existence lies the Soul-Spirit, designated by the Pāli term attā and the Sanskrit term ātman. The Soul-Spirit is understood in Arahanism as the true spiritual subject, while the embodied personality and the five aggregates constitute its temporary worldly manifestation.

This distinction is essential. Arahanism does not simply teach that an ordinary human being possesses a Soul in the same way that someone possesses a house, a garment, or an object. Such language can inadvertently preserve the very worldly identity that spiritual investigation must examine. It places the familiar personality in the position of the owner and relegates the Soul to the position of something owned.

The deeper Arahanist proposition reverses this relationship: the Soul-Spirit is not merely an object possessed by the worldly person; the worldly person is a temporary manifestation through which the Soul-Spirit participates in worldly existence.

This is not an easy distinction to grasp because ordinary language is constructed around the experiences and assumptions of worldly life. We habitually speak as though the embodied individual were the ultimate subject of experience. Arahanism asks us to investigate that assumption rather than accept it unquestioningly.

The purpose of this inquiry is not to establish another intellectual identity to which one can become attached. It is to understand the relationship between the Soul-Spirit, the five aggregates, worldly bondage, physical death, and the possibility of liberation.

2). Why “I Have a Soul” Can Be Misleading

Consider the familiar statement, “I have a Soul.”

Grammatically, the statement establishes two positions. First, there is an “I” who possesses something. Second, there is a Soul that belongs to this “I.” The speaker assumes that the person who utters the sentence is already an independently established subject, and that the Soul is an additional entity possessed by that subject.

But what exactly is this “I”?

If the “I” refers to the physical body, then the body is being treated as the owner of the Soul. If it refers to the familiar personality, then the personality is being placed above the Soul in the relationship of possession. If it refers to the ordinary sense of self constructed from memories, feelings, desires, opinions, and social identity, then a changing collection of worldly experiences is being treated as the ultimate subject to which the Soul belongs.

From the standpoint of Arahanism, this is a fundamental confusion.

The body is subject to physical change. Feelings arise and pass away. Perceptions depend upon conditions. Mental formations change in response to circumstances. Consciousness associated with worldly experience is likewise conditioned. None of these changing processes, considered in itself, provides a satisfactory basis for identifying the familiar worldly personality as the ultimate spiritual subject.

If the Soul-Spirit is the deeper reality that Arahanist practice seeks to realize, then the ordinary personality cannot simply be assumed to be its owner. Doing so would make the temporary worldly identity the foundation of the very spiritual reality through which that identity is to be understood.

For this reason, Arahanism distinguishes between the habitual worldly statement “I have a Soul” and the deeper spiritual orientation expressed as “I am the Soul-Spirit manifesting through a temporary worldly existence.”

The second formulation changes the direction of inquiry. Instead of beginning with the familiar personality and adding a Soul to it, we begin with the Soul-Spirit as the true subject and investigate how worldly identity arises through the aggregates.

This distinction must not be reduced to a grammatical trick. Changing a sentence does not itself produce liberation. A person can repeat the words “I am the Soul-Spirit” while remaining deeply attached to bodily identity, worldly desires, fear, anger, and delusion. The statement becomes spiritually meaningful only when it directs practice toward the relinquishment of worldly identification and the purification of the mind-heart.

The point is not to replace one verbal formula with another. It is to reconsider what we take ourselves to be.

3). The Five Aggregates as the Temporary Structure of Worldly Existence

In the Pāli teachings, the five aggregates are rūpa, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, and viññāṇa.

They are commonly translated as form, feeling, perception, formations, and sense generated consciousness. Together, they provide a framework for examining the physical and mental processes through which ordinary human experience occurs.

Rūpa refers to material form, including the physical body. Vedanā refers to feeling, particularly the pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful tone of experience. Saññā concerns perception and recognition. Saṅkhārā encompasses volitional and other conditioned mental formations. Viññāṇa refers to sense generated consciousness associated with worldly experience.

These are not five independent objects stored inside a person. They are interrelated aspects of conditioned existence. Through them, the world is encountered, interpreted, desired, resisted, remembered, and acted upon.

The body provides the material basis of ordinary human life. Feeling gives external worldly experience its affective tone. Perception identifies and interprets what is encountered. Mental formations shape intentions, reactions, habits, and patterns of thought that are directed toward the outside world. Sense generated consciousness are the assets gathered from lived experience and stores in the brain/mind and heart, which makes particular experiences manifest internally.

From childhood onward, people learn to identify with this changing arrangement. The body is taken to be “me”; feelings become “my happiness” or “my suffering”; perceptions become “my understanding”; thoughts become “my opinions”; and consciousness is assumed to establish an enduring personal identity. The aggregates are therefore not merely experienced. They become the foundation upon which the worldly sense of “I” is constructed.

Arahanism asks practitioners to examine this identification carefully.

The body is undeniably experienced as the body. Feelings are undeniably experienced as feelings. Thoughts and perceptions arise in lived experience. But does the fact that these processes occur establish that they are the ultimate spiritual identity of the one who experiences them?

Arahanism answers no. It interprets the five aggregates as the temporary worldly manifestation and burden through which the Soul-Spirit participates in embodied existence. The aggregates provide the structure of worldly experience, but they are not, in themselves, the true Soul-Spirit.

This position requires an important qualification when discussing the Pāli Canon. The early Buddhist discourses examine the five aggregates as conditioned, impermanent, and unsuitable for identification as a permanent self. This rejection of identification with the aggregates is understood logically as the existence of a true spiritual subject, rather than as a sufficient basis for concluding that no Soul-Spirit exists.

4). Anattā: What Is Not the True Soul-Spirit?

The teaching of anattā is central to this inquiry.

In the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59), Gautama Buddha examines the five aggregates and explains why they should not be regarded as “mine,” “I am this,” or “this is my self.” The discourse directs attention to the conditioned and unsatisfactory nature of the worldly aggregates and encourages disidentification from them.

Arahanism places particular emphasis on this movement away from worldly identification.

If the body were the true and sovereign self, one might expect to command it completely: “Let my body never age; let it never become ill; let it never change.” But the body does not obey such commands. It is subject to conditions beyond personal control.

The same inquiry can be applied to feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness. They arise and change according to conditions. They cannot simply be ordered to remain permanently pleasant, consistent, or under complete personal control.

The practical conclusion is that the worldly aggregates should not be treated as an unchanging spiritual identity. They are processes conditioned by the universal laws including the law of decay and death, and attachment to them as the ultimate self or soul-spirit (Attā / Ātman) creates a basis for fear, frustration, and bondage.

Arahanism draws a further conclusion from this teaching: what is not the true Soul-Spirit should not be mistaken for the true Soul-Spirit. The body's impermanence does not, by itself, establish the Soul-Spirit's existence; equally, the rejection of the worldly aggregates as the true identity does not, by itself, establish that no spiritual subject of Attā / Ātman, which transcends the world, exists beyond them. The latter is the distinct metaphysical position affirmed by Arahanism.

This is where careful language matters. In the Pāli discourse, anattā is applied to the aggregates, and the practitioner is instructed not to identify with them. Arahanism interprets this disidentification as part of a wider path toward recognizing the Soul-Spirit (Attā / Ātman) beyond the temporary worldly personality, and beyond the world.

The practitioner must therefore avoid two different errors.

The first is to mistake the body and personality for the whole of one's being. The second is to suppose that merely adopting a belief about the Soul-Spirit is equivalent to realizing it. The first confuses the temporary manifestation with the true spiritual subject; the second substitutes an intellectual conclusion for the work of liberation.

The Arahanist path requires both discernment and transformation.

5). The Burden and the Bearer: Understanding the Bhāra Sutta

A particularly important text for this discussion is the Bhāra Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.22), the Discourse on the Burden.

The discourse identifies the five aggregates subject to clinging as a burden. It then speaks of the bearer of that burden and explains that craving is the force through which the burden is taken up, while the abandoning of craving constitutes the laying down of the burden.

This imagery offers a powerful way to understand the spiritual problem.

A burden is something carried. It is not identical to the bearer who carries it. If a person carries a heavy load for many years, the load may shape that person's posture, movement, daily activities, and sense of what is possible. The person may become so accustomed to carrying it that the burden is treated as inseparable from life itself. Nevertheless, the distinction between the one who bears the load and the load being carried remains conceptually meaningful.

Arahanism applies this distinction to embodied existence. The five aggregates are understood as the burden of worldly manifestation, while the Soul-Spirit, understood through the purified Citta, is identified as the deeper spiritual bearer.

With the Soul-Spirit identified as the true self, the bearer, the metaphor illuminates the true purpose of renunciation. Liberation does not mean improving the burden until it becomes permanently comfortable. Nor does it mean decorating the burden, acquiring a more prestigious burden, or constructing a worldly identity around carrying it successfully. It means abandoning the worldly craving and clinging through which the burden is taken up and sustained.

Consider how the burden operates in ordinary life.

A person becomes attached to the body and fears its decline. Another becomes attached to praise and is distressed by criticism. Another builds an identity around possessions, relationships, family, status, or intellectual achievement. When these conditions change, the person experiences the loss not merely as an external event but as a threat to the self.

The burden is thus sustained by more than physical existence. It is sustained by craving, attachment, fear, aversion, anger, ignorance, and identification. The aggregates become the basis of bondage when they are appropriated and clung to as “me” and “mine.”

Arahanism understands the bearer as needing to become free from this bondage. The goal is not to make the worldly personality more secure within the world but to end the worldly craving and attachment that bind the Soul-Spirit to worldly existence.

The metaphor must not be misunderstood, however. It does not imply that an unliberated person can simply declare the body irrelevant and abandon ordinary responsibilities. While embodied life continues, ethical conduct, discipline, sense restraint, wisdom, and the purification of the mind-heart remain indispensable. The burden is laid down through the ending of worldly craving and clinging, not through neglect, contempt for the body, or mere verbal rejection of worldly life.

title: Our Buddhist Garden
content:
Wutai Shan Buddhist Garden

A Mandala of Wisdom and Compassion in Canada

A sanctuary of peace, learning, and compassion — inspired by Mount Wutai, renewed in Canada

  • Location: Cavan–Monaghan, Ontario, Canada
  • The Buddhist Garden On Google Map
  • Website: https://thebuddhistgarden.com
  • Tour Reservation Portal: https://wutaishan-g6mjg7ij.manus.space/

Nestled in the rolling hills of Ontario, the Wutai Shan Buddhist Garden stands as one of the most serene and majestic Buddhist cultural sites in North America. Inspired by the sacred Mount Wutai of China, this Garden reimagines the Five Terraces of Wisdom through architecture, art, and contemplative landscape design. Each hall, statue, and pathway has been built with devotion and precision, blending Tang-dynasty artistry with Canadian natural beauty.

This guided walk introduces the Garden’s key landmarks — from the radiant Maitreya Buddha at the entrance to the tranquil Wisdom Lake, from the towering Grand Buddha Hall to the Five Platforms of Mañjuśrī, each revealing a facet of the path toward wisdom, compassion, and peace.

Wutai shan Buddhist Garden is inspired by Mount Wutai in China, one of the Four Sacred Mountains of mahayana Buddhism, but every structure here has been built anew in Canada with the same devotion and precision.


1. Main Gate (山门)

  • Traditional three-arch layout symbolizing the Three Trainings — Sīla (Ethical Conduct), Samādhi (Concentration), Paññā (Wisdom).
  • Constructed in Tang-style architecture with bronze-tiled roof and carved wood doors.
  • Beyond the gate lies a long central axis representing the spiritual journey inward — from the worldly to the sacred.

2. Grand Buddha Hall (大雄宝殿)

Summary:

  • The heart of the complex — a Tang-dynasty–style wooden structure, 15 m high, built using traditional mortise-and-tenon joinery without nails.
  • Houses the Three Great Buddhas:
    • Bhaiṣajyaguru (Medicine Buddha) in the East — healing wisdom.
    • Gautama Buddha in the Center — enlightenment in this world.
    • Amitābha Buddha in the West — infinite compassion.
  • Two flanking Bodhisattvas: Mañjuśrī (Wisdom) and Samantabhadra (Practice).
  • The hall’s redwood carvings depict the Eighty-Eight Buddhas; the bronze roof tiles (61 tons total) gleam gold under sunlight — symbol of incorruptible truth.

Main Buddha Hall (大雄宝殿)

The Main Buddha Hall is the spiritual heart of the Wutai Shan Buddhist Garden. It stands as one of the largest and most authentic Tang-dynasty–style wooden temples ever built in North America.

The hall measures about 44 metres in length, 30 metres in depth, and 15 metres in height, with a total area of approximately 1,400 square metres. The lower two levels are reinforced concrete, while the upper hall is a complete wooden structure built using traditional Tang-era techniques — mortise-and-tenon joints without nails.

All major components, including beams, columns, and brackets (dougong), are made from imported hardwoods such as rosewood, camphor, and yew. The roof is covered with more than 24,000 bronze tiles weighing around 61 tonnes, bringing the total roof structure to about 600 tonnes. This gives the building both durability and a soft golden luster that glows under sunlight.

Inside the hall are the Three Great Buddhas:

  • Bhaiṣajyaguru (Medicine Buddha) in the East — symbol of healing and restoration.
  • Gautama Buddha in the Center — symbol of enlightenment and the rediscovery of the path.
  • Amitābha Buddha in the West — symbol of infinite light and compassion.

On each side stand two great Bodhisattvas: Mañjuśrī (Wisdom) on the left and Samantabhadra (Practice) on the right. Together they represent the union of wisdom and virtuous conduct.

The inner walls are decorated with carved redwood panels gilded in gold, depicting the Eighty-Eight Buddhas of the Past. These works were crafted by master artisans and assembled piece by piece by hand.

The architectural design follows Tang-dynasty proportion — broad rooflines, deep eaves, and graceful simplicity — expressing both strength and serenity. The open interior space, supported by interlocking bracket sets, allows the central Buddha platform to remain unobstructed, embodying the principle of spaciousness and harmony.

Today, this hall stands not only as a place of worship but also as a living testament to the preservation of ancient craftsmanship in a modern world — a bridge between continents, and between faith and artistry.

(note): The structure is the largest Tang-style wooden Buddha Hall in North America.

3. Shan Cai Hall (善财堂)

  • Multipurpose cultural hall used for art exhibitions, concerts, and educational programs.
  • Currently hosts the Rangbala Thangka Art Exhibition — featuring more than fifty authentic Tibetan thangkas from Sichuan, hand-painted with natural pigments and gold.
  • Emphasize cultural exchange: “Art is a bridge between devotion and understanding.”

Shan Cai Hall is named after Shan Cai (善财童子) in Chinese — in Sanskrit as Sudhana, the youth who embodies the seeker’s path toward perfect wisdom.

In Buddhist tradition, Sudhana was a devoted disciple of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, the embodiment of wisdom. The story of his pilgrimage appears in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra (Flower Ornament Scripture), in the section known as the Gandavyūha chapter — one of the most beautiful allegories of spiritual awakening in world literature.

Following Mañjuśrī’s instruction, the young Sudhana set out on a vast pilgrimage to visit fifty-three teachers — men, women, monks, nuns, householders, kings, courtesans, and deities — each revealing to him a different aspect of the Bodhisattva Path.
Through humility, perseverance, and pure aspiration, he learned that wisdom is not found in isolation, but through compassion and service in every encounter.

At the end of his journey, Sudhana reunited with Mañjuśrī and realized that all those he had met were reflections of the one enlightened mind. His pilgrimage symbolizes the living path of spiritual maturity — the movement from curiosity to insight, from seeking to awakening.

Therefore, Shan Cai Hall in this Garden represents the union of learning and practice, the place where knowledge becomes experience and where wisdom is embodied through culture, art, and education.
It is here that exhibitions, concerts, and community programs are held — continuing Sudhana’s journey of learning through encounter and shared inspiration.

4. Avalokiteśvara Shrine (观音殿 / Guanyin Hall)

  • Dedicated to Avalokiteśvara (Guanyin), the Bodhisattva of Compassion.
  • The hall contains multiple standing and seated Guanyin statues in diverse iconography — representing universal compassion in all forms.
  • The interior design follows a lotus motif — symbol of purity arising from the world’s impurity.

5. Kṣitigarbha Hall (地藏殿 / Dìzàng Diàn)

Dedicated to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva (地藏菩薩) — the Bodhisattva of Great Vows, Compassion, and Deliverance. His vow embodies the limitless compassion and unshakeable resolve to rescue all beings from suffering. Inside the hall, the main statue of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva is portrayed in monk’s robes, holding a wish-fulfilling jewel in one hand and a staff of liberation in the other. Flanking him are often the Ten Kings of the Underworld, representing the karmic process of judgment and purification.

6. Pilgrim’s Path and The Five Platforms (五台)

On this land, five terraces or platforms (五台) have been established: East, South, West, North, and Central. Each holds a bronze statue of Mañjuśrī, representing one of the Five Wisdoms of Enlightenment.
Together, they form a living mandala — a circle of wisdom harmonizing heaven, earth, and mind.

Imagine the Garden not just as landscape, but as a sacred field of awareness, where each direction expresses a different aspect of enlightenment.

1). Eastern Platform (東台) — “Platform of Clarity”

  • Element: Air / Dawn
  • Wisdom: Mirror-like Wisdom (大圓鏡智)
  • Colour: Blue
  • Statue: Blue Mañjuśrī — calm, reflective, holding the sword of insight.

The Eastern Platform faces the rising sun. From this direction comes light — symbolizing the awakening of awareness that reflects reality just as it is. This is the Mirror-like Wisdom, the mind that sees all phenomena clearly, without distortion. Here, Mañjuśrī’s sword represents clarity that cuts through confusion. Visitors often begin their walk here, as dawn marks the birth of wisdom.

2). Southern Platform (南台) — “Platform of Harmony”

  • Element: Fire / Noon
  • Wisdom: Wisdom of Equality (平等性智)
  • Colour: Yellow
  • Statue: Yellow Mañjuśrī — compassionate, radiating warmth.

“The Southern Platform represents warmth and vitality. Its wisdom is the Wisdom of Equality — the insight that sees all beings as equal in nature, beyond division of self and other. The fields and open sky of the south remind us that compassion is expansive like sunlight, embracing all without bias. Here, Mañjuśrī smiles — teaching that wisdom and kindness are never separate.”

3). Western Platform (西台) — “Platform of Discernment”

  • Element: Water / Sunset
  • Wisdom: Wisdom of Subtle Discernment (妙觀察智)
  • Colour: Red
  • Statue: Red Mañjuśrī — seated in meditation, holding a lotus and scripture.

The Western Platform faces the setting sun. It embodies the Wisdom of Discernment — the ability to distinguish truth from illusion, and to understand the unique nature of all things. The soft evening light teaches reflection and insight. Here, Mañjuśrī observes with compassion — reminding us that true discernment is gentle, never harsh.

4). Northern Platform (北台 / Běitái) — “Platform of Action”

  • Element: Wind / Midnight
  • Wisdom: Wisdom of Accomplishment (成所作智)
  • Colour: White
  • Statue: White Mañjuśrī — standing, holding a staff or vajra.

The Northern Platform stands highest and feels the coldest wind. It represents purity, discipline, and resolve — the Wisdom of Accomplishment. Just as the northern stars guide travelers, this wisdom guides all compassionate actions in the world. It is not enough to see truth; one must embody it through right conduct. This platform honours all who dedicate themselves to selfless service.

5). Central Platform (中台) — “Platform of Unity”

  • Element: Space / Stillness
  • Wisdom: Dharmadhātu Wisdom (法界體性智) — the all-encompassing wisdom of the awakened mind.
  • Colour: Gold or Green
  • Statue: Golden Mañjuśrī — serene, seated on a lion throne.

At the centre lies the heart of the mandala. The Central Platform unites the four directions — representing the totality of wisdom and the still point within all motion. Here, all distinctions dissolve; every direction becomes one. This is the realization of Mañjuśrī himself — wisdom that is boundless, luminous, and free.

The path around the Five Platforms is more than a walk — it is a mandalic pilgrimage. Beginning in the East with clarity, passing through harmony, discernment, and action, one returns to the Centre — to unity, stillness, and liberation.

These Five Platforms are living reflections. Here, wisdom is not distant. It is alive in every direction, in every breath, and in the quietness of this Canadian sky. May all who walk these terraces awaken the same luminous mind that Mañjuśrī represents — the mind of pure wisdom and compassion.

7. Monastic Residence & Dining Hall

  • Living quarters for resident bhikkhus and visiting practitioners.
  • Visitors may observe mindful eating in silence in the dining hall, symbolizing gratitude and restraint.

title: The Arahanist Path
content:
The Arahanist Path – 7 Day Meditation Retreat

This 7-day intensive retreat is a rare opportunity to enter the direct training established by Gautama Buddha, the Supreme Arahant, for those awakening to seek full liberation from the world. The Arahanist Path is a precise and demanding training aimed at dismantling the forces that bind the mind to worldly existence and initiating a profound transformation that transcends human limits—going beyond the human condition to become more than human.

Rooted in the threefold training of Sīla (systematic withdrawal from worldly engagement), Samādhi (stabilization and elevation of the mind from the world), and Paññā (direct penetrative wisdom into worldly phenomena), this retreat guides participants through a progressive internal transformation. The training reveals, step by step, the cosmology of how this world operates and the multidimensional nature of human existence.

Participants will be led through the Liberation Triad:
• Disenchanted from the World (Nibbidā) — seeing clearly the instability and burden of worldly life
• Fading off Worldly Passion (Virāga) — the cooling and release of craving and emotional entanglement
• Liberated from the World (Vimutti) — the direct realization of freedom beyond the world’s binding field

A defining feature of this retreat is open doctrinal clarification. Students are encouraged to ask questions throughout the training. Doubt is not suppressed—it is examined, challenged, and resolved, establishing right understanding and firm confidence in the path.

The image of the lotus rising from mud toward the sun expresses the entire training: from immersion in the world to purification, elevation, and emergence into clarity.

Participants should come prepared not merely to “experience meditation,” but to undergo a genuine shift—from participation in the world toward release from it.

Now Accepting Invitations Worldwide

title: One Day Meditation Retreat
content:
One Day Meditation Retreat: Purification, Wisdom, and Freedom

What Does It Mean to Be Truly Human?

Every human being eventually encounters questions that cannot be answered by material success, technology, or worldly achievement.

  • What is a human being?
  • Why is there suffering?
  • What is a good life?
  • What survives death?
  • How should one live?
  • What is ultimate freedom?

These questions have occupied the greatest spiritual traditions throughout history. Yet in today's world, they are often ignored, replaced by endless distraction, entertainment, and the pursuit of external success.

This one-day meditation retreat invites you to return to these timeless questions—not merely through intellectual discussion, but through direct contemplation and meditation.

Meditation as a Path of Purification and Freedom

Meditation is far more than a technique for reducing stress or improving concentration.

According to the Buddha, meditation is a path of purification. It is a systematic training that gradually frees the mind from attachment, hatred, confusion, and fear. As the mind becomes purified, wisdom naturally arises. With wisdom comes genuine inner freedom.

This retreat introduces meditation as it was originally taught within the Theravāda Buddhist tradition—a practical path aimed at liberation rather than self-improvement alone.

Whether you are completely new to meditation or have practiced for many years, the retreat provides an opportunity to deepen your understanding of both meditation and the purpose of spiritual practice.

Authentic Buddha's Teachings

Many modern presentations of Buddhism focus primarily on mindfulness, relaxation, or psychological well-being. While these can be valuable, they represent only a small part of the Buddha's teaching.

This retreat returns to the heart of the Theravāda tradition:

  • Authentic teachings of the historical Gautama Buddha
  • Meditation grounded in ethical purification
  • Wisdom through direct investigation
  • A coherent understanding of the spiritual path
  • Genuine liberation as the ultimate goal

Participants are encouraged not simply to accept ideas, but to investigate them carefully through both practice and thoughtful reflection.

A Retreat of Inquiry

Spiritual growth begins with honest questions.

Rather than avoiding difficult topics, this retreat welcomes them.

Throughout the day, Bhante Mudita encourages participants to ask questions openly and examine long-held assumptions. Doubts are explored respectfully, and doctrinal questions are addressed with clarity based upon the true teachings of Gautama Buddha.

This is not merely a meditation workshop.

It is an opportunity for genuine spiritual inquiry.

Beyond the Confusion of Modern Life

Modern society offers more information than ever before, yet many people experience increasing confusion, anxiety, and uncertainty.

This Meditation Retreat creates space to step outside this constant noise.

During the retreat you will experience periods of guided meditation, silent contemplation, Dhamma teachings, discussion, and opportunities for personal reflection.

The atmosphere is intentionally simple, peaceful, and conducive to inner transformation.

Transformation Begins Within

Real transformation does not occur by changing the external world.

It begins by transforming the mind.

As the Buddha taught, purification of mind is the foundation for wisdom, compassion, and freedom.

This retreat offers practical methods for beginning—or deepening—that transformation.

Retreat Leader

Bhante Mudita, Bhikkhu Thera

Bhante Mudita is a Theravāda Buddhist Bhikkhu dedicated to preserving and teaching the authentic path of liberation found in Gautama Buddha's original teachings. His teaching style combines careful doctrinal explanation with practical meditation instruction, encouraging participants to understand the Dhamma through both reason and direct experience.

Venue

Wutai Shan Meditation Center

Hosted by:

  • Buddhist College of Canada
  • Center for Liberation Studies

Online Registration:

You Are Welcome

Whether you are exploring Buddhism for the first time, seeking a deeper meditation practice, or searching for answers to life's fundamental questions, you are warmly invited to attend.

Come with curiosity.

Come with questions.

Come with an open mind.

Perhaps the most important question is not simply:

"What is meditation?"

But rather:

How can a human being become truly free?

We invite you to spend a day exploring that question through meditation, wisdom, and the authentic teachings of the Buddha.

We look forward to welcoming you to Meditation Retreat: Purification, Wisdom, and Freedom.

title: Books
content:
BOOKS & ONGOING WORKS

The Writings of Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera

The Intellectual Foundation of My Writings

The writings of Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera are guided by an Arahanist intellectual foundation, with a singular purpose: to seek, examine, and communicate the truth concerning spiritual existence and Gautama's original liberation teaching.

The following principles guide this body of work:

1. Truth is the objective.
Truth is the ultimate purpose of intellectual and spiritual inquiry. Our concern is to recognise what is true, examine it carefully, and communicate it faithfully.

2. Gautama's original liberation teaching is central.
The early Pāḷi suttas still constitute the primary textual foundation of this inquiry. The words, terminology, and teachings preserved in these discourses deserve direct and careful examination.

3. The wider Indian spiritual heritage is essential.
The inquiry draws upon the three major bodies of Indian spiritual literature: Vedic, Jain, and Pāḷi sources. Together, they provide an extensive textual foundation for examining spiritual existence, consciousness, renunciation, and liberation.

4. Vedic knowledge deserves its proper standing.
Vedic knowledge, including the teachings concerning Ātman and Brahman, the Munis, and the Upaniṣads, is approached with the seriousness and respect it deserves as an integral part of India's spiritual heritage.

5. Arahanism provides the intellectual standpoint.
Arahanism is the framework through which these questions are examined, with Gautama's liberation teaching at its centre. It is not simply a subdivision of Buddhism or the Śramaṇa tradition, but a distinct commitment to recovering, articulating, and preserving the liberation teaching of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

6. The pursuit of truth takes precedence over the study of religious developments.
These writings are concerned principally with identifying and communicating truth, rather than tracing the historical evolution of religious doctrines or cataloguing their subsequent additions and transformations.

7. Textual precision is indispensable.
Every examination must remain attentive to original terminology, linguistic context, textual evidence, and the precise meaning of the teachings. Conclusions must arise from careful investigation rather than inherited assumptions.

A Guiding Principle

Seek the truth. Examine the evidence. Communicate what is true.

These principles guide my books, essays, translations, commentaries, and ongoing research. They reflect a sustained commitment to the pursuit of truth and the recovery of Gautama's original liberation teaching.

SAMĀDHI

The Arahanist System of Yogic and Meditative Training

Integrating Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra with Gautama's Path to Liberation

Attā, Citta, and Viññāṇa: Recovering the Soul-Spirit of Gautama’s Liberation Teaching - An Arahanist Examination of the Five Aggregates, Anattā, and Consciousness in the Wider Indian Spiritual Heritage

Attā, Citta, and Viññāṇa: Recovering the Soul-Spirit of Gautama’s Liberation Teaching presents a fundamental re-examination of the nature of human existence and the path to liberation taught by Gautama, the Supreme Arahant. Drawing upon the Pāḷi Suttas, particularly the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā, this work investigates the spiritual significance of Attā (Soul-Spirit), Citta (Mind-Heart), and Viññāṇa (sense-generated consciousness). It challenges the dominant interpretation of Anattā as a universal denial of Soul-Spirit and examines what the ancient renunciants actually cultivated, disciplined, and sought to liberate.

Situated within the wider Indian spiritual heritage, this book seeks to recover Gautama’s true liberation teaching that, in the Arahanist assessment, has been obscured through centuries of doctrinal mis-interpretation. It establishes an important foundation for the contemporary articulation of Arahanism—the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant—grounded in the Sutta and Vinaya, with renunciation and Arahantship at its centre. This work is an invitation to re-examine inherited assumptions, return to the testimonies of the ancient elders, and renew the pursuit of the Deathless.

Vandanā Pūjā: Homage and Veneration

A carefully selected collection of essential Theravāda Pāli chants, accompanied by literal English translations and commentary where necessary to clarify their original meaning. It then presents the teachings of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant, and the spiritual training of his early disciples, exploring the traditional Theravāda path of Sīla, Samādhi, Paññā, and renunciation directed toward Arahantship. It also introduces the Arahanist Order of Canada and its commitment to preserving and transmitting Arahanism—the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Voices of Liberation
Theragāthā & Therīgāthā: Verses of the Elder Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs on the Path to the Realm of Nibbāna

Volume I, Volume II, Volume III, Volume IV,

A direct and uncompromising re-examination of anattā, using the testimony of the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā to challenge the interpretation of anattā as the denial of Self or Soul-spirit and to recover the renunciant path toward vimutti-Complete liberation from the world and into the Deathless Realm of Nibbāna.

Alongside the literal translation of the verses is an extensive, practice-oriented commentary examining their Pāli terminology, doctrinal implications, philosophical assumptions, and soteriological direction.

Bhagavad-Gītā: A Theravāda Buddhist Reading

Volume I, Volume II

Bhagavad-Gītā: A Theravāda Buddhist Reading offers a fresh reading of the Bhagavad-Gītā through a Theravāda perspective, examining its Sanskrit teachings on Ātman, knowledge, action, renunciation, and liberation alongside the Pāli teachings of Gautama the Supreme Arahant. It brings to light both the shared ancient Indian spiritual vocabulary underlying these traditions and the fundamentally different paths through which they understand ultimate freedom.

Bhante Mudita approaches the Gītā not only as a scholar but as a practicing Yogi bhikkhu, drawing upon years of monastic training at Pa-Auk Forest Monastery and Meditation Center in Myanmar, sustained samādhi practice, Pāli study, and life within Gautama’s Saṅgha. His reading therefore approaches the Gītā not through intellectual comparison alone, but through the perspective of yogic practice, renunciation, meditative realization, and the lived pursuit of liberation.

A provocative Theravāda Buddhist reading of the Bhagavad-Gītā that explores the spiritual subconscious of ancient India and examines its competing claims about karma, renunciation, meditation, divinity, immortality, and liberation. By placing Kṛṣṇa’s teachings alongside Gautama’s renunciate path, volume II asks whether paths described as “liberation” truly lead to the same destination—and invites readers to distinguish religious promises from directly realized truth.

The Life and Teachings of St. Paul

Volume I: Renunciant Spirituality in Early Christianity: A Buddhist Perspective

Volume II: Pauline Christianity Through the Lens of Theravāda Buddhism

The Life and Teachings of St. Paul offers a bold comparative investigation into one of the most important questions in religious history:

What historical and spiritual connections may exist between the ancient Buddhist renunciant tradition of India and the emergence of early Christianity in the Mediterranean world?

At its core, Volume I examines St. Paul as a renunciant and spiritual teacher while exploring the historical and spiritual connections between Early Christianity and Theravāda Buddhism. It focuses especially on their shared emphasis on renunciation, moral purification, non-harming, compassion, contemplative transformation, and liberation from worldly bondage.

Volume II examines St. Paul’s teachings through the liberative framework of Theravāda Buddhism, revealing structural parallels in renunciation, moral purification, universal compassion, non-harming, and transformation of consciousness. It explores how Pauline Christianity and Theravāda Buddhism, despite profound doctrinal differences, address the common human quest for freedom from worldly bondage and the cultivation of a higher spiritual life.

The Arahanism Suttas: Handbook for Walking the Path of Complete Liberation

A structured restoration of Gautama the Supreme Arahant’s liberation path through direct translation and doctrinal analysis of early Pāli suttas. It guides the reader from renunciation and purification of the citta to complete liberation from the world and realization of Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm.

The Mindful Body, the Awakened Mind: Cultivating Presence, Energy, and Discernment for Personal Transformation

This book guides practitioners through discernment, purification, and independent awareness (Anissito), cultivating a clear, value-aligned mind capable of freedom from worldly attachment and oriented toward liberation. A companion book for Kayagatasati Meditation Program.

Seven Days of Renunciation: Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā — The Path of Liberation: Study Guide for the Seven-Day Ordination Program

A structured guide to the renunciant training of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, offering a direct and practical entry into the path of liberation from worldly existence toward Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm.

Body in Body: The Art of Inner Seeing – A Complete Guide to Satipaṭṭhāna and Liberation from the World

A precise, uncompromising restoration of Satipaṭṭhāna teaching that guides practitioners through the systematic, layered higher seeing (“body in body,” “feeling in feelings,” “citta in citta,” “dhammā in dhammā”) to directly reveal how the luminous citta can stand full independence (anissito) and no clinging (“na ca kiñci loke upādiyati”) to the worldly, and reach Nibbāna-dhātu.

The Complete Mindfulness Training Toward Liberation: The Union of Satipaṭṭhāna (Foundational Mindfulness) and Anussati (Higher Mindfulness)

A complete system of mindfulness training that unites four Satipaṭṭhāna (foundational mindfulness) and ten Anussati (higher mindfulness), transforming awareness from worldly dependence to independent clarity (anissito). It reveals how mindfulness can lead beyond the cycle of aging and death into the deathless realm of Nibbāna.

Original Buddhism: The Psychotherapy of Gautama Buddha
Healing the Mind, Living the Values, and Walking the Path to the Deathless

Born from the question that drove Gautama Buddha to leave his palace, this book reveals Buddhism as a daring and complete path of escape from aging and death. It restores the Middle Exit and the reality of Nibbāna-dhātu, presenting liberation as a true departure from the world into the Deathless Realm.

THE SVASTIKA 卍 — SYMBOL OF THE SOLAR LAW
The Āryan Lineage of Light and the Path Beyond the Cosmos

The forgotten Solar meaning of the svastika — the ancient emblem of light, order, and ascent carried across Eurasia by the early Aryan migrations. It reveals how this universal symbol reaches its final fulfillment in the awakening of Gautama Buddha, restoring the Middle Exit and the Solar Law of Sīla–Samādhi–Paññā for our age.

Electric Dreams & Black Mirror
The Artificial World, the Human Mind, and the Future Already Written

As artificial worlds reshape perception, identity, and consciousness, we are living in an age where technology curates our reality and fragment our identity, this book shows how Gautama Buddha’s Path offers the only stable refuge: the restoration of the inner self and the true freedom. It is a manual for remaining human — truly human — in a synthetic world. 

The Healing Stream: From Gautama Buddha to the Desert Fathers
How the Ancient Path of Liberation Became the Monastic Soul of Christianity

A sweeping historical and doctrinal journey revealing how Gautama Buddha’s original Path of Liberation flowed through the Therapeutae, Essenes, and Desert Fathers to become the contemplative heart of Christian monasticism — one continuous Healing Stream guiding humanity toward the Deathless.

Beyond the Highest Heaven: Why Ascension Is Not the End
The Ancient Quest for Immortality and the Buddha’s Path Beyond the Universe

How humanity’s ancient quest for immortality through ladders of ascent — from Ṛṣis, Siddhas, and Pharaohs etc. — finds its true fulfillment only in Gautama Buddha’s discovery of the Middle Exit, beyond the universe into the Deathless.

Messiah of the East and West
The Universal Path of Liberation

Revealing how the Buddha’s path of insight and the Messiah’s path of grace are two converging currents of one eternal way, guiding humanity beyond suffering and death into the deathless.

Beyond the Universe
Gautama’s Rediscovery of the Path of Liberation

It unveils how the Buddha reopened the lawful gate beyond the universe, calling the manussa lineage to purify the citta, extinguish defilements, and step into the deathless realm of Nibbāna-dhātu.

The Buddha’s Face: From History to Myth
How Aryan Lineage, Greek Art, and Egyptian Archetypes Shaped the Image of the Enlightened One

佛像：從歷史到神話
雅利安血統、非洲記憶與希臘-埃及藝術如何塑造了覺悟者的形象

Temples of the Dawn: Ancient Beacons, Lost Civilizations, and the Buddha’s Path Beyond Fire and Light

黎明廟宇：古老的燈塔、失落的文明與佛陀超越火與光的道路 

The Path of the Awakened: An Inner Journey Beyond Conditioning

This concise and comprehensive guide serves as a valuable resource for Theravada monks, offering a collection of commonly utilized Vinaya rules for reference in daily conduct. It provides a convenient tool for monks seeking guidance in their spiritual practices.

Offers a rigorous scholarly investigation into the doctrinal foundations and practical applications of early Buddhism … the Buddha’s renunciation… his path to liberation and culminating in a nuanced examination of the concept of Nibbāna and its associated realm, Nibbāna-Dhātu.
