title: Arahanist Training Brahmacariya
content:
The Arahanist Training System

From the Law of Values to Complete Liberation

III. Brahmacariya — The Discipline of Restraint

From Values to Renunciant Discipline

Whereas Brahmavihāra establishes the Law of Values within the individual, Brahmacariya develops the discipline of sense restraint and the systematic training of progressive withdrawal of the citta from the world.

Brahmacariya is central to the Arahanist path because the pursuit of liberation from the world requires more than living according to good values. The practitioner must also examine and restrain the sensual desires, habits, and attachments through which citta remains entangled in worldly existence.

Brahmacariya therefore encompasses a disciplined way of life, grounded in Sīla and progressively developed through more comprehensive precepts. It requires restraint in bodily conduct, speech, sensual activity, and the pursuit of gratification. For those who undertake full renunciation, it includes the celibate life of a Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī.

The precepts are not merely a list of prohibitions. They are a training system through which the practitioner progressively reorganizes daily life around restraint rather than sensual impulse.

Arahanism provides a graded structure of Sīla, allowing people to begin training according to their circumstances while making the direction of progression clear: from foundational ethical conduct of Five Precepts towards comprehensive restraint and full renunciant commitment of Bhikkhu and Bhikkhuni.

Stage 1 — The Five Precepts: Foundational Sīla, Ethical Lay Person

The Five Precepts provide the initial foundation for practitioners who remain householders.

They train the practitioner to refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants that lead to heedlessness or loss of restraint.

This foundation establishes basic responsibility for one’s actions and their consequences. The practitioner begins to restrain harmful impulses, develop reliability, and bring everyday conduct into alignment with the Law of Values.

The Five Precepts are the starting point of systematic training, not the completion of the Arahanist path. They establish a basis upon which more comprehensive discipline can be undertaken.

Stage 2 — The Eight Uposatha Precepts: Part-Time Renunciant Training for Lay Person

The Eight Precepts deepen restraint by extending beyond the basic ethical obligations of household life. They introduce two essential components of renunciant training: celibacy and sense restraint (Brahmacariya), and the progressive withdrawal from external sources of happiness towards the cultivation of inner happiness.

The Eight Precepts include refraining from killing, stealing, sexual activity, false speech, intoxicants, eating at inappropriate times, entertainment and adornment, and the use of high or luxurious beds and seats.

The first component is celibacy and sense restraint (Brahmacariya). By abstaining from sexual activity and reducing engagement with sensual stimulation, the practitioner begins to loosen the connection between happiness and the gratification of bodily desires. The purpose is not merely to prohibit particular activities, but to train citta to become less dependent upon sensual satisfaction. The practitioner learns to exercise restraint over impulses and gradually develops greater independence from the demands of the senses.

The second component is the strategic reduction of external sources of happiness and pleasure. Ordinary human life is sustained, in part, by the pursuit of happiness, enjoyment, and emotional satisfaction. People naturally seek pleasure because happiness and joy are important dimensions of human life. Renunciation, however, requires us to examine where this happiness originates and whether it can provide a stable foundation for our existence.

Happiness derived from the external world is inherently unstable. Sensory pleasures depend upon circumstances, possessions, relationships, entertainment, recognition, and changing physical conditions. These sources of satisfaction may be pleasant, but they are transient and impermanent. What brings pleasure today may disappear tomorrow; what once satisfied the mind may eventually become insufficient or produce further craving. When citta depends upon these external conditions for its happiness, it remains vulnerable to the changes and uncertainties of worldly existence.

For this reason, Arahanist training does not simply remove sources of pleasure and leave the practitioner feeling deprived. It deliberately reduces dependence upon external happiness so that the practitioner can cultivate a more stable, inwardly grounded happiness that does not depend upon the changing conditions of the world.

As sensual stimulation, entertainment, adornment, and other sources of worldly gratification are reduced, the practitioner creates space for inner stillness, unification, and joy arising from cultivation. Through meditation and the development of citta, one learns to discover happiness that is less dependent upon external circumstances. This inner happiness such as from Brahmavihara is divine or Brahmic happiness: a joy associated with inner refinement, divine states of consciousness, and freedom from habitual dependence upon sensual gratification.

This transition is essential to the psychology of renunciation. Human beings need happiness and joy; therefore, sustainable renunciation cannot be understood merely as the suppression of pleasure. The practitioner must also cultivate inner source of happiness. As dependence upon worldly pleasure diminishes, inner happiness becomes increasingly important, enabling the practitioner to relinquish external gratification without experiencing renunciation merely as loss, deprivation, or suffering.

The strategic purpose is to sever citta’s dependence upon the world while preserving and deepening its capacity for happiness and joy. The practitioner gradually learns that a fulfilling inner life does not require the continuous pursuit of external stimulation. This makes restraint more sustainable and prepares citta for deeper Samādhi and further progress along the liberation path.

The Eight Precepts therefore provide an opportunity to practise a renunciant orientation without feeling miserable. During these periods of intensive training, practitioners can experience how celibacy, sense restraint, simplicity, and the reduction of external pleasures affect the mind. They can begin to cultivate inner happiness and discover the possibility of living with greater contentment and independence from worldly conditions.

In this way, the Eight Precepts serve as a bridge between ordinary household discipline and a more sustained commitment to Brahmacariya and deeper renunciation. They teach the practitioner not merely to abandon certain pleasures, but to develop the inner resources necessary to live happily without depending upon them.

Stage 3 — The Eight Precepts: Full-Time Lay Renunciant Discipline

For practitioners who are prepared to maintain the Eight Precepts continuously, Arahanism provides a more intensive form of full-time lay discipline.

Here, the Eight Precepts is no longer confined to occasional observance days or temporary retreats. It becomes the organizing principle of daily life.

The practitioner maintains the precepts as a sustained commitment, reduces sensual and social distractions, and creates conditions more supportive of meditation, simplicity, and the progressive withdrawal from worldly entanglements.

This stage calls for a deliberate reorientation of one’s life. The practitioner must consider how living arrangements, daily activities, relationships, consumption, and personal habits either support or undermine restraint.

Full-time observance of the Eight Precepts is a more intensive form of training, but it remains distinct from formal monastic ordination. It prepares the practitioner for greater discipline while preserving the distinction between lay observance and the responsibilities of the ordained Saṅgha.

Stage 4 — Pabbajjā: Professional Renunciant Training

Pabbajjā marks a decisive transition from a Lay Person into the monastic renunciant life.

The practitioner leaves household life and undertakes the life of a novice monastic renunciant, training under the guidance of an experienced monastic teacher. In the standard Theravāda novice framework, this stage is associated with the Ten Precepts.

The Ten Precepts extend the discipline of restraint from the Eight Precepts and establish a more comprehensive renunciant way of life. In addition to the foundational Eight Precepts, they include abstention from handling money according to the applicable training framework.

At this stage, renunciation is no longer simply a temporary discipline adopted alongside household responsibilities. It becomes the practitioner’s central commitment.

The novice learns to live with simplicity, sense restraint, humility, voluntary poverty, and dependence upon the support of the religious community. Daily life is organized around Sīla, meditation, study, service, and the guidance of the teacher.

Pabbajjā is therefore a major step in Brahmacariya. It provides the formal setting for sustained renunciant training and prepares the practitioner for the responsibilities and discipline of full ordination.

Furthermore, by refraining from using money, one further reduces happiness derived from the external world, which requires greater inner happiness to sustain overall happiness and maintain the renunciant life.

Stage 5 — Full Upasampadā Ordination: Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī

Full Upasampadā ordination establishes the practitioner within the fully ordained monastic Saṅgha, with its comprehensive system of precepts, communal responsibilities, and disciplinary procedures.

The fully ordained Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī undertakes a life governed by Pātimokkha, literally means “path toward liberation”, Brahmacariya: celibacy and sense restraint, simplicity, voluntary poverty, and adherence to the monastic discipline are no longer casual practices; they are integral commitments of the renunciant life.

Full ordination brings responsibilities that extend beyond personal observance. The monastic must preserve the integrity of the discipline, maintain appropriate relationships within the Saṅgha, receive instruction, and serve as a custodian of the Dhamma through conduct and practice.

The Vinaya is central to this training. It provides the disciplinary framework through which monastic conduct, communal life, and the integrity of renunciation are maintained. The specific obligations may differ in our Arahanist Order of Canada, a Canadian monastic tradition and ordination lineage, adjusted according to the Canadian specific social and natural environment.

For Arahanism, full renunciation is not simply a change of clothing, title, or social identity. It is a comprehensive commitment to the liberation path. The purpose of the discipline is to support the progressive purification of citta and the ending of the attachments that sustain worldly bondage.

The ordained life represents the fullest institutional commitment to Brahmacariya and the renunciant orientation of Arahanism.

“Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṁ brahmacariyaṁ, kataṁ karaṇīyaṁ, nāparaṁ itthattāyāti.”

“Destroyed is birth in this world, the holy life (Brahmacariya) has been fulfilled, what had to be done is done, there is no more returning to this worldly existence.”

IV. The Integration of Brahmavihāra and Brahmacariya

Brahmavihāra and Brahmacariya address complementary dimensions of the practitioner’s development.

Brahmavihāra cultivates the values that should govern the mind: kindness, compassion, Brahmic joy, and transcendental release. Brahmacariya establishes the sense restraint and discipline required to sever the citta from worldly existence by bringing conduct, sensual activity, and daily life under training.

Values without restraint may remain aspirations that are repeatedly defeated by impulse. Restraint without the cultivation of values may become a merely external discipline, lacking the warmth, integrity, and divine orientation that should govern the practitioner.

Their integration produces a more complete training:

  • Brahmavihāra develops the value-oriented character of the individual.
  • Brahmacariya establishes sense restraint to untie the citta from the worldly bondage.
  • Sīla provides the structured discipline through which conduct is trained.
  • Samādhi develops the concentration of a unified mind required for deeper practice.
  • Paññā develops liberating discernment, wisdom and empowerment.
  • Nibbidā is disenchantment with worldly existence.
  • Virāga is the fading of worldly passion.
  • Vimutti is complete liberation from the world.

This progression expresses the direction of Arahanist training. Values and virtues establish the foundation; sense restraint and discipline untie the citta from worldly bondage; concentration and wisdom support disenchantment and dispassion; and the path culminates in liberation from worldly bondage.

The stages are related, but they are not interchangeable. A person may become ethically accomplished without attaining deep Samādhi. A person may attain concentration without completing the work of liberation. The practitioner must therefore continue training rather than mistaking one achievement for the final goal.

V. The Purpose of Arahanist Training

The purpose of Arahanist training is not merely to produce ethical householders, disciplined meditators, or socially responsible members of a community. These are valuable developments, but the complete purpose of the path extends further.

Training is directed towards the purification of citta from rāga, dosa, and moha, the progressive withdrawal from worldly attachment, and the attainment of Vimutti.

Brahmavihāra establishes the Law of Values within the individual. Brahmacariya trains the practitioner in sense restraint and disciplined conduct that eventually untie the citta from worldly bondage. Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā form the practical foundation for the further progression through Nibbidā and Virāga towards Vimutti.

Every stage has its proper value. The Five Precepts establish foundational responsibility. The Eight Precepts deepen restraint and start to walk on the path of liberation. Pabbajjā establishes the novice in the renunciant life under training. Full ordination places the practitioner within the comprehensive discipline of the Bhikkhu/ Bhikkhuni Saṅgha. Throughout this progression, the practitioner must continue cultivating the values that make restraint principled, stable, and beneficial.

The training is therefore both personal and communal. Each practitioner is responsible for the cultivation of their own citta, while the community preserves the values, discipline, teaching, and conditions that support serious practice.

Arahanism welcomes sincere practitioners who are prepared to begin with foundational training and gradually deepen their commitment. Not everyone begins at the same stage, and not everyone will immediately undertake full renunciation. What matters is that the direction of training is understood and that each stage is undertaken sincerely.

For those called to full renunciation, Brahmacariya becomes the organizing principle of life. The aim is to leave behind the ordinary pursuit of worldly gratification and devote oneself to the direct path of liberation from the worldly bondage.

The Arahanist training system is a progressive path: live according to the Law of Values, establish Sīla, restrain the senses, cultivate Samādhi, develop Paññā, become disenchanted with worldly bondage, relinquish worldly passion, and realize Vimutti.

This is the discipline of Arahanism: the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

title: 10 Marks Part 11
content:
ARAHANISM

The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant

3. Brahmacariya (Holy Life)

The Cornerstone of Liberation

The Structural Foundation for Transcending the Sex Realm

1) The Meaning of Brahmacariya

Brahmacariya is the structural foundation of the liberation path.

Brahmacariya means:

  • The holy life
  • The life of purity
  • The complete renunciation of sexuality
  • The restraint over sensuality

Brahmacariya establishes a decisive shift in existence:

from immersion in the sex realm (kāma-dhātu) to the path of transcendence beyond it.

This is a cosmological act, not a moral preference.
It is the beginning of liberation from the structure of worldly conditioned existence.

2) The Cosmological Context: The Three Realms

Existence unfolds within three realms:

  • Kāma-dhātu — the sex realm, governed by sexuality and sensory craving
  • Rūpa-dhātu — the fine-matter realm, refined form beyond coarse sensuality
  • Arūpa-dhātu — the formless realm, formless and infinite existence

The human condition belongs to kāma-dhātu, the realm of sexuality.

Sexuality is the defining force of this realm:

  • It includes male and female
  • It drives sexual craving (taṇhā)
  • It sustains becoming (bhava) within this realm

As long as sexuality remains active, the being remains bound to kāma-dhātu.

Brahmacariya directly addresses this condition.

3) Brahmacariya as Transcendence of the Sex Realm

Brahmacariya is the practice that enables exit from kāma-dhātu.

The renunciation of sexuality:

  • Cuts the central bond to the sex realm
  • Withdraws the mind from sensual entanglement
  • Reorients citta toward higher realms of existence

Celibacy is therefore a cosmological function.

Through Brahmacariya:

  • The pull of sensuality weakens
  • The mind becomes clear
  • The conditions for entry into rūpa-dhātu arise

This marks the upward movement beyond the human condition of sensual existence.

4) Celibacy as Indispensable Discipline

Celibacy stands at the core of Brahmacariya.

Sexual activity binds the being through:

  • Desire and craving
  • Identity formation
  • Emotional attachment
  • Biological continuation of existence

Brahmacariya requires:

  • Complete abstinence from sexual activity
  • Guarding of the senses
  • Withdrawal from sensual stimulation
  • Simplification of life

This discipline purifies citta at its root.

Without celibacy, the structure of kāma-dhātu remains intact.
With celibacy, the foundation of that realm begins to dissolve.

5) Brahmacariya within the Path Structure

The path unfolds as:

  • Sīla — stabilizing life
  • Samādhi — stabilizing the mind
  • Paññā — liberating through wisdom

Brahmacariya supports and completes all three:

  • Sīla reaches purity through sexual restraint
  • Samādhi deepens as sensual agitation ceases
  • Paññā penetrates clearly when sexual craving subsides

Brahmacariya acts as the unifying condition that allows the path to mature.

6) The Life of the Bhikkhu

The bhikkhu lives Brahmacariya fully.

This life includes:

  • Renunciation of household existence
  • Complete celibacy
  • Discipline under Vinaya
  • Continuous cultivation of citta

Brahmacariya defines the renunciant.

It expresses the path in lived form:

a life directed entirely toward liberation from the world (loka).

7) Fulfillment of the Holy Life

Brahmacariya culminates in completion.

At arahantship, the declaration is made:

“Birth is ended, brahmacariya (the holy life) fulfilled, what had to be done has been done, There is no more for this state of being.”

“Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyāti.”

This statement reveals:

  • Brahmacariya reaches fulfillment
  • The cycle of involuntary worldly birth ends
  • no future Return to the worldly existence (loka bhava)

The holy life achieves its purpose:
complete transcendence of the structures that sustain worldly existence (loka bhava).

8) The Indispensable Condition for Liberation

Brahmacariya is essential to the path.

It establishes:

  • Freedom from sexual bondage
  • Release from the sex realm
  • Conditions for higher realization

Through Brahmacariya:

  • The mind becomes clear and steady
  • sexual energy is redirected to spiritual pursuits
  • Liberation becomes attainable

Brahmacariya is the foundation that enables transcendence from sex realm (kāma-dhātu) toward the Deathless realm (Nibbāna-dhātu).

9) The Path Beyond the Sex Realm

The path of Arahanism leads beyond worldly conditioned existence.

Brahmacariya marks the decisive movement:

  • From sexuality → to purity
  • From kāma-dhātu → to higher realms
  • From bondage → to release

It establishes the ground for the final realization:

Birth is ended.
brahmacariya (The holy life) is fulfilled.
What had to be done is done.

This is the completion of Brahmacariya.
This is the stepstone to arahantship.

title: 10 Marks Part 10
content:
ARAHANISM

The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant

2. Awakening (Buddhahood)

Seeing the World Clearly. Realizing the Mind’s Freedom.

Awakening begins not with belief, but with correct seeing.
Gautama Buddha’s realization starts from a direct recognition:

The world itself is the field of dukkha.

1) The World as the Field of Dukkha

This does not mean the world contains only pain.
It means something more exact:

The world cannot provide lasting refuge.

  • Pleasure exists — but cannot endure
  • Beauty exists — but must fade
  • Love exists — but cannot escape separation
  • Achievement exists — but cannot resist decline

All are governed by the same law:

  • Whatever is born must age
  • Whatever ages must decay
  • Whatever decays must die

This is not pessimism.
This is diagnosis.

2) Dukkha is Structural, Not Emotional

Dukkha is often misunderstood as suffering in the emotional sense.
In GAUTAMA Buddha’s teaching, it is far deeper:

Dukkha is the condition of worldly existence itself.

  • It is not merely pain, grief, or fear
  • It is the instability of all that arises (anicca)
  • It is the inability of the world to provide permanence

Even joy is included — not because it is wrong,
but because it cannot be secured.

3) The Two Governing Laws of the World

Awakening requires seeing the structure of worldly existence clearly.
The world operates under two inseparable laws:

The Law of Decay

  • All things age, decline, and dissolve
  • No form of existence is exempt
  • Decay is structural, not accidental

The Law of Power

  • Life is sustained through struggle and competition
  • Survival depends on strength, adaptation, and defense
  • Peace is not the default state of the world

Nothing can last. Nothing can fully rest.

4) Why the Mind Suffers

The problem is not the world alone.
The problem is dependency.

The citta(mind-heart) seeks:

  • stability
  • safety
  • continuity

But it places this trust in what cannot provide it.

Thus suffering arises:

Not because the world is wrong —
but because the mind relies on what must collapse.

5) The Mind as the Patient

In this system, the patient is not the world.
It is the citta.

  • The body ages — but does not suffer
  • The world changes — but does not despair
  • The mind suffers — because it clings

Gautama Buddha’s path is therefore therapeutic:

to free the citta from dependence on the world.

6) Symptom vs. Structure

Fear, grief, anxiety, and distress are symptoms.
They are not the root.

The root is:

existence within a system governed by decay and power.

Relief may calm symptoms.
Only structural insight opens the way to liberation.

7) Story vs. Process

The untrained mind creates stories:

  • “Why did this happen?”
  • “This should not be.”
  • “This is unfair.”

Awakening shifts attention from story to process:

  • arising and passing
  • attachment and reaction
  • clinging and release

Not personal narrative — but universal law.

8) The Turning Insight

When seen clearly, the conclusion becomes unavoidable:

The world cannot be a final refuge.

This insight is not despair.
It is the beginning of wisdom (paññā).

Only when false refuge is abandoned
can true freedom be sought.

9) Anissito — Pure Unworldly Awareness

At the mature stage of awakening, the citta enters a new mode:

Anissito — independent of the world.

  • Awareness remains
  • Knowing continues
  • Clinging ceases

The body is known — but not identified with
Feelings are known — but not depended upon
Mind is known — but not confined

Awareness stands without support from the world.

10) Proof of the Soul (Atta / Ātman)

In this state:

  • Awareness persists without dependence on the world
  • It does not collapse when not attached to the world
  • It is not constructed by the worldly aggregates

This reveals:

The citta is real, enduring, and capable of independence.

It is not annihilated.
It is purified and liberated.

11) The Meaning of Awakening

Awakening (Buddhahood) is the full realization of:

  • The world as dukkha
  • The mind as bound by dependency
  • The possibility of complete release

Awakening is the direct seeing that transforms the structure of the mind.

12) The Direction of the Path

Once awakening begins, the direction becomes clear:

  • Not improvement within the world
  • Not identity or belief
  • Not emotional management

But:

Withdrawal, purification, and transcendence

Leading toward:

→ Anissito (independent)
→ Complete liberation (Vimutti)
→ Entry into Nibbāna-Dhātu, the deathless realm

Awakening is the moment the mind stops seeking refuge in the world.

Seeing clearly, it withdraws.
Freed from dependence, it becomes capable of liberation.

title: 10 Marks Part 12
content:
ARAHANISM

The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant

4. Pabbajjā (Renunciation)

1) The Foundation of the Arahanist Path

At the heart of Arahanism stands Pabbajjā — the decisive act of renunciation. It is the conscious turning away from the world and the formal entry into a life wholly directed toward liberation.

The term Pabbajjā means “renunciation,” or “departure from the household state.” It signifies leaving behind worldly life and entering Brahmacariya — the disciplined path of training oriented toward the realization of Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless Realm.

Pabbajjā marks the first irreversible threshold of the Middle Exit (Majjhimā Nissaraṇa). It is the point at which the practitioner no longer organizes life around the world, but around liberation from it.

2) The Renunciant Impulse

Before his awakening, Gautama Buddha lived within the fullness of worldly privilege. Yet through direct observation, he discerned the governing conditions of existence: aging, suffering, and death. These are structural limits of the world — conditions that no power, wealth, or identity can overcome.

At the same time, he encountered the figure of the renunciant — one who had stepped out of worldly life in search of transcendence of human limits. This revealed a different trajectory for human existence: a life not aimed at refinement within the world, but at exit from the world.

This recognition gave rise to the Great Renunciation. Gautama left behind status, security, and relational identity, and entered the life of a seeker. Through disciplined training, he brought this path to completion, realizing Arahatta and abiding in Nibbāna-dhātu (Tathāgata).

Having completed the path, he restored the renunciant system in a precise and transmissible form — establishing Pabbajjā as the formal gateway into the Arahanist training.

3) An Ancient Lineage of Renunciation

Pabbajjā did not originate with Gautama the great arahant. The renunciant practice had long existed in ancient cultures as a living tradition of seekers （Isi (Pali) / Ṛṣi, Rishi (Sanskrit) / Xiān, 仙 (Chinese)） who withdrew from society to dwell in solitary forest and practice samadhi, and super-human state. They are often called “seer,” “sage,” “holy man,” “Immortal” or “Transcendent”. In the Pali Canon, Gautama the great arahant is often called Mahesi (maha-isi,The Great Seer), or Isisattama (The Seventh Seer among the Sages) or Isigili (The mountain that “swallows” the seers).

These renunciants cultivated:

  • samadhi, deep meditative absorption
  • tapas, including fasting, disciplined restraint
  • inquiry into consciousness and multi-dimensioanal cosmic existence

Gautama joined this group of solitary forest dwellers, perfected its highest potential, reformed and restructured it into a complete system leading to liberation beyond aging and death.

Thus, in Arahanism, Pabbajjā is both ancient in origin and perfected in form.

4) Pabbajjā as Structured Withdrawal (Sīla)

Renunciation in Arahanism is not symbolic. It is technical withdrawal — the first stage of the Middle Exit.

Sīla functions as a graded system of disengagement from the world:

(1) Lay Foundation — Initial Withdrawal

  • Five Precepts (Pañca-sīla)
    Establishes moral stability and restrains coarse defilements.
  • Eight Precepts (Uposatha-sīla)
    Introduces simplified living, celibacy, and reduced sensory engagement.
    This stage creates a transitional field between lay life and renunciation.

This level prepares the citta by weakening habitual outward flow.

(2) Pabbajjā — Novice Renunciation (Sāmaṇera / Sāmaṇerī)

Pabbajjā is the formal act of Renunciation.

The practitioner:

  • leaves household identity
  • relinquishes wealth and personal ownership
  • enters a life governed by discipline (sikkhāpada)

The novice undertakes the Ten Precepts, including:

  • abstaining from killing
  • abstaining from taking what is not given
  • abstaining from sexual activity
  • abstaining from false speech
  • abstaining from intoxicants
  • abstaining from eating after noon
  • abstaining from entertainment and adornment
  • abstaining from luxurious beds
  • abstaining from handling money

At this stage, renunciation becomes structural. Life is reorganized around restraint, simplicity, and training.

(3) Upasampadā — Full Ordination (Bhikkhu / Bhikkhunī)

Upasampadā completes the renunciant transition.

The practitioner fully enters the Vinaya system:

  • complete celibacy
  • total economic renunciation
  • regulated conduct and communal discipline
  • sustained meditative training
  • continuous development of paññā

This stage establishes total withdrawal from worldly identity and economic systems. The renunciant no longer participates in the structures that generate worldly attachment.

5) Why Renunciation Is Structurally Necessary

The household life is inherently organized around:

  • family obligation
  • economic production
  • social identity
  • sensory engagement

These generate continuous outward movement of the citta, reinforcing rāga (worldly craving and attachment), dosa (survival instincts of fear and anger), and moha (ignorance and delusion of not knowing the liberation path).

Pabbajjā interrupts this system.

It creates a controlled environment in which:

  • sensory input is minimized
  • responsibilities are simplified
  • worldly identity is reduced
  • attention is redirected inward

Renunciation therefore functions as a protective boundary condition for Samādhi.

Without this withdrawal, deep stabilization of the mind remains structurally obstructed.

6) The Forest Orientation

From the earliest formation of the Saṅgha, Gautama directed renunciants toward secluded environments (Arañña) — forests, mountains, and remote dwellings.

These conditions cultivate:

  • solitude
  • vigilance (sati)
  • simplicity of living
  • direct observation of the mind

This orientation is expressed in the ancient discourse Khaggavisāṇa Sutta (The Rhinoceros Horn), which presents the ideal of the solitary practitioner living independently, free from entanglement of worldly life.

The forest is not symbolic. It is a functional training environment that supports disengagement from the sensory and social field.

7) Pabbajjā as the Gateway to the Middle Exit

Pabbajjā is the entry point into the Arahanist Path.

It marks the moment when intention becomes existential commitment:

  • the world is no longer the field of fulfillment
  • liberation becomes the sole orientation

Through this act, the practitioner enters Brahmacariya — a life structured entirely around:

  • Sīla (withdrawal)
  • Samādhi (stabilization and elevation of mind)
  • Paññā (direct realization of the exit)

From this point forward, every aspect of life is aligned toward one end:

Vimutti — liberation, and abiding in Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless Realm beyond the world.

title: 10 Marks Part 13
content:
ARAHANISM

The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant

5. Arahantship (Arahatta)

1) Complete Liberation Beyond the World

Arahantship (Arahatta) is the consummation of the Arahanist Path — the full purification of the citta and the complete release from the world’s jurisdiction. It is the realization of Vimutti, liberation, and abiding in Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless Realm.

This path to Arahantship is a path of purification (visuddhi-magga). It is a precise and lawful process through which the citta is purified of the three governing distortions:

  • Rāga — worldly craving and attachment
  • Dosa — survival-instinct of fear and anger
  • Moha — ignorance of the liberation path and delusion regarding reality

Arahantship is therefore the completion of purification, where these forces are uprooted at their origin and no longer organize experience.

2) the training triad — Sīla · Samādhi · Paññā as One Continuum

The Three Trainings are structurally inseparable:

  • Sīla withdraws the citta from the world
  • Samādhi unifies and lifts the citta beyond the sensory field
  • Paññā reveals the exit and the Deathless

Together they form the training triad for Middle Exit (Majjhimā Nissaraṇa) — the precise route of liberation.

Break this continuity, and the path fragments.
Maintain it, and liberation unfolds lawfully.

Correcting Structural Misunderstandings

restores the functional integrity of the training:

  • Sīla as architecture of withdrawal, not JUST moralism
  • Samādhi as lifting power, not relaxation technique
  • Paññā as exit-knowledge, not philosophical analysis

When separated, these lose transformative force.
When unified, the path unfolds with precision and inevitability.

3) Paññā — The Middle Way as Majjhimā Nissaraṇa, The Middle Exit

The Middle Way, as taught by Gautama the Supreme Arahant, is not moderation. It is Majjhimā Nissaraṇa — the Middle Exit: the path by which the citta leaves the cosmos and enters Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm.

The common interpretation reduces the teaching to balance — managing desire, calming emotion, improving life within the world. This belongs to worldly continuity, not liberation from the world.

Tapas traditionally functioned as inner refinement that strengthens Samādhi and supports ascent. Later misunderstanding distorted it into self-torture, replacing inner purification with physical hardship.

The Middle Exit avoids two extremes:

  • Kāma-loka — sensual entanglement that binds through sexual and sensual craving and attachment
  • Arūpa-loka — cosmic absorption that dissolves individuality

Both remain within saṃsāra.

The Middle Way is neither indulgence nor dissolution. It is the exit through the Rūpa-loka.

Liberation unfolds through the Rūpa realm as the exit point, culminating in transcendence of the world into Nibbāna-dhātu.

This is a sovereign departure, not migration within the cosmos.

4) The Liberation Triad — A Single Therapeutic Arc

The training of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā functions as one continuous and integrated movement. It operates as a single therapeutic arc, culminating in:

Nibbidā → Virāga → Vimutti

This sequence is the natural unfolding of purification when the training is complete.

Why This Arc Is Therapeutic

The path revealed by Gautama THE SUPREME ARAHANT functions as psychotherapy in its original and technical sense:

  • it diagnoses the condition as bondage to the world
  • it identifies causes: rāga, dosa, moha
  • it applies treatment: Sīla, Samādhi, Paññā
  • it completes the cure through Vimutti into Nibbāna-dhātu

This therapeutic arc heals in four dimensions:

  • Conduct — through Sīla (withdrawal from harmful structures)
  • Emotion — through Samādhi (stabilization and elevation)
  • Perception — through Paññā (direct seeing)
  • Identity — through Vimutti (complete exit from worldly self-structure)

This is a total cure, not management. The system that generates bondage is dismantled.

5) Gotrabhū — The Change of Lineage

At the culmination of insight sharpened by stable Samādhi, the citta reaches a decisive threshold:

Gotrabhū — the change of lineage

This is a single, irreversible mind-moment in which:

  • the orientation of consciousness shifts completely
  • the practitioner crosses from puthujjana-gotra (worldling lineage)
    to ariya-gotra (noble lineage)

The Structural Shift

Before this point:

  • the mind takes worldly conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) as its field
  • it organizes experience around the false self or ego

At Gotrabhū:

  • the mind turns away from all worldly conditioned formations
  • it takes the deathless realm — Nibbāna-dhātu — as its object

A new governing law replaces the old. The system of worldly becoming is overridden.

Entry into the ariyan Lineage

when This transition unfolds, the practitioner:

  • enters the group of the Noble beings (ariya-sāvaka-saṅgha)
  • joins a lineage extending across human and celestial realms
  • participates in ariyan lineage with the new identity of Gautama

This is an existential integration, not symbolic affiliation.

Irreversible Reorientation

Following Gotrabhū:

  • identity as gautama is established
  • the lower fetters of world binding forces are cut
  • the trajectory toward full liberation is set

The citta is now aligned with the Deathless realm.

6) The Maturation of the Liberation Triad

Nibbidā — Disenchantment FROM THE WORLD

  • Clear seeing produces disenchantment.
  • The world loses emotional and existential appeal.
  • Perception becomes free from projection and illusion.

Nibbidā is clarity. The mind recognizes the limits of all WORLDLY conditioned existence.

Virāga — Fading of WORLDLY Attachment

  • WORLDLY Craving dissolves without suppression.
  • Delight in THE worldly fades naturally.
  • The gravitational pull of WORLDLY existence loses its force.

Virāga is the cooling of the fires OF rāga, dosa, moha. The citta disengages from all WORLDLY objects of attachment.

Vimutti — Liberation FROM THE WORLD

  • Final disengagement from all WORLDLY conditioned domains
  • Freedom from the jurisdiction of saṃsāra
  • Stable orientation in Nibbāna-dhātu

Vimutti is not transformation into another state of WORLDLY becoming.
It is complete exit from the system of WORLDLY becoming.

7) Completion of the Path: The Arahantship

At Arahantship:

  • all fetters that bind citta to the world are eradicated
  • all defilements are extinguished
  • the training is fulfilled

The classical realization stands complete:

“Birth is ended, brahmacariya (the holy life) fulfilled, what had to be done has been done, There is no more for this state of being.”

“Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyāti.”

Worldly becoming has ended fully and finally.

The Arahant embodies Vimutti.

Freedom from Worldly Jurisdiction

  • no further rebirth-generating kamma
  • no compulsion toward worldly becoming
  • complete independence from saṃsāric processes

Continuity Without Bondage

  • life continue out of the worldly jurisdiction
  • experience unfolds without worldly attachment and suffering

Orientation to the Deathless Realm

  • the citta abides aligned with Nibbāna-dhātu
  • Brahma-vihāra qualities manifest spontaneously
  • perception operates free from distortion

The Arahant lives in the world yet remains fully unbound by it.

Arahantship is the completion of Gautama the Supreme Arahant’s Liberation Path.

  • the citta is purified
  • the world is unbound
  • liberation is realized

This is not belief.
This is not philosophy.

This is the fully operational path of liberation restored and completed by Gautama the Supreme Arahant.

title: Arahanism Part 5
content:
Arahanism vs. Buddhism

Awakening Within the World or Liberation Beyond It

24. A Historical Timeline of the Paradigm Shift from the Age of Arahanism to the Age of Buddhism

1). The Central Question: What Happened to the Liberation Path?

How did a spiritual tradition centred on renunciation and the complete liberation of the individual come to encompass so many different ideals, practices, philosophical systems, and understandings of spiritual attainment? How did the pursuit of Arahantship, which Arahanism identifies as the defining purpose of Gautama’s teaching, become overshadowed by the pursuit of Buddhahood and the Bodhisattva ideal?

These questions cannot be answered merely by comparing doctrines as they exist today. They require us to examine the historical development of the traditions, the transmission of their scriptures, and the gradual transformation of their spiritual aspirations.

Arahanism proposes that the history of this transformation can be understood as a paradigm shift: from an age in which renunciant liberation stood at the centre of Gautama’s teaching to an age in which a broader and increasingly diverse conception of Buddhism became dominant.

The term Arahanism, as used here, is a name for the liberation-centred path that Arahanism understands as the essential purpose of Gautama’s teaching. It does not imply that the early renunciants historically organized themselves under this name. Rather, it identifies the defining orientation of their path: renunciation of worldly bondage and the attainment of Arahantship.

The following timeline sets out the historical framework for this interpretation. Some dates derive from traditional Buddhist chronicles; others are approximate historical reconstructions. The argument that these developments constitute a transition from the Age of Arahanism to the Age of Buddhism is the interpretation advanced by Arahanism.

2). The Age of Renunciant Liberation: Gautama and the Brahmanical and Śramaṇa Traditions

Approximately the fifth to sixth centuries BCE — Gautama’s inheritance and reformulation of ancient Indian spiritual traditions

Gautama emerged within a rich and diverse spiritual landscape shaped by both Brahmanical and Śramaṇa traditions. To understand the significance of his teaching, it is necessary to recognize this broader inheritance rather than portray him simply as a figure who rejected the religious world from which he emerged.

The Brahmanical tradition preserved an extensive heritage of sacred knowledge, ritual, philosophical inquiry, and reflection on the nature of ultimate reality. Alongside it, the Śramaṇa traditions cultivated renunciation, ascetic discipline, meditation, and the pursuit of liberation from the conditions of ordinary existence. These traditions were neither identical nor entirely separate. They developed in interaction, sometimes sharing questions and practices while differing profoundly in their answers.

Gautama’s teaching arose within this wider environment. Arahanism understands his achievement as a profound reformulation of both inheritances: the integration of spiritual knowledge with the discipline of renunciation and samādhi, directed towards a definitive realization of liberation.

Gautama as a Reformer of the Brahmanical Tradition

Gautama’s criticisms of Brahmins and Brahmanical practices should not automatically be interpreted as a rejection of the entire Brahmanical heritage. In the early Buddhist texts, his criticism often targets particular claims to spiritual authority, ritual practices, inherited status, and the conduct of those who claimed Brahminical distinction without possessing the qualities that would justify it.

The distinction matters. To criticize the degeneration of a tradition is not necessarily to deny everything that tradition has preserved. A reformer may challenge those who have misunderstood, misused, or failed to embody their inheritance while continuing to recognize the significance of the questions and truths that originally animated it.

Arahanism interprets Gautama in this light. His criticism of Brahmanical religion should be understood in relation to his pursuit of genuine spiritual realization, not reduced to a simple rejection of everything associated with the Vedas or the Brahmanical world.

The Pāli epithet vedagū, associated with profound knowledge or mastery on the Vedas, is particularly relevant to this inquiry. Its significance deserves careful examination when considering how Gautama positioned himself in relation to the language and concepts of his religious environment. For Arahanism, it invites us to reconsider the wrong portrayals of Gautama as wholly detached from the Brahmanical intellectual and spiritual inheritance.

Arahanism also maintains that Gautama did not deny the existence of the Ātman or Soul. Arahanism interprets his teaching on anattā as a rejection of identifying the true Self/ Soul with the five aggregates and the worldly ego, rather than as a declaration that no Soul exists for humans. This is a major point of disagreement between Arahanism and many contemporary academic and Buddhist interpretations. It therefore requires direct engagement with the relevant early texts and their competing interpretations.

The central Arahanist argument is that Gautama’s relationship with the Brahmanical tradition must be investigated rather than predetermined by the assumption that he rejected its entire spiritual inheritance and the existence of the Ātman or Soul.

Gautama and the Śramaṇa Tradition of Renunciation

The Śramaṇa traditions provide another essential context for understanding Gautama’s path. Ancient India was home to renunciants who left household life in pursuit of spiritual freedom. Through ascetic discipline, meditation, sensory restraint, and philosophical inquiry, they sought to overcome the limitations of human existence.

The Jain tradition and other renunciant communities developed their own teachings and disciplines within this broader environment. Their doctrines may differ from Gautama’s to some degree, but their presence demonstrates that renunciation and liberation were central concerns in the spiritual landscape of ancient India.

Gautama did not merely reproduce every practice or doctrine he encountered. His path involved critical examination, disciplined cultivation, and realization. The significance of his teaching lies in the distinctive way he organized the spiritual life around the attainment of liberation.

For Arahanism, samādhi and renunciant discipline are essential to understanding this achievement. Knowledge cannot be separated from the transformation of the practitioner, and spiritual inquiry cannot be fulfilled merely by possessing ideas about or awakening to certain reality. The practitioner must undertake the discipline through which worldly attachment is abandoned, the mind-heart is purified, and liberation is realized.

The Śramaṇa inheritance thus provides the context for Gautama’s emphasis on worldly renunciation, while his engagement with the broader Brahmanical heritage opens further questions about knowledge and truth, ultimate reality, and the meaning of spiritual attainment.

The Synthesis: A Distinctive Path to Liberation

Arahanism understands Gautama as a reformer who brought these inheritances to a new height. He did not simply preserve an existing Brahmanical system, nor did he merely reproduce the practices of the Śramaṇa communities. He established a distinctive path in which renunciation, sense restraint, samādhi, and liberating wisdom were directed towards the attainment of Arahantship.

This interpretation challenges the familiar picture of Buddhism promoted by mainstream academia as a movement defined principally by its rejection of Brahmanical thought. Arahanism instead asks whether Gautama’s achievement is better understood through the transformation of inherited spiritual resources into a path with a clearly defined liberating purpose.

The distinction is fundamental. Gautama’s greatness, in the Arahanist understanding, lies not in the creation of a new religious identity for its own sake, but in his realization and teaching of a path that leads beyond worldly bondage.

His teaching must therefore be examined in relation to both its historical inheritance and its ultimate objective. The question is not simply which earlier tradition he accepted or rejected. It is how he distinguished genuine spiritual realization from inherited knowledge, ritual, and practices that fail to bring liberation.

For Arahanism, this is the defining achievement of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant: the reformulation of the spiritual quest into a path of complete renunciation and liberation.

The history that follows must be understood against this background. If Gautama’s teaching emerged through a distinctive engagement with the Brahmanical and Śramaṇa traditions, then the subsequent development of Buddhism must be evaluated by asking whether this liberation-centred purpose remained intact, or whether it gradually became obscured as new interpretations and spiritual ideals gained prominence.

3). The Five-Hundred-Year Prophecy: A Warning About the Future of the True Dhamma

Traditionally attributed to Gautama in the Vinaya

The Theravada Pali Canon Vinaya contains a prediction associated with the establishment of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha: that the duration of Gautama’s True Dhamma would last only five hundred years. Versions of this prediction occur in several other Vinaya traditions as well, although its interpretation in the commentary may differ, some commentors may think it should be 5000 years instead for example.

Within the traditional framework, this prediction invites reflection on the vulnerability of a spiritual teaching as it passes from one generation to another.

A teaching may survive institutionally while its original purpose becomes increasingly obscured and difficult to recognize. Its texts may continue to be recited, its monasteries may remain active, and its followers may sincerely believe that they preserve the tradition. Yet the question remains: does the living practice retain the same orientation towards liberation from the world that defined the teaching at its beginning?

Arahanism interprets the five-hundred-year prophecy as a historical fact and a warning that the continued existence of a religious institution does not necessarily guarantee the continued primacy of its founding purpose.

The distinction is crucial. The disappearance or decline of the True Dhamma need not be understood simply as the physical disappearance of monks, monasteries, scriptures, or religious communities. From the perspective of Arahanism, the more fundamental danger is that the path to complete liberation from the world may become obscured even while the name and outward forms of the tradition endure.

The five-hundred-year period therefore provides an important traditional reference point for the historical inquiry that follows. It should not, however, be treated as independently verified proof that the teaching disappeared at a precise date.

The question is not merely how long a tradition survives. It is whether the purpose for which it was established remains at its centre.

4). The Third Buddhist Council: A Traditional Turning Point

Approximately 250 BCE — The reign of King Asoka

According to the Theravāda chronicles, a Third Buddhist Council was convened at Pāṭaliputta during the reign of King Asoka, traditionally dated to approximately 250 BCE. The account associates the council with the elder Moggaliputta Tissa and describes efforts to establish doctrinal boundaries, address disputed teachings, and reaffirm the community’s understanding of the Dhamma. The chronicles also connect the council with the dispatch of missions to other regions, including Sri Lanka.

Asoka’s inscriptions demonstrate his involvement to support the Saṅgha to conduct the council meeting trying to unify the Dhamma and Vinaya, the Theravāda chronicles give much details of this historical event. Many other traditions may have forgotten this history, but luckily the Theravāda lineage remembers its own history.

It presents a moment when the growing religious community now become national wide of the whole northern Indian continent faced the problem of distinguishing teachings regarded as authentic from teachings regarded as incompatible with its understanding of the Dhamma. It also portrays the state’s patronage as giving the Saṅgha greater public recognition and enabling the transmission of its teachings beyond its original centres and on a world wide stage.

Arahanism treats this period as an important point of departure for examining the subsequent institutional history of the tradition. It does not require us to assume that every event in the traditional account can be independently verified, nor that a single council definitively settled every question of doctrine.

The deeper issue is the relationship between the preservation of a teaching and the interpretation of that teaching.

Gautama’s teaching was transmitted orally, interpreted by successive generations, and preserved within communities that developed under different historical circumstances, carried on by people with diverse spiritual and cultural background. In such a process, questions inevitably arise concerning the relationship between inherited formulations and the purpose they are intended to serve.

Arahanism uses a criterion directly came from Gautama own instruction for addressing these questions: teachings must be examined according to the direction in which they lead the practitioner. Do they lead towards the abandonment of worldly craving and attachment, the eradication of defilements, and complete liberation? Or do they primarily encourage continued involvement in worldly existence, even when that involvement is expressed in religious or spiritual language?

This criterion is central to Arahanism’s understanding of the True Dhamma.

5). The Pāli Canon: Preservation, Development, and the Question of Authenticity

From the early centuries after Gautama to the first century BCE

The teachings attributed to Gautama were transmitted orally for generations before the Pāli Canon was committed to writing, according to the Theravāda tradition, in Sri Lanka around 30 BCE.

Traditional accounts associate this undertaking with 12 years of famine, decades of political instability including civil wars and invasions from southern Indian continent, and thus caused danger to the continuity of monastic learning. According the Theravada accounts, after decades of war (termed as hundred of years of war) and years of famine, it is difficult to find monks can recite big portions of the Pali Canon. The decision to write down the texts was thus decided as a means of protecting the teachings against the risk that oral transmission might fail.

The preservation of the Pāli Canon was therefore a major development in the history of Theravāda Buddhism. It provided a durable textual foundation for the tradition and helped establish the collection that became authoritative across much of Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia.

Yet the act of preservation also raises a question that remains important to Arahanism: how should we understand the relationship between the surviving collection and the original teaching?

The existence of a canon does not, by itself, establish that every text within it originated directly with Gautama or that every passage expresses an identical conception of liberation. The collection contains different genres, styles of exposition, and presentations of spiritual practice. Its texts must therefore be read with attention to their context, purpose, and relationship to the central path.

Arahanism does not regard the Pāli Canon as dispensable. On the contrary, it recognizes the Canon as indispensable to the study of Gautama’s original teaching. Its concern is that the Canon should not be treated as though every element within it necessarily carries the same historical status or serves the same spiritual purpose.

The question is not whether the Canon should be preserved. It is how its contents should be understood and evaluated.

For Arahanism, the decisive criterion remains liberation. Teachings that guide practitioners towards worldly renunciation, the purification of citta, the eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha, and the attainment of Arahantship stand at the centre of the inquiry. Other materials must be considered in relation to that purpose rather than automatically treated as equivalent expressions of it.

This approach invites a distinction between the preservation of a textual collection and the preservation of the governing principle of liberation from the world.

title: Arahanism Part 6
content:
Arahanism vs. Buddhism

Awakening Within the World or Liberation Beyond It

6). The Jātakas: Moral Instruction and the Changing Image of Gautama

Evidence of circulation by the third century BCE; development over a longer period

The Jātaka tradition became an important part of Theravada Pali Canon and Buddhist literature. These narratives concern Gautama’s supposed former births and are widely associated with moral instruction, generosity, sacrifice, patience, and other virtues. Stories identified as Jātakas were represented in early Buddhist art, while the collection preserved in the Pāli Canon comprises hundreds of verses associated with former-birth narratives. The prose commentary familiar to many readers is a distinct textual layer whose development cannot simply be assigned to Gautama’s lifetime.

Arahanism considers the spiritual implications of this fictional literary completely negative. It is untrue, and cause the paradigm shift of the spiritual focus from renunciant liberation toward lay people’s worldly merit hunting cravings, and eventually give birth to Mahayana counter movement which replaced the renunciants focused world transcendence liberation path.

When Gautama is presented through stories of his supposed former lives, readers encounter a figure whose long spiritual journey includes acts of generosity, extraordinary sacrifice, moral excellence, and the accumulation of virtues across many existences. These narratives can provide ethical instruction and inspire admiration. But they can also shape the way people understand the purpose of spiritual practice. And most importantly they are not facts and truth.

A reader who identifies with these stories may come to regard the accumulation of merit and the perfection of virtues over successive lives as the principal model of spiritual achievement. The question of complete renunciation and the attainment of Arahantship may consequently recede from view.

This is the critical point for Arahanism.

The issue is not whether moral virtues are valuable. Nor is it whether stories can communicate ethical lessons. The issue is whether a particular model of spiritual aspiration directs people towards the end of worldly bondage or encourages them to understand religious life primarily as the accumulation of merits within the world of repeated existence.

Arahanism interprets the growing prominence of former-birth narratives and, later, the Bodhisattva ideal as part of a broader transformation in the imagination of Buddhist practice. The figure of Gautama could increasingly be contemplated not only as the renunciant who attained liberation and taught others to do likewise, but also as a future Buddha whose long career of preparation could become a model for spiritual aspiration.

This development of course should not be reduced to a single date or claimed to have originated exclusively in the Jātakas. There could be manipulating forces behind as well. The relationship between Jātaka literature, the Bodhisattva ideal, and the emergence of Mahāyāna is not only as we see on the surface. Nevertheless, Arahanism sees in this literary tradition an important example of how the emphasis of a religious tradition can shift without the abandonment of its older texts.

A tradition may preserve narratives associated with liberation from the world while gradually directing popular attention, or collective consciousness, towards a different ideal.

7). The Bhagavad-Gītā and the Wider Renunciant Question

A parallel witness to ancient Indian concerns about liberation

The second chapter of the Bhagavad-Gītā presents a sustained discussion of renunciants based liberation from the world, with topics such as wisdom, disciplined action, equanimity, freedom from desire, and the restraint of the senses. This chapter is estimated to be inserted into the Gītā around 200 BCE and thus provides a valuable window to investigate how the renunciation based liberation path was perceived by the general populace.

The other chapters of Bhagavad-Gītā the presents other religious practices and philosophical framework, including Karma-yoga, represent the emerging Mahayana movement and their practices, as a wider ancient Indian spiritual movement about spiritual freedom.

The Jain tradition and other śramaṇa communities likewise emphasize renunciation, discipline, and liberation. Their doctrines may not be identical to those of Gautama, but their presence helps to understand the wider renunciants based world transcendence liberation path, instead of the later lay people centered merit accumulation rituals as we see in Mahayana. Jainism traditionally always questioned the ordinary household life and pursued release through rigorous spiritual practice.

For Arahanism, this wider context matters because it prevents the history of renunciant liberation from being understood solely through the later institutional boundaries of Buddhism.

The search for freedom from worldly attachment, the cultivation of sense control, withdrawal from the world, and the aspiration to transcend human existence were not concerns that belonged exclusively to one later Buddhist denomination. They were part of a broader religious environment in which Gautama’s distinctive teaching took shape.

The chapters of the Bhagavad-Gītā, estimated to be compiled during a period of 200 BCE and 200 AD, is therefore a valuable windows to see how renunciants based world transcendence liberation path was challenged by a broader spiritual movement with lay people centered spirituality.

8). The Missions to Sri Lanka and the Formation of the Theravāda Tradition

Traditionally dated around 250 BCE after the 3rd council meeting during King Asoka’s reign

The Theravāda chronicles associate the reign of King Asoka with missions that carried the teachings of the Saṅgha beyond the Indian heartland. Among the most significant was the mission to Sri Lanka traditionally associated with the elder Mahinda (Pali speaking).

According to this account, the establishment of the monastic tradition in Sri Lanka became a decisive stage in the transmission of the lineage that would later be known as Theravāda. Sri Lanka subsequently became a major centre for the preservation and study of Pāli literature, and its monastic tradition played an important role in the transmission of the Canon to later generations as we see today.

The importance of this history should not be underestimated. The preservation of the Pāli Canon in Sri Lanka and its subsequent transmission to regions including Myanmar and Thailand helped sustain a major living tradition of monastic discipline, textual study, and meditation.

From the perspective of Arahanism, however, the preservation of a lineage and the preservation of the original purpose of a teaching remain related but distinct questions.

A lineage can preserve scriptures, ordination, and institutions across centuries. Whether its living interpretation consistently gives primacy to complete liberation from the world is a further question—one that must be examined through its teachings and practices.

Arahanism does not need to deny the historical importance of Theravāda to make this distinction. Rather, it seeks to recover what it regards as the liberation-centred purpose that the tradition was established to preserve.

9). The Emergence of Mahāyāna: A Broader Conception of the Spiritual Ideal

Around the beginning of the Common Era, with further developments over subsequent centuries

Although the Jātaka literature, developed from about 300 BCE and onward, can be treated as the source of Mahāyāna. The emergence of Mahāyāna was a gradual process rather than a single historical event. Early Mahāyāna texts formally appeared in written texts around the turn of the Common Era, and the movement further developed over subsequent centuries, with the growing prominence of the Bodhisattva ideal (influenced by the Jātaka literature) becomes a significant development in the history of Buddhist thought.

In Mahāyāna traditions, the Bodhisattva aspiration became central to a vision of spiritual practice directed towards Buddhahood (which unlike Arahant, a lay person can achieve, how convenient!) and, in many formulations, the liberation and welfare of all sentient beings. This represented a different ordering of spiritual goals from the one Arahanism places at the centre of Gautama’s teaching.

Arahanism interprets this development as a paradigm shift.

The defining question changes from how the practitioner can attain Arahantship and bring worldly bondage to an end to how the practitioner should pursue the Bodhisattva path and ultimately attain Buddhahood. The meaning of the highest spiritual ideal is correspondingly reconfigured.

This does not mean that every Mahāyāna practitioner abandoned renunciation, that every Mahāyāna text rejected Arahantship, or that the historical relationship between Mahāyāna and earlier Buddhist communities can be reduced to a simple conflict between two completely separate institutions. Early Mahāyāna developed within a complex Buddhist environment, and its relationship with existing monastic communities was varied.

Arahanism’s argument concerns the governing ideal rather than the personal sincerity of individual practitioners.

When Buddhahood becomes the supreme spiritual aspiration, the renunciant pursuit of Arahantship no longer necessarily occupies the same position it holds within Arahanism. Even when renunciation and meditation continue, it just remains at appearance level, and their place within the larger spiritual framework is understood differently.

For Arahanism, this is the central significance of the shift: the path of liberation is no longer necessarily the organizing principle of the entire spiritual system.

10). Nāgārjuna and the Philosophical Transformation of Buddhist Thought

Approximately at 200 CE

Nāgārjuna, a lay person often referred as Bodhisattva, became one of the most influential philosophers associated with Mahāyāna Buddhism. His writings helped establish the philosophical foundations of Madhyamaka, particularly its analysis of emptiness and its critique of intrinsic existence.

The significance of Nāgārjuna for Arahanism is as a mark that the renunciants based liberation path was completely overshadowed by lay people centered Mahāyāna movement. Not only as a religious movement, but also completely obscured Gautama’s dhamma with increasingly sophisticated philosophical systems on emptiness and the denial of human soul. Arahanism thus regard this as clear evidence of spiritual decline, and marks the complete abandonment of the liberation path.

Its concerns are fundamental: Do they clarify the path to the end of worldly bondage? Do they strengthen renunciation and the discipline of liberation? Or does philosophical inquiry become an independent enterprise whose sophistication gradually obscures the practical purpose of the path?

This is the question Arahanism brings to the study of Buddhist intellectual history.

The emergence of new schools of thought demonstrates that the history of Buddhism was not simply the passive transmission of an unchanged body of doctrine. It involved interpretation, debate, the development of new conceptual frameworks, and the redefinition of spiritual ideals.

For Arahanism, the decisive issue is these developments completely distorted the primacy of Gautama’s liberation path or place it within a substantially different vision of spiritual attainment.

11). From the Age of Arahanism to the Age of Buddhism

A gradual transformation over the centuries after the induction of the Jatāka Literature

The preceding timeline does not establish that the liberation path disappeared at a precise moment or that every later Buddhist tradition abandoned renunciation. Theravāda in Sri Lanka preserved a powerful monastic and textual tradition, while in Indian continent it evolves quickly into Mahāyāna traditions which completely steps away from the liberation path. We are lucky that traces of Arahanism is more or less still preserved in the Sri Lankan Pali Canon that we today can use to restore the age of Arahanism.

In the age of Arahanism, the defining purpose of the path was complete liberation from worldly bondage. Renunciation, sense control, discipline, concentration, insight, and the eradication of defilements were organized around that end.

In what Arahanism calls the Age of Buddhism, the spiritual landscape became increasingly diverse. New philosophical systems, new scriptural traditions, different conceptions of Buddhahood, and the growing prominence of the Bodhisattva ideal expanded the range of goals and interpretations associated with Buddhism. But what’s in common among them is stepping away from the renunciation and liberation from the world: the attainment of Arahantship ceased to be the uncontested organizing ideal across the Buddhist world.

This is the paradigm shift that Arahanism seeks to identify.

It is not a claim that every later development was without value, nor that every later practitioner misunderstood Gautama. It is a claim about the relationship between a tradition’s founding purpose and the ideals that eventually come to define it.

A teaching may retain its name, its scriptures, and many of its practices while its central spiritual question changes.

12). The Five-Hundred-Year Question Revisited

The Gautama’s prediction in Theravada Vinaya text that His True Dhamma would endure for five hundred years invites us to reconsider what it means for a teaching to survive.

If survival means only the continued existence of scriptures, institutions, monastic communities, and religious observances, then the history of Buddhism clearly demonstrates the extraordinary endurance of the tradition. If, however, survival also requires the continued primacy of a particular path and spiritual goal, the question becomes more difficult.

Arahanism interprets the first several centuries after Gautama as a period in which the renunciant path remained foundational, even as the transmission and interpretation of the teaching developed. It then understands the increasing prominence of alternative spiritual ideals as part of a longer process through which the original purpose became less clearly distinguished from other aspirations.

The five-hundred-year prophecy cannot, by itself, prove this interpretation. Nor can the Third Council, the writing down of the Pāli Canon, the Jātaka literature, or the emergence of Mahāyāna independently establish the precise moment at which a paradigm shift occurred.

Taken together, however, these developments provide the historical setting for the question Arahanism raises: can the preservation of a religious tradition guarantee the preservation of its original purpose?

Arahanism answers that question by returning to the goal itself.

The criterion of authenticity is not simply antiquity, institutional continuity, scriptural authority, or the number of people who accept a teaching. It is the direction in which the teaching leads. A path intended for complete liberation from the world must be evaluated by whether it leads towards the abandonment of worldly craving and bondage, the eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha, and the attainment of Arahantship.

For Arahanism, this is the essential distinction between preserving the outward inheritance of a tradition and restoring its liberation-centred purpose.

13). Arahanism: The Restoration of the Liberation Path

The historical developments outlined here do not remove the need for careful study of the Pāli Canon, nor do they permit us to treat every question of Buddhist history as settled. They instead provide a framework for examining the relationship between the surviving traditions and the purpose that Arahanism identifies as fundamental to Gautama’s teaching.

Arahanism does not present itself as the invention of a new destination. It presents itself as a call to restore the primacy of a particular destination: Arahantship and complete liberation from worldly bondage.

Its emphasis is therefore not on adding another ideal to an already diverse spiritual landscape. It is on asking whether the original liberation goal has been obscured by the growth of competing ideals, and whether it can once again be placed at the centre of spiritual life.

This is why the distinction between the Age of Arahanism and the Age of Buddhism matters.

It directs attention away from the mere continuity of names and institutions and towards the purpose of the path itself. It asks readers to distinguish between spiritual development within the world and the pursuit of complete liberation from worldly bondage. It asks whether renunciation remains central or has become one option among many. And it asks whether the highest goal is understood as Arahantship or has been redefined through a different conception of Buddhahood, and the invention of numerous unverifiable Buddha identities.

These are not merely historical questions. They are questions about the direction of one’s own spiritual life.

If the purpose of Gautama’s teaching was complete liberation from worldly bondage, then the restoration of that purpose requires more than preserving ancient texts or venerating historical figures. It requires the recovery of the discipline, renunciation, and practical orientation through which liberation is pursued.

Arahanism therefore calls for both historical reconsideration and practical renewal: a careful examination of the inherited tradition, followed by a renewed commitment to the path that leads towards the end of worldly bondage.

The history of a teaching is important. But the purpose of a liberation path is ultimately realized not in the chronology of its institutions, but in the lives of those who practise it.

The Age of Buddhism may have reshaped the religious landscape. Arahanism seeks to reopen the question of liberation at its centre: Is the ultimate goal to become a Buddha, or to attain Arahantship and complete liberation from worldly bondage?

Arahanism — The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.
