title: Project
content:
Property for Monastic Training and Spiritual Education

Phase One: Establishing a Home for the Liberation Path

The Arahanist Order of Canada is seeking a suitable property in Southern Ontario to establish a religious and contemplative centre as the first phase of a longer-term plan to develop a Theravāda Buddhist monastic training centre—a Buddhist seminary dedicated to renunciation, meditation, Dhamma education, and the training of future bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs.

Phase One focuses on securing a suitable building that can serve as a Dhamma hall and place of worship, meditation, and spiritual education. A former church or chapel would be particularly suitable because it may already provide the spacious gathering hall needed for these activities. A property with a separate house, rectory, or other residential accommodation would be especially valuable.

Phase Two will focus on developing suitable residential facilities for monastic training, retreat accommodation, and the formation of prospective monastics. By proceeding in stages, we hope to establish the centre responsibly, making the best possible use of existing buildings and available resources while avoiding unnecessary construction expenses and regulatory complications.

Phase One: A Dhamma Hall and Place of Worship

Our immediate priority is to find a building suitable for regular meditation, Dhamma instruction, religious gatherings, and contemplative programs.

We are particularly interested in former churches, chapels, and other religious properties that are underused, becoming available through congregational restructuring, or seeking a new long-term purpose.

A former church could provide a suitable main hall for meditation and teaching while continuing to serve as a place of worship. Where a congregation wishes to preserve its Christian worship and activities, we would welcome discussions about shared use, provided the arrangement is suitable for both communities.

A separate rectory, clergy residence, or house on the property would be an additional advantage. Such accommodation could support the initial needs of resident monastics while providing a foundation for the centre's future development.

We are also open to suitable schools, retreat centres, and other institutional properties that can accommodate the intended religious activities.

Our aim is to identify a building that can be put to use with minimal unnecessary conversion, expense, and regulatory uncertainty.

Acoustic Suitability for Meditation

An important consideration is the acoustic character of the proposed Dhamma hall.

Our community conducts contemplative programs involving crystal singing bowls and other resonant instruments, alongside silent meditation and Dhamma instruction. We therefore seek a quiet, spacious hall with pleasant natural acoustics, allowing sustained tones to resonate clearly without excessive or distracting echoes.

Good sound isolation from neighbouring properties is also important, allowing regular meditation and contemplative programs to take place without unnecessarily disturbing nearby residents or other occupants.

Former churches and chapels may be promising candidates because of their spacious interiors and distinctive acoustic qualities. However, each property would need to be assessed individually to determine its suitability.

Phase Two: Developing a Monastic Training Residence

The longer-term vision is to develop a dedicated residence and training environment for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, together with appropriate accommodation for short-term retreats.

The centre will aspire to function as a Arahanist seminary, integrating disciplined monastic living, Dhamma study, meditation, and the practical requirements of renunciant training.

Depending on the property and available resources, Phase Two may involve adapting existing residential buildings, expanding suitable accommodation, or developing additional facilities where permitted.

The objective is to establish an environment where prospective monastics can prepare for and undertake the renunciant life, supported by suitable accommodation, systematic spiritual education, and sustained meditation practice.

We intend to develop this phase gradually, according to the centre's needs, the suitability of the property, and the resources available.

Property Requirements and Permitted Use

We are seeking a suitable property in Southern Ontario, preferably within reasonable driving distance of the Kawartha Lakes area, Kitchener, and the Greater Toronto Area.

Our preferred property would include:

  • An existing church sanctuary, chapel, or spacious hall suitable for meditation and religious gatherings.
  • A quiet interior with pleasant natural acoustics and good sound isolation.
  • A separate house, rectory, or other residential building, if available.
  • Sufficient parking and practical access for monastics, visitors, and program participants.
  • The potential to accommodate future monastic residence and training facilities.

We are also open to properties that meet the essential requirements without satisfying every preference.

The legal suitability of a property is equally important. We will need to establish whether its existing zoning, permitted uses, occupancy arrangements, and building conditions can accommodate the proposed religious activities and, where applicable, residential use, retreat accommodation, and future monastic training.

Our aim is to find a property where Phase One can begin with minimal conversion and expense, while leaving a realistic path for future development.

Supporting the Project Through Dana

In Theravāda Buddhist countries such as Myanmar, Thailand, and Sri Lanka, monasteries and monastic training institutions have traditionally depended on the generosity of lay supporters. Through dāna—the practice of giving—supporters help provide the material conditions necessary for monastic life, Dhamma education, and the continuation of the renunciant tradition.

The Arahanist Order of Canada seeks to develop this same spirit of generosity and shared responsibility in Canada.

Through Padma Refuge Foundation, a Canadian registered religious charity, we aim to seek donations and other forms of support toward establishing the centre. Contributions may help secure a suitable property, prepare the Dhamma hall, provide essential facilities, and, in the longer term, develop accommodation for monastic training.

We also welcome inquiries from individuals, families, Buddhist communities, charitable foundations, and potential benefactors who may be interested in supporting the project through financial contributions, property donations, or other appropriate arrangements.

Subject to the charity's policies and applicable Canadian requirements, we would like to explore ways of recognizing substantial supporters, including the possibility of priority access to designated facilities or priority booking for certain programs. Any such arrangements would need to be clearly defined and consistent with the charitable purpose of the project.

Our intention is to build a sustainable foundation for monastic training through generosity, cooperation, and the responsible use of resources.

An Opportunity to Preserve and Renew a Spiritual Space

We recognize that some churches and religious institutions face declining attendance, rising maintenance costs, or uncertainty about the future use of their buildings. Yet these properties may still possess considerable spiritual, architectural, and community value.

Where appropriate, shared use could allow an existing Christian congregation to continue its worship and activities while our community uses designated facilities at other times. Such an arrangement could also help share operating expenses and keep the building in meaningful religious use.

We would approach these opportunities with respect for the property's existing traditions and a commitment to constructive cooperation.

An Invitation to Cooperate

The establishment of a Dhamma hall is the first practical step toward our longer-term vision of a Theravāda Arahanist monastic training centre in Southern Ontario.

We welcome inquiries from churches, dioceses, religious organizations, charitable foundations, property owners, and individuals who may know of a suitable property or wish to support this initiative.

We are open to a range of possibilities, including a donated property, charitable transfer, affordable long-term lease, shared-use arrangement, substantially discounted property, or manageable purchase.

A building that no longer meets the needs of one congregation may offer a new opportunity to serve as a place of worship, contemplation, and spiritual education for future generations.

If you have or know of a suitable property, are exploring the future of an underused religious building, or wish to support the development of this centre, we warmly invite you to get in touch.

title: 10 Marks Part 5
content:
TEN MARKS OF ARAHANISM

5. The Brahma Law of Values Is the Foundation of the Noble Human Way

1). The Two Laws Governing Existence

Arahanism distinguishes between two fundamentally different orders of existence: the Cosmic Law of Power and the Brahma Law of Values.

The Cosmic Law of Power is the order of competition, domination, and survival through strength. Within the world, beings struggle to secure their existence, protect their interests, and prevail over competing forces. Strength can determine outcomes, the powerful can exploit the vulnerable, and one being's survival may come at the expense of another. This order operates through the struggle for existence, in which power can become an instrument of domination and exploitation.

The Brahma Law of Values, by contrast, establishes a higher ethical order founded upon kindness, compassion, brahmic joy, transcendental release, justice, fairness, and respect for others. Under this law, strength carries responsibility. Those capable of protecting others should not exploit their vulnerability; power should serve the welfare of life rather than become an instrument of oppression.

The distinction is not that strength itself is evil, but that strength can serve fundamentally different purposes. Under the Cosmic Law of Power, it can establish domination. Under the Brahma Law of Values, it is governed by ethical principles and directed towards protection, responsibility, and the common good.

These two laws represent two different ways of conducting existence. One places power at the centre of relationships; the other places values at the centre of conduct.

2). The Brahma Lineage and the Noble Human Way

Arahanism understands Brahma as the higher spiritual source associated with the noble lineage of humanity. Within this doctrine, the Brahma Law of Values is not merely an ethical system invented by human society. It is a higher dimensional order of values transmitted through the Brahma lineage and preserved as the foundation of noble human existence.

Humanity on Earth is understood, within the Arahanist account of human origins, as possessing a dual inheritance: a connection with the Brahma lineage and an animal ancestry associated with the primate world. These two sources provide the doctrinal basis for understanding the tension between noble values and primitive power-driven impulses in human conduct.

Consequently, human beings possess the capacity to choose which order they will embody. We can organize our lives around competition, domination, and selfish advantage, or we can cultivate kindness, compassion, restraint, justice, and responsibility.

The Noble Human Way (Manussa) is the way of existence aligned with the Brahma Law of Values. It requires the deliberate cultivation of the qualities that distinguish noble human conduct from behaviour governed primarily by instinct, aggression, and the struggle for power.

This choice has consequences for both the individual and society. A person who cultivates noble values transforms the disposition of the mind; a community that establishes these values as guiding principles creates the conditions for a more civilized human order.

3). The Four Brahmavihāras: The Individual Foundation of the Law of Values

At the individual level, the Brahma Law of Values is embodied through the Four Brahmavihāras, the Brahmic abodes for the mind: mettā, karuṇā, muditā, and upekkhā.

These four qualities are not simply desirable emotions. In Arahanism, they are divine ordered emotions and foundational forms of mental cultivation through which the citta is purified, stabilized, and progressively aligned with the Noble Human Way.

Mettā — Kindness

Mettā is the cultivation of goodwill towards living beings. It counters hostility and ill-will, replacing the impulse to harm with a disposition towards the welfare of others. Through mettā, the individual learns to regard others without making personal advantage the governing principle of every relationship.

Karuṇā — Compassion

Karuṇā is the response to suffering through concern for those who experience it. It counters cruelty, hardness, and indifference. Compassion inclines a person to relieve suffering rather than exploit vulnerability, establishing protection of the weak as an expression of noble strength.

Muditā — Brahmic Joy

Muditā at human level may exhibit as Sympathetic Joy, at divine level, it is merely a joy of being part of the cosmic mankind lineage. For humans, it is the ability to rejoice in the happiness, welfare, and good fortune of others. It counters envy, jealousy, and the contraction of the mind that arises when another person's success is regarded as a personal loss.

Within the Arahanist understanding of the Brahma lineage, muditā also expresses an expansive joy in the cultivation and flourishing of noble qualities. The individual learns to welcome the elevation of others rather than experience their advancement as a threat.

Upekkhā — Transcendental Release

Upekkhā at human level may exhibit as Equanimity, a balanced impartiality, free from excessive attachment, aversion, and personal favoritism. It counters reactive judgment and helps the individual maintain composure when confronting changing circumstances, conflicting interests, and the suffering of others.

At divine level, upekkhā is Transcendental Release, the progressive elevation of the citta towards higher dimensional spiritual refinement. Its cultivation at the human level establishes a foundation of balance and impartiality; its higher dimensional development is within the broader path of meditation and liberation belongs to the further transformation of consciousness.

Together, the four Brahmavihāras cultivate goodwill, compassion, joy, and ascension. Through repeated practice, these qualities can become stable dispositions rather than occasional emotional responses.

Their function is to transform the inner basis of conduct: reducing hostility, cruelty, envy, and agitation while establishing a citta increasingly aligned with the Brahma Law of Values, and governed by noble values rather than impulse, selfishness, or the pursuit of power.

4). From Individual Purification to Civilized Society

The Law of Values has both an individual and a collective dimension.

At the individual level, the Brahmavihāras cultivate the inner qualities required for noble conduct. At the collective level, these values find expression through the principles and institutions by which human beings organize their relationships and govern their common affairs.

A civilized society cannot be established through strength, legislation, or institutional structures alone. Its stability depends upon the values that guide the people who exercise power and the principles that determine how power may legitimately be used.

The Brahma Law of Values therefore provides an divine and ethical foundation for the development of a noble human civilization.

Its principal collective expressions include the following:

Justice: The impartial recognition of wrongdoing, the protection of those who suffer harm, and the restoration of a just order. Justice requires that power and personal interest do not determine the application of moral standards.

Fairness: The consistent application of principles without improper favoritism. Fairness requires that individuals be treated according to relevant and defensible standards rather than the arbitrary preferences of those in authority.

Equality: The recognition that differences in strength, wealth, status, or social position do not justify the exploitation or degradation of others. Equality expresses the extension of goodwill and compassion beyond personal preference and privileged relationships.

Democracy: The sharing of responsibility for collective affairs through participation, deliberation, and accountable governance. In the Arahanist framework, democracy fulfils its noblest purpose when collective power is restrained by ethical values and directed towards the common good.

These principles give social and political expression to the Law of Values. They are not identical to the four Brahmavihāras, nor are they exhausted by them. Rather, they extend the underlying ethical orientation of the Brahmavihāras into the organization of collective life.

5). The Supporting Virtues of a Noble Civilization

The stability of a value-based civilization requires additional virtues that enable its principles to endure across generations and remain effective under pressure.

Loyalty and Commitment establish continuity in relationships and dedication to a community or higher principle. Noble loyalty remains governed by conscience rather than blind allegiance.

Self-Sacrifice expresses the willingness to place a worthy principle or the welfare of others above personal advantage when circumstances require it. It prevents self-interest from becoming the ultimate measure of conduct.

Chivalry represents the ethical restraint of strength. It requires those who possess power or ability to exercise them with dignity, consideration, and a willingness to protect the vulnerable.

Integrity establishes consistency between declared principles and actual behaviour. Without integrity, a society may profess noble values while continuing to operate through deception, exploitation, and hypocrisy.

Responsibility requires individuals to recognize their obligations and accept the consequences of their actions. It connects personal conduct with the welfare of the wider community.

Discipline sustains ethical conduct through continued restraint and training. It ensures that noble values are maintained even when immediate impulses or personal interests encourage their abandonment.

Wisdom (paññā) enables individuals and communities to discern consequences, recognize the limitations of immediate gratification, and make decisions in accordance with deeper principles.

Respect recognizes the dignity and legitimate claims of others. It sustains harmonious relationships while allowing appropriate differences in responsibility, role, and function.

Together, these virtues reinforce the collective expression of the Law of Values. Justice requires integrity; responsibility requires discipline; chivalry requires restraint; and loyalty requires wisdom. Each virtue supports the others, helping to prevent the degeneration of a value-based order into a system governed primarily by personal advantage and domination.

The purpose is not to eliminate strength or differences among human beings, but to establish the ethical principles by which strength, authority, and individual capabilities are exercised.

6). Brahmavihāra, Brahmacariya, and the Purification of the Citta

Within Arahanism, the Brahma Law of Values also has a direct relationship with the spiritual path.

The cultivation of the Brahmavihāras purifies the emotional basis of the citta. However, noble and divine emotions must be accompanied by restraint in conduct if their influence is to become stable and enduring.

This is the role of sīla and brahmacariya.

Sīla establishes sense restraint in bodily and verbal conduct. It prevents the individual from repeatedly reinforcing the very patterns of hostility, exploitation, and uncontrolled desire that the cultivation of noble values seeks to overcome.

Brahmacariya, the noble or holy life, extends this principle into a disciplined way of living. Through renunciation, sense restraint, celibacy, and the abandonment of worldly entanglements, the practitioner progressively withdraws the mind-heart from the worldly conditions that perpetuate attachment and agitation.

The Brahmavihāras and brahmacariya therefore serve complementary functions. The former cultivate the inner qualities of noble conduct; the latter establishes a way of life that protects and deepens spiritual development.

The Law of Values provides the ethical foundation, while disciplined practice transforms that foundation into a stable way of being.

For the Arahanist, however, the cultivation of noble values is not the final objective of the liberation path. A civilized human existence and the attainment of Arahantship are distinct, though related, dimensions of the doctrine. The former concerns the values behind human conduct; the latter concerns liberation from worldly bondage.

7). The Foundation of the Noble Human Way

The Brahma Law of Values establishes the foundation upon which a noble human civilization can be built. It directs power towards protection, relationships towards mutual respect, and collective institutions towards justice and responsibility.

Its individual foundation is the cultivation of the four Brahmavihāras. Its collective expression is a civilization governed by justice, fairness, equality, and responsible cooperation. Its supporting virtues include integrity, discipline, wisdom, loyalty, and self-restraint. Within the spiritual path, its cultivation is strengthened by sīla and brahmacariya.

These dimensions form a connected order in which inner purification supports noble conduct, noble conduct supports civilized relationships, and civilized institutions provide a social expression of the values cultivated by individuals.

Arahanism therefore maintains that humanity's highest potential cannot be realized through power alone. Strength without values can produce domination; knowledge without integrity can serve exploitation; and social organization without compassion can preserve injustice.

The Noble Human Way begins when human beings choose to govern their conduct according to the Brahma Law of Values rather than allowing the struggle for power to determine their relationships.

The Brahma Law of Values is thus the foundation of the Noble Human Way: the higher divine and ethical order through which human beings cultivate the citta, govern their conduct, and establish a civilized existence aligned with Brahma Law of Values.

title: 10 Marks Part 6
content:
TEN MARKS OF ARAHANISM

6. Brahmacariya: The Complete Practice for Arahantship

Brahmacariya as the Complete Course of Practice

Arahanism establishes Brahmacariya, the holy life, as the complete course of practice directed towards Arahantship. It encompasses renunciation, celibacy, sense restraint, disciplined withdrawal, meditation, wisdom, and the progressive abandonment of worldly attachment. It is the entire disciplined way of life through which the practitioner pursues the complete transcendence of worldly bondage.

The purpose of Brahmacariya is to fulfil the ancient quest for liberation from the world. Through the progressive cultivation of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, the practitioner develops Nibbidā (disenchantment from the world), Virāga (fading of worldly passion), and Vimutti (liberation from worldly bondage). The holy life culminates in Arahantship, the fulfilment of the task of liberation from the worldly bondage.

The Arahant's declaration expresses this completion: Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā.

“Birth is exhausted, the holy life brahmacariya has been fulfilled, what had to be done has been done, and there is no further coming back to this state of being.”

Brahmacariya is therefore the entire course of practice, from the initial renunciation of household worldly life to the fulfilment of Arahantship.

1). Brahmacariya and the Transcendence of Kāma-Dhātu

Within Arahanism, Brahmacariya has a decisive role in overcoming attachment to the sexual and sensual realm (kāma-dhātu). It establishes complete renunciation of sexuality, restraint over sensuality, and the progressive purification of Citta at its root.

Sexuality is a fundamental feature of sensual existence. Male and female embodiment, sexual attraction, and the craving associated with sensual gratification sustain powerful attachments to worldly life in kāma-dhātu. These attachments contribute to taṇhā (craving) and bhava (worldly becoming or manifestation), perpetuating involvement in worldly conditioned existence.

As long as sexual craving continues to govern the mind, the practitioner remains vulnerable to the attractions and attachments associated with reincarnation the sexual and sensual realm (kāma-dhātu). Brahmacariya directly addresses this pattern by abandoning sexual activity and cultivating freedom from sensual dependence.

Through strict celibacy, the practitioner withdraws from the habitual pursuit of sexual gratification, weakens the patterns of craving associated with sensuality, and establishes conditions favourable to mental clarity, concentration, and deeper meditation.

Brahmacariya thus marks a decisive transition in the direction of spiritual development: from immersion in sensual existence towards the cultivation of the mind for higher meditative attainments and, ultimately, liberation from worldly bondage.

In the Arahanist framework, this transition can be expressed as the movement from attachment to kāma-dhātu towards the pursuit of the Deathless Realm, Nibbāna-dhātu.

Complete celibacy is therefore not merely a rule of personal morality. It is a central discipline of the holy life, directed towards the abandonment of sexual and sensual craving and the attainment of Arahantship.

2). Taming Soul-Spirit through the Holy Life

In Arahanism, the practice of Brahmacariya also concerns the taming of Soul-Spirit through the purification and transformation of the mind-heart, Citta.

According to the Arahanist understanding of Soul-Spirit (Attā), Citta is the mind-heart through which the Soul-Spirit experiences and engages with the world. Left to its habitual inclinations, Citta tends towards sensual attachment, reactive emotions, and the pursuit of worldly gratification. Like water flowing without direction, the mind follows established tendencies unless it is deliberately trained.

Brahmacariya provides the disciplined framework for this training. Through Sīla, the practitioner restrains unwholesome conduct and prevents the continual reinforcement of worldly attachments. Through Samādhi, the mind develops concentration, stability, and the capacity to remain independent of external stimulation. Through Paññā, the practitioner develops the understanding required to abandon worldly attachment to worldly conditioned existence.

This progression supports the transformation expressed through three successive dimensions of the path:

  • Nibbidā — Disenchantment from the world: The mind progressively loses its fascination with worldly existence and recognizes the limitations of worldly conditioned phenomena.
  • Virāga — Fading of Worldly Passion: Worldly passion and craving diminish as the mind relinquishes its worldly attachment to sensual gratification and worldly becoming or manifestation (bhava).
  • Vimutti — Liberation from worldly bondage: The mind is freed from the bondage sustained by worldly craving and clinging.

These are not merely intellectual conclusions. They represent the progressive transformation of the practitioner's relationship with the world.

The purpose of taming Citta is not simply to become calmer while continuing to depend upon worldly gratification. It is to develop the Sīla, samādhi, and paññā required for the complete abandonment of worldly bondage.

Within Arahanism, Brahmacariya therefore unites sense restraint, disciplined wirthdrawal, mental cultivation, and wisdom into a single course of practice directed towards the Deathless.

3). The Progressive Arc of Sīla: From Ethical Living to Total Renunciation

Sīla is often understood as a system of ethical conduct governing how people behave towards one another. Arahanism recognizes this function but places Sīla within a more comprehensive renunciants’ liberation path framework is: the progressive withdrawal of the practitioner from worldly dependence.

The different levels of precept training establish increasingly demanding forms of restraint. They provide a structured progression from ethical lay life through yogi training and novice renunciation to the complete discipline of a fully ordained Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī.

The Five Precepts: Ethical Human Life

The Five Precepts establish the foundation of wholesome conduct for laypeople. They restrain harmful bodily and verbal actions and cultivate the conditions for an ethical life.

At this level, the practitioner remains within ordinary lay society, participating in family, economic, and social life while undertaking moral discipline.

The Five Precepts are therefore the starting point of ethical training. They establish restraint, but they do not require the complete abandonment of sexuality or the renunciation of worldly life.

The Uposatha Eight Precepts: The Beginning of Yogi Training

The Eight Precepts introduce a more intensive form of spiritual discipline, traditionally undertaken on Uposatha days and on other occasions devoted to practice.

The decisive distinction between the Five and Eight Precepts is the abandonment of sexual activity, even only for a day. Whereas the Five Precepts prohibit sexual misconduct, the Eight Precepts require temporary complete celibacy through the observance of abrahmacariyā veramaṇī.

This transition changes the purpose of restraint. The practitioner is no longer concerned only with avoiding harmful conduct but deliberately withdraws from sensual gratification to cultivate the mind.

The remaining precepts further reduce dependence on external sources of pleasure. Abstaining from entertainment, adornment, luxurious sleeping arrangements, and eating after midday reduces opportunities for habitual sensory gratification.

These disciplines are intended to loosen the mind's dependence on external stimulation and encourage the cultivation of inner well-being through spiritual practice.

As sensual preoccupations diminish, the practitioner can devote greater attention to pāmojja (gladness), pīti (rapture or spiritual joy), sukha (happiness or well-being), and the development of Samādhi.

Full-Time Eight Precepts: Upāsaka and Upāsikā Yogi Training

When a lay practitioner progresses from periodic Uposatha observance to a sustained commitment to spiritual training, the next stage is to undertake the Eight Precepts full-timely as an Upāsaka or Upāsikā. This marks a transition from ordinary ethical lay life to a disciplined course of preparation for renunciation.

Within Arahanism, full-time Upāsaka/Upāsikā training is a formal requirement of the path towards novice ordination. Practitioners are expected to reside in a training monastery, where their daily lives can be organized around celibacy, ethical restraint, meditation, spiritual study, and the cultivation of inner discipline. By withdrawing from ordinary household routines and reducing dependence on external sources of pleasure, they learn to establish a way of life increasingly directed towards liberation from worldly bondage.

This training is not merely the daily observance of eight rules. It is a sustained period of preparation in which practitioners develop the discipline, maturity, and stability required for the more comprehensive renunciation of pabbajjā. They learn to maintain celibacy, regulate their daily activities, cultivate inner joy through spiritual practice, and progressively reduce their dependence on worldly relationships, entertainment, bodily comforts, and material interests.

Arahanism establishes a minimum training period of one to two years for full-time Upāsaka/Upāsikā practice before progression to the Ten Precepts novice renunciation. This period provides the time necessary to establish a stable foundation of Sīla, deepen Samādhi, and prepare the practitioner for the responsibilities and demands of renunciant life.

The Upāsaka/Upāsikā stage therefore serves as a formal bridge between ethical lay life and renunciation. It allows practitioners to experience the demands of sustained celibacy and disciplined living before undertaking the more comprehensive commitments of a novice.

Upon completing this stage and satisfying the requirements of the Arahanist training system, the practitioner may proceed to the Ten Precepts and enter pabbajjā as a Sāmaṇera or Sāmaṇerī. This subsequent stage requires a further minimum of two to three years of training before progression to full ordination, in accordance with the requirements of the Arahanist Order.

The progression is therefore deliberate and structured: periodic Eight Precept observance introduces yogi training; full-time Upāsaka/Upāsikā training establishes sustained discipline; and novice renunciation deepens the practitioner's separation from ordinary worldly life. Each stage prepares the practitioner for the next, progressively organizing the whole of life around the ultimate objective of Arahantship.

The Ten Precepts: The Beginning of Renunciant Life

The Ten Precepts mark a further transition: pabbajjā, the renunciation of household life as a novice monastic under training (sāmaṇera or sāmaṇerī).

The novice abandons ordinary household life and undertakes a more comprehensive discipline of renunciation. This includes celibacy, simplicity, voluntary poverty and restraint from the economic transactions associated with personal wealth and financial accumulation.

The prohibition concerning the handling of gold and silver, expressed in the Vinaya as jātarūpa-rajata-paṭiggahaṇā, forms an important part of the traditional renunciant discipline. Its purpose is not merely to simplify personal finances but to establish a way of life distinct from the pursuit and possession of worldly wealth.

Under this discipline, the novice depends upon the support of the monastic community, the charity behind, and lay donors rather than organizing life around personal accumulation and economic independence.

The transition to renunciation therefore changes the practitioner's entire relationship with worldly security. Time, conduct, and daily life become increasingly organized around spiritual training.

The Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Upasampadā Ordination: Complete Renunciant Training

Full Upasampadā ordination establishes the Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī within the complete monastic discipline governed by the relevant Pātimokkha Vinaya.

The fully ordained Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī undertakes a comprehensive system of sense restraint and communal discipline. Celibacy, simplicity, voluntary poverty, dependence upon alms, and the abandonment of ordinary household life provide the framework for sustained cultivation of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā.

In the Arahanist understanding, this is the complete institutional form of the holy life: the practitioner has renounced the household existence and undertaken the disciplined course of practice directed towards Arahantship.

The monastic vocation is not fulfilled merely by entering the Saṅgha or maintaining its external rules. The discipline must serve its ultimate purpose: the eradication of worldly craving and attachment and the realization of liberation.

Gautama expressed the spiritual relationship between himself and his disciples through the image of disciples as his Dhamma-born children and heirs to the Dhamma rather than to material things. This principle captures the spirit of renunciation: the practitioner inherits and embodies Gautama’s Dhamma through disciplined practice rather than through the acquisition of worldly possessions.

4). The Progressive Structure of Renunciant Training

The progression can be summarized as follows:

This progression describes increasingly intensive forms of discipline. The stages differ in their obligations, duration, and relationship to lay or monastic life, while sharing a common direction: the progressive reduction of worldly attachment and the cultivation of the conditions necessary for liberation from worldly bondage.

The Eight Precepts, for example, can be undertaken periodically or maintained daily. Daily observance by a layperson represents sustained yogi training, but it does not itself constitute formal monastic ordination.

Likewise, full Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī ordination establishes the complete monastic discipline, but Arahantship requires the successful fulfilment of the path rather than external observance alone.

The significance of the progression lies in its organizing principle: Sīla develops from ethical restraint into a comprehensive discipline of worldly renunciation.

5). Sīla as the Progressive Withdrawal from the World

Within Arahanism, Sīla is not merely a static collection of social rules intended to make worldly life more pleasant, or miserable. It is an essential component of the course of practice through which the practitioner progressively withdraws from worldly bondage.

Worldly phenomena and conditioned formations—dhammesu and saṅkhāresu, understood within their respective contexts—belong to conditioned existence. They arise and change under the governing conditions of the world and are subject to impermanence, decay, and dissolution.

The practitioner who seeks Arahantship must therefore do more than behave ethically within the world. The practitioner must understand the limitations of worldly conditioned existence and abandon the worldly craving and clinging that sustain bondage to it.

The progression from the Five Precepts through the Eight and Ten Precepts to the full monastic discipline provides an increasingly comprehensive framework for this work.

Through Sīla, the practitioner restrains the bodily and verbal conduct through which unwholesome tendencies are reinforced. Through Samādhi, the mind develops stability and collectedness that generates Tapas, the primordial spiritual force that is necessary and indispensable to purify the citta. Through Paññā, the practitioner develops the wisdom required to abandon ignorance and worldly attachment.

This training addresses the three fundamental defilements:

  • Rāga — worldly craving and attachment.
  • Dosa — fear, anger, aversion, hostility, violence, and related reactive tendencies.
  • Moha — ignorance and delusion concerning the nature of existence and the path to liberation from worldly bondage.

The purpose is not merely to suppress these tendencies temporarily, but to bring about their complete eradication through the fulfilment of the path.

Sīla provides the discipline required for this progression. It protects the practitioner from continually renewing the patterns of conduct that reinforce attachment, while preparing the mind for deeper Samādhi and the liberating work of Paññā.

6). The Fulfilment of Brahmacariya in Arahantship

The ultimate objective of Brahmacariya is Arahantship.

The holy life is undertaken to accomplish what ordinary worldly existence cannot accomplish by itself: the complete ending of the worldly craving and clinging that sustain bondage to worldly conditioned existence.

Its fulfilment is expressed in the Arahant's declaration:

Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā.

“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been fulfilled, what had to be done has been done, and there is no further coming back to this state of being.”

The declaration identifies the completion of the spiritual task. The practitioner has fulfilled the holy life and accomplished what was necessary for liberation from worldly bondage.

Within Arahanism, Arahantship is understood as the transcendence of worldly bondage and the attainment of the Deathless realm, Nibbāna-dhātu. It is not simply a state of ethical excellence, psychological well-being, or temporary meditative absorption. It is the culmination of the entire course of renunciation, sense restraint, mental cultivation, and wisdom.

The quest that begins with the recognition of the limitations of worldly existence reaches its fulfilment when the causes of worldly bondage have been eradicated.

Brahmacariya therefore encompasses the complete course of practice: the renunciation of worldly life, the progressive purification of conduct, the taming and stabilization of Citta, the cultivation of wisdom, and the realization of Arahantship.

Brahmacariya is the complete practice for Arahantship. Its purpose is fulfilled when the holy life has accomplished its task, worldly bondage has been eradicated, and the practitioner has attained liberation from worldly bondage.

title: 10 Marks Part 7
content:
TEN MARKS OF ARAHANISM

7. Inner Happiness and Joy Are the Foundation of Renunciation

Arahanism establishes a principle that is frequently misunderstood in spiritual practice: renunciation requires not only the relinquishment of worldly pleasures but also the deliberate cultivation of inner happiness and joy. A practitioner cannot build a sustainable life of renunciation simply by removing sources of pleasure from the external world. The practitioner must develop the inner capacity for happiness that makes such renunciation possible, fulfilling, and sustainable.

The path towards Arahantship requires a progressive withdrawal from worldly gratification. Through the Eight Precepts, practitioners deliberately reduce their dependence on sensory pleasures, entertainment, bodily indulgence, and other sources of external satisfaction. Those who undertake full-time Upāsaka or Upāsikā training sustain these disciplines as a way of life. Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs go further, completely relinquishing worldly life and accepting the comprehensive discipline of the renunciant path.

These restrictions are purposeful. They reduce the conditions through which worldly craving is repeatedly stimulated and reinforced. Yet they also raise a fundamental practical question: when a practitioner deliberately relinquishes the ordinary sources of worldly happiness, what will sustain the happiness necessary to continue living and practising?

Arahanism answers directly: inner happiness and joy must be cultivated as an essential part of the path.

Renunciation is not a programme of making oneself unhappy. Its purpose is to free the practitioner from dependence on worldly gratification and direct the Citta towards liberation from worldly bondage. To teach practitioners to relinquish external pleasures without teaching them to cultivate inner happiness is to neglect an essential dimension of renunciant training. The reduction of external gratification and the cultivation of inner happiness must proceed together.

1). Non-Attachment Does Not Mean Rejection of Inner Happiness

A common misunderstanding of non-attachment is that happiness itself should be regarded with suspicion. When practitioners experience happiness, rapture, or tranquillity during Samādhi, they may be warned not to become attached to these experiences. This is non-sense. It becomes misleading when it encourages practitioners to distrust inner happiness simply because it is pleasant.

Arahanism rejects this indiscriminate treatment of happiness.

The essential question is not whether happiness exists, but where it originates and what relationship it establishes between the Citta and the world. Happiness derived from worldly gratification can reinforce dependence on external objects, sensory stimulation, possessions, relationships, and changing circumstances. Happiness cultivated through spiritual practice can instead help the Citta become less dependent on those conditions.

These two forms of happiness must not be treated as though they have the same spiritual significance. One can strengthen worldly attachment; the other can help the practitioner withdraw from it.

When happiness arises through sense restraint, disciplined withdrawal, renunciation, meditation, concentration, and the purification of the mind-heart, it should not automatically be classified as an obstacle. Such happiness can demonstrate that the practitioner no longer needs to rely exclusively on external gratification for well-being. It can encourage further cultivation, strengthen confidence in the path, and make the renunciant life more sustainable.

The distinction is essential: non-attachment to worldly gratification does not require indifference towards the wholesome happiness cultivated within the Citta.

The practitioner should learn to recognize this happiness, cultivate it wisely, and allow it to support the work of liberation from worldly bondage. The objective is not to suppress every experience of joy, but to transform the source of happiness and progressively free the mind from worldly dependence.

2). The Eight Precepts Require the Cultivation of Inner Happiness

The relationship between renunciation and happiness becomes particularly clear when we examine the Eight Precepts.

The Eight Precepts are not merely an expanded list of moral prohibitions. They establish a practical discipline through which the practitioner deliberately reduces dependence on ordinary sources of worldly pleasure. Full celibacy replaces sexual activity; abstention from entertainment and adornment reduces sensory stimulation; abstention from eating after midday limits the pursuit of bodily gratification; and restrictions concerning luxurious beds and seats encourage simplicity.

These disciplines are intended to change the practitioner's relationship with pleasure. They create opportunities to observe worldly craving, reduce habitual dependence on sensory gratification, and direct attention towards the cultivation of the mind.

Yet the removal of external pleasures is only one dimension of the training. The practitioner must also develop the capacity to experience contentment and joy through spiritual cultivation. Otherwise, the discipline risks becoming an exercise in deprivation, with the mind continually longing for the pleasures it has relinquished.

Arahanism therefore places inner happiness at the centre of this process. As external gratification is deliberately reduced, the practitioner must learn to cultivate happiness through Sīla, meditation, Samādhi, spiritual understanding, and alignment with Brahma divine values.

This is not an invitation to replace one form of sensory indulgence with an endless pursuit of pleasurable meditation. It is a call to develop a different foundation for well-being: one that becomes progressively less dependent on external acquisition and increasingly rooted in the qualities of the Citta.

The Eight Precepts reduce dependence on external happiness; the cultivation of inner happiness makes that reduction sustainable.

3). Inner Happiness Is Essential to the Renunciant Life

The principle becomes even more significant when practitioners progress towards full-time renunciation.

A full-time Upāsaka or Upāsikā undertakes the Eight Precepts continuously as part of a disciplined spiritual life. A Sāmaṇera or Sāmaṇerī enters novice renunciation under the Ten Precepts, while a fully ordained Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī accepts the comprehensive discipline of monastic life. Through these stages, ordinary worldly activities, sensual pursuits, and worldly connections are progressively reduced.

The renunciant cannot depend on the same pattern of happiness as a householder. Much of what ordinarily structures a person's sense of satisfaction—sexual relationships, entertainment, material acquisition, social recognition, and the pursuit of sensory pleasure—no longer occupies the same place in life.

A renunciant path that neglects inner happiness therefore leaves a crucial question unanswered: how is the practitioner to sustain contentment while deliberately relinquishing these familiar sources of satisfaction?

Arahanism holds that the answer must be found through the cultivation of the Citta. The practitioner develops happiness through ethical living, simplicity, seclusion, meditation, concentration, and the progressive purification of the mind-heart. Such happiness supports the discipline of Brahmacariya and helps the practitioner maintain a life devoted to liberation from worldly bondage.

The Theragāthā offers compelling spiritual testimony to this relationship between renunciation and joy. The elder monks constantly express their appreciation of solitude, seclusion, freedom from worldly burdens, and the happiness associated with contemplative life. Their verses do not portray renunciation simply as the loss of ordinary pleasures. They also express the contentment and joy discovered through a different way of living.

This is an important lesson for Arahanist training. Renunciation must be accompanied by the discovery of a positive source of happiness. The practitioner must learn not only how to leave worldly gratification behind, but also how to live well without depending upon it.

Inner happiness is therefore not a luxury added to monastic discipline. It is part of the spiritual foundation that allows the practitioner to sustain that discipline over the course of a life devoted to Arahantship.

4). Inner Happiness Must Become a Characteristic of the Citta

Arahanism teaches that inner happiness should be deliberately cultivated and progressively stabilized as a quality of the mind-heart.

The practitioner should not treat spiritual joy as an accidental occurrence that appears during meditation and must then be dismissed. Happiness arising through wholesome cultivation is a quality to understand, develop, and integrate into one's spiritual life.

Through Sīla, the practitioner experiences the contentment associated with ethical conduct and freedom from remorse. Through renunciation, the practitioner develops gladness in relinquishing worldly burdens. Through Samādhi, the mind may experience tranquillity, rapture, concentration, and profound well-being from higher dimensional experiences. Through Paññā, the practitioner gains a deeper understanding of worldly conditions and becomes increasingly capable of turning away from the worldly attachments that sustain suffering.

These developments reinforce one another. Ethical discipline supports contentment; contentment encourages spiritual cultivation; meditation deepens inner well-being; and the experience of happiness independent of worldly acquisition can strengthen the resolve to continue renunciation.

Arahanism therefore seeks a transformation in the practitioner's habitual source of happiness. Rather than continually seeking satisfaction through external stimulation, the practitioner develops the capacity to find contentment within the cultivated Citta.

The aim is not to guarantee a particular pleasant feeling at every moment. Nor does every meditative experience necessarily indicate spiritual progress. The aim is to develop a stable spiritual orientation in which inner happiness, composure, and joy become increasingly available through practice and increasingly independent of worldly gratification.

This is the difference between a life organized around the pursuit of external pleasure and a life organized around the cultivation of the mind-heart.

5). Brahmic Joy and the Divine Values of Humanity

Inner happiness also has a moral and spiritual dimension. The cultivation of the Brahmavihāras—Mettā, Karuṇā, Muditā, and Upekkhā—develops a noble disposition of the Citta.

Muditā, brahmic joy, is particularly important because it demonstrates that happiness need not depend on personal acquisition or advantage. One can rejoice simply because one is part of the divine lineage of mankind. Such joy arises through a cultivated mind rather than through the satisfaction of a personal desire.

Within the Arahanist understanding of human spiritual nature, Brahmic joy expresses a divine spiritual inheritance. It reflects an orientation towards compassion, generosity, integrity, fairness, and the well-being of others rather than towards competition, domination, jealousy, or personal gratification.

This form of joy supports the Brahma Law of Values. It allows happiness to become associated with goodness itself. The practitioner learns to rejoice in what is noble and wholesome, gradually changing the inner values that govern thought, intention, and conduct. When the Citta cultivates Brahmic joy, goodness in another person can itself become a source of happiness.

Inner happiness thus contributes not only to renunciation but also to the development of a noble human character. It helps the practitioner move beyond a life governed by personal gratification and towards one informed by divine spiritual values.

6). Inner Happiness as a Signature of Transcendence

Arahanism understands happiness and joy within the wider framework of its teaching on Nibbāna-dhātu. In the Arahanist doctrine, Nibbāna is understood as the Deathless realm, whose characteristics include peace, purity, stability, and happiness beyond the conditions governing our worldly existence.

True happiness (sukha) and joy (pīti–muditā) are understood in this context as more than responses to favorable external conditions. They can arise through worldly withdrawal, purification, and alignment with divine values. They express the capacity of the Citta to develop qualities that are not dependent on the acquisition of worldly pleasures.

Inner happiness and joy are therefore energies of ascent, lifting the Citta beyond habitual dependence on the sensory field. They are also signatures of transcendence, expressing the direction of spiritual development away from worldly gratification and towards liberation. Inner happiness sustains the practitioner through renunciation, supports the development of Samādhi, and helps weaken dependence on worldly gratification.

Arahanism therefore treats inner happiness as a positive spiritual force whose proper cultivation advances the practitioner towards the ultimate objective of Arahantship.

7). Attā-saraṇa and Dhamma-saraṇa: Taking Refuge in the Inner Soul-Spirit of Transformation

The teaching expressed in the words attā-dīpa, attā-saraṇa; dhamma-dīpa, dhamma-saraṇa is central to the Arahanist understanding of spiritual development: take refuge in one's Attā / Soul-Spirit and make one's Attā / Soul-Spirit one's island; take refuge in Gautama’s true Dhamma and make the true Dhamma one's island.

In the Arahanist interpretation, Attā refers to Soul-Spirit, the spiritual essence of a human being. Taking refuge in one's Soul-Spirit means recognizing the inner spiritual reality towards which the practice is directed, rather than placing ultimate reliance upon the unstable conditions of the external world. Taking refuge in the Dhamma means relying upon the teaching and practice through which the practitioner transforms or purifies the Soul-Spirit and advances towards liberation from worldly bondage.

This transformation includes the cultivation of inner happiness and joy. Through Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, the practitioner disciplines and purifies the mind-heart Citta which envelops the Soul-Spirit, develops noble qualities, and reduces dependence on worldly gratification. The happiness arising through this transformation should be recognized as part of the practitioner's spiritual development.

The practitioner therefore has reason to value and cultivate this inner happiness. It is not a worldly possession that must be acquired and defended. It is a wholesome quality developed through spiritual practice, helping the practitioner sustain worldly renunciation and orient life towards liberation from worldly bondage.

Taking refuge in one’s Soul-Spirit and Gautama’s Dhamma, or using Gautama’s Dhamma to transform our Soul-Spirit, thus gives inner happiness a place within the complete path. The practitioner does not rely exclusively on the external world to sustain well-being, but progressively cultivates the inner qualities that support the life of Brahmacariya.

Conclusion: Renunciation Must Be Sustained by Inner Happiness

The Seventh Mark establishes a principle that should guide the whole of Arahanist training: the relinquishment of worldly pleasures must be accompanied by the cultivation of inner happiness and joy.

The Eight Precepts deliberately reduce external gratification. Full-time Upāsaka and Upāsikā training sustains this discipline. Novice and full ordination deepen the renunciant commitment, progressively separating the practitioner from ordinary household life and worldly pursuits. At every stage, the practitioner must cultivate more inner happiness that sustains the journey.

Arahanism therefore challenges the idea that non-attachment requires suspicion towards happiness itself. The relevant distinction is between happiness that reinforces dependence on the external world and happiness cultivated through the purification of the Citta. The former can strengthen worldly bondage; the latter can help the practitioner transcend it.

The path requires both relinquishment and cultivation: relinquishment of the external pleasures that sustain worldly dependence, and cultivation of the inner happiness that makes renunciation sustainable. As the practitioner advances through Sīla, Samādhi, Paññā, Nibbidā, Virāga, and Vimutti, inner happiness supports the renunciant life and helps direct the Citta towards Arahantship.

True happiness (sukha) and joy (pīti–muditā) are not products of worldly conditions. They arise through worldly withdrawal, purification, and alignment with divine values. They are energies of ascent, lifting the Citta beyond the sensory field, and signatures of transcendence, expressing the inner transformation through which the practitioner moves towards liberation.

title: 10 Marks Part 8
content:
TEN MARKS OF ARAHANISM

8. Gautama’s True Dhamma Rests on Duality; Non-Dual Awakening Is Wrong Awakening

The Noble Law of Values and the Transcendence of the Cosmic Natural Order

The Cosmic Natural Order and the Noble Law of Values

Arahanism distinguishes between the natural operation of the universe and the Noble Law of Values that governs the path of liberation from worldly bondage.

The universe operates through its own governing laws, encompassing the arising, transformation, decay, and dissolution of worldly phenomena. Within this cosmic order, oppositions and differences arise as part of natural processes. Yet the natural operation of the universe, considered in itself, does not establish the ethical discipline required for liberation from worldly bondage.

Arahanism characterizes this natural orientation as non-dual naturalism: an understanding that emphasizes the underlying unity of cosmic processes and seeks to transcend distinctions within worldly existence. When this approach is elevated into a doctrine of final liberation, Arahanism argues, it risks confusing accommodation to the cosmic order with emancipation from it.

The noble way of mankind requires a fundamentally different orientation. Human beings must consciously distinguish wholesome from unwholesome, purity from defilement, and conduct that supports liberation from conduct that perpetuates bondage. These distinctions establish the foundation of the Law of Values and provide the operational framework for the cultivation of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā.

This is the dualistic vision that Arahanism associates with the Manussa lineage and the noble (Ariyan) mode of existence. Its defining characteristic is not the mere recognition that differences exist, but the deliberate alignment of one's conduct and consciousness with wholesome values. The practitioner must cultivate virtue, abandon defilement, develop the Brahmavihāras, and undertake the discipline of Brahmacariya. Through this process, the citta is progressively purified and released from its attachment to worldly existence.

The distinction between the natural and the noble ways is therefore a distinction between two fundamentally different orientations. One remains within the operation of the cosmic order; the other deliberately cultivates the values and disciplines required to transcend worldly bondage.

Arahanism does not regard the natural order itself as a moral agent. Rather, it maintains that natural processes alone do not provide the ethical direction necessary for liberation. The Law of Values requires conscious discernment, moral responsibility, and sustained purification. It is through this deliberate cultivation, not through the passive acceptance of cosmic unity, that the practitioner follows Gautama's path toward complete release from worldly bondage.

Non-dual naturalism, when treated as the final goal, remains oriented toward the cosmic order. Noble Dualism directs the practitioner toward the transcendence of that order. The former seeks to overcome distinctions within worldly existence; the latter employs the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome, bondage and liberation, as the foundation of the path beyond it.

This is why Arahanism regards Noble Dualism as the defining principle of its liberation path. It expresses the civilized and noble way of mankind: a way governed by conscious values, ethical discipline, and the deliberate purification of the citta, directed toward the Deathless rather than continued participation in worldly becoming.

title: 10 Marks Part 9
content:
TEN MARKS OF ARAHANISM

9. The Liberation Path Is Ancient, Universal, and Open to All Who Seek It

The Ancient Path of the Cosmic Human Lineage

Arahanism understands the Liberation Path as an ancient path rediscovered by Gautama, the Supreme Arahant. Its significance extends beyond the history of one religion, one civilization, or one planet. It belongs to a deeper question concerning the place of mankind within the cosmos: whether beings who recognize the limitations of worldly existence can consciously seek a way beyond it.

The path is ancient because liberation is not merely a new philosophy invented by a historical teacher. Gautama rediscovered and taught the way to complete release from worldly bondage. His achievement was not simply to improve the conditions of life within the world, but to reveal a path by which a practitioner could purify the citta, sever attachment to worldly existence, and exit the univer to join the Deathless realm.

The path is universal because Arahanism understands the human lineage as extending beyond the boundaries of any single earthly society or historical age. Humanity, in this understanding, is distinguished by its capacity to question the nature of existence itself. A human being can ask whether worldly happiness is sufficient, whether everything conditioned by the universal laws must eventually change and decay, and whether a form of existence beyond these limitations is possible. The search for permanence, freedom, and ultimate release expresses this distinctive potential of the Manussa lineage.

Arahanism therefore does not regard humanity's highest purpose as merely surviving, reproducing, acquiring possessions, or securing a more comfortable position within the world. These activities may belong to ordinary worldly existence, but the human capacity for reflection and aspiration opens another possibility: the deliberate pursuit of liberation from the conditions that govern that worldly existence.

The Dignity of the Manussa Lineage

Within Arahanism's cosmological understanding, the human lineage occupies a distinctive place in the Liberation Path. Not every form of life is understood to possess the same eligibility for entry into Gautama's renunciant lineage. The Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī traditions are specifically human forms of renunciant life, established for those who undertake the discipline required to pursue Arahantship.

This distinction is not a declaration that other beings have no worth. It concerns the particular capacity and responsibility associated with the human path. The human being can consciously recognize worldly bondage, make a commitment to purification, and undertake the disciplined training through which liberation from worldly bondage becomes the governing purpose of life.

For this reason, Arahanism calls upon human beings to recognize the significance of their lineage. To be human is to possess an opportunity that should not be treated casually: the opportunity to seek a truth beyond worldly advantage, to cultivate a purified citta, and to direct one's existence toward the Deathless.

One should therefore rejoice in the opportunity to belong to the Manussa lineage and to encounter Gautama's Liberation Path. This joy is not pride based on superiority over others. It is muditā: gladness in the precious opportunity to pursue the Noble Path and in the possibility that human existence can be directed toward complete liberation from worldly bondage.

A person who recognizes this opportunity should not regard renunciation as a loss of life's highest possibilities. Renunciation is the deliberate use of the human opportunity for its highest purpose.

From Birth Lineage to Liberation-Oriented Lineage

Arahanism further distinguishes biological birth from the spiritual direction a person chooses to cultivate. A human being may be born into a family, culture, nation, and society whose ordinary purposes are directed toward worldly existence. Yet birth alone does not determine the final orientation of the citta.

A person must consciously choose the direction of purification. Rather than allowing worldly desires, inherited assumptions, and social expectations to determine the course of life, the aspirant begins to examine these conditions and to withdraw from attachment to them. Through Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, the practitioner cultivates a different relationship with existence. The purpose of life becomes not the indefinite continuation of worldly becoming or manifestation, but the attainment of liberation from it.

Arahanism describes this as a transformation of spiritual lineage: a movement away from an orientation governed by worldly continuation and toward a liberation-oriented lineage of practice. The aspirant does not achieve this transformation merely by adopting a new label or professing a new belief. It requires conscious commitment, sustained purification, and a willingness to reorganize one's life around the Liberation Path.

The Pāli term gotrabhū has a specific technical meaning in Theravāda, associated with a transition preceding the supramundane path of stream-entry. Arahanism's such reflection on spiritual lineage invites further consideration of how a person's spiritual orientation can undergo a decisive transformation as the path toward liberation from worldly bondage unfolds.

In the distinctive cosmological language of Arahanism, this transformation may be described as choosing a Brahma-oriented source and lineage rather than passively following the conditions inherited from ordinary worldly existence. Such a choice must become real through purification. It is not accomplished through ancestry, declaration, or aspiration alone, but through the sustained discipline of the Liberation Path.

Open to All Who Sincerely Seek Liberation

The Liberation Path is open to all who sincerely seek it and are prepared to undertake the necessary training. No nationality, social position, earthly culture, or previous religious identity grants exclusive ownership of the path. The decisive question is whether a person is willing to recognize worldly bondage and undertake the work of purification of the mind-heart citta.

Yet openness does not mean that liberation is effortless or that every aspiration automatically reaches its goal. A person may encounter the teaching, appreciate its ideas, and begin practising its principles without yet making the commitment required for complete renunciation. The opportunity is open, but its realization demands sustained effort and transformation.

Arahanism therefore invites sincere aspirants to approach Gautama's teaching with joy, seriousness, and confidence. The human opportunity is precious because it can be used for something greater than worldly achievement. Through the cultivation of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, and through the progressive abandonment of rāga, dosa, and moha, the aspirant prepares for the path toward complete release.

The ancient path rediscovered by Gautama is not the possession of a single people or historical moment. It is the Liberation Path offered to those who recognize the limitations of worldly existence and are prepared to seek the Deathless.

The opportunity is universal; the commitment must be personal. The path is open to all who seek liberation from worldly bondage, and each aspirant must undertake the work of purification of the citta for themselves.

10. Arahanism Is the Path of Complete Renunciation

The Commitment Required for Complete Liberation

Arahanism directs its entire discipline toward one goal: Arahantship, the complete liberation of the citta from worldly bondage. It does not present renunciation as an optional lifestyle preference or as one spiritual approach among many equally sufficient alternatives. Renunciation is the organizing principle of the Liberation Path because the goal itself requires a decisive withdrawal from worldly existence.

Arahanism holds that the attainment of Arahantship requires the abandonment of household identity and the undertaking of full renunciation as a Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī. Lay practice can cultivate generosity, ethical conduct, concentration, wisdom, and a sincere aspiration for liberation. It can prepare a person for the renunciant life. Yet Arahanism does not regard continued lay identity as the final and suitable vehicle inducive for attaining Arahantship.

The distinction between preparation and consummation is essential. One may recognize the limitations of worldly life while continuing to live according to its ordinary structures. One may cultivate virtue while retaining household responsibilities, possessions, relationships, and social identities. Such practice can be valuable, but the complete Liberation Path requires a more fundamental commitment: the deliberate reorientation of one's entire life toward release from worldly bondage.

Renunciation is therefore not merely a change of clothing, residence, or social status. It is a commitment to make liberation the governing purpose of existence. The external discipline of the Bhikkhu or Bhikkhunī provides the structure within which this commitment can be enacted and sustained.

Independence: The Aspiration to Become Anissita

The renunciant's first governing aspiration is independence from worldly dependence. Arahanism uses the Pāli term anissita to express this direction: the practitioner seeks not to remain supported by attachment to worldly existence, but to become free from the dependence that binds the citta to it.

Ordinary life is shaped by dependence on possessions, status, family, relationship, security, sensory satisfaction, social recognition, and the continuation of familiar identities. Even when these conditions bring comfort, they remain within a world subject to change and dissolution. If the citta depends upon them for its ultimate security, its freedom remains incomplete.

Arahanist renunciation therefore seeks inner sovereignty: not the power to control the world, but freedom from being governed by attachment to it. This independence cannot be established by declaration alone. It must be cultivated through sense restraint, concentration, wisdom, and the gradual abandonment of the mental conditions that perpetuate worldly bondage.

The renunciant does not withdraw from worldly life merely because the world is unpleasant. The deeper purpose is to stop making worldly existence the foundation of ultimate security and fulfilment. The goal is freedom from dependence on the world itself.

Purification: Visuddhi of the Citta

Complete renunciation requires the purification of the citta. Leaving household life without transforming the mind would amount to a change of circumstances rather than the fulfilment of the Liberation Path.

Arahanism places the eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha at the centre of this purification. Rāga encompasses worldly craving and attachment; dosa encompasses fear, anger, aversion, hatred, violence, and related forms of hostility; moha encompasses ignorance and delusion, including failure to understand the path beyond worldly bondage.

These defilements are not overcome merely by adopting the outward appearance of a renunciant. They must be recognized, restrained, weakened, and ultimately eradicated. Renunciant discipline provides the conditions for this work by reducing entanglement with worldly pursuits, cultivating concentration that induces Tapas, the primordial spiritual force, and directing this Tapas, time, energy, and attention toward purification.

Sīla establishes the discipline of conduct. Samādhi develops the concentration of the mind and induces Tapas. Paññā penetrates the nature of worldly conditioned existence and supports the abandonment of worldly attachment. These are not separate accomplishments pursued without relation to one another. They work together as the practical foundation for the purification of the citta.

The renunciant life is therefore a sustained commitment to transformation. Its measure is not the appearance of holiness, the possession of religious knowledge, or recognition by others. Its measure is the actual purification of the citta and the progressive release from the conditions that maintain worldly bondage.

Withdrawal from the World: Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā

Renunciation becomes effective through practice. Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā form the principal framework through which the practitioner withdraws from worldly entanglement and develops the conditions for liberation.

Sīla is more than a code of social respectability. In Arahanism, it is a progressive discipline of withdrawal. The practitioner learns to restrain bodily and verbal conduct, abandon activities that intensify defilement, and reduce dependence on worldly gratification. For the fully ordained renunciant, this discipline is embodied in the Vinaya and the obligations of the monastic life.

Samādhi directs the mind away from its habitual scattering among worldly objects and concerns. Through sustained training, the practitioner develops the concentration and the power of Tapas necessary for deeper examination and purification. Paññā then clarifies the nature of worldly conditioned existence, enabling the practitioner to recognize why worldly attachment cannot provide the ultimate freedom being sought.

The three work together. Without Sīla, the practitioner continues to feed the very entanglements from which liberation is sought. Without Samādhi, the mind remains unstable and vulnerable to its habitual patterns. Without Paññā, restraint and concentration do not by themselves complete the work of liberation.

Arahanism therefore treats the renunciant life as an integrated discipline rather than a collection of religious observances. Conduct, mental development, and wisdom must converge upon the same purpose: the cessation of worldly bondage.

Nibbāna-Dhātu: The Deathless Goal

The ultimate purpose of complete renunciation is not simply to become calmer, more virtuous, more detached, or better adapted to the conditions of the world. These qualities have their place in the training, but Arahanism directs the path toward a goal beyond worldly existence.

Arahanism understands Nibbāna-Dhātu as the Deathless realm, distinct from the conditioned universe and its governing conditions of arising, decay, and dissolution. Liberation therefore cannot be reduced to a psychological state, an experience of cosmic unity, or an improved way of living within the world. Its consummation is the release sought through the complete eradication of the defilements and the ending of bondage to worldly existence.

This is why complete renunciation is indispensable within Arahanism. If the goal is complete release, the whole discipline must be oriented toward that release. The practitioner cannot make continued participation in worldly life the final purpose while simultaneously treating transcendence of worldly bondage as the ultimate goal.

Renunciation does not mean that the practitioner must despise other people or abandon compassion. The cultivation of mettā, karuṇā, muditā, and upekkhā remains integral to the noble way. The renunciant withdraws from worldly entanglement in order to purify the citta, not to cultivate indifference or hostility toward beings.

The Total Commitment of the Renunciant

Arahanism is therefore the path of those who commit themselves to the entire discipline of liberation. Its essential orientation can be expressed through four interrelated commitments:

  • Realize independence — anissita: cease making worldly existence the foundation of ultimate security and seek freedom from worldly dependence.
  • Purify the citta — visuddhi: undertake the sustained eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha.
  • Withdraw from worldly bondage: cultivate Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā within the discipline of complete renunciation.
  • Realize the Deathless goal: direct the whole path toward Nibbāna-Dhātu, understood in Arahanism as beyond the conditioned universe.

These commitments describe one integrated way of life. Independence establishes its direction; purification transforms the citta; renunciant discipline gives the transformation its practical form; and the Deathless provides its ultimate goal.

The ninth mark affirms that the Liberation Path is ancient, universal, and open to all who sincerely seek it. The tenth clarifies what following that path to its consummation requires. Openness to the path does not remove the demands of the path. The opportunity may be offered broadly, but complete liberation requires the total commitment of renunciation.

Arahanism is not simply a philosophy of liberation or a practice for improving worldly life. It is the path of complete renunciation from the world, directed toward the complete release of the citta from worldly bondage and the attainment of the Deathless realm.
