title: Meditation Retreat Part 4
content:
The Arahanist Training for Arahantship

Samatha, Vipassanā, and the Liberation Path of Gautama

11. The Four Approaches as a Practical Framework for Our Retreat

The four approaches are not merely theoretical classifications. They provide a framework for understanding how meditation training can be adapted to the practitioner.

Our retreat uses this framework to guide instruction and practice.

For the Practitioner Who Needs Mental Stability

Some practitioners arrive with little experience of sustained meditation. Their attention is easily distracted, their minds are restless, and they may find it difficult to remain with a meditation object.

For them, the initial emphasis may be on samatha.

They learn to establish a stable posture, maintain attention, recognize distraction, and return patiently to the meditation object. The objective is to develop sufficient concentration for more sustained investigation.

Vipassanā is introduced and developed in relation to their growing stability.

For the Practitioner Who Relies Heavily on Reflection

Other practitioners have studied the Dhamma extensively or naturally approach meditation through analysis.

They may understand many principles but struggle to settle the mind.

For these practitioners, the training emphasizes the transition from conceptual investigation to direct meditation. They learn to recognize when further thinking is useful and when it has become an obstacle to concentration.

Samatha is developed as a necessary complement to their existing interest in vipassanā.

For the Practitioner Developing Both Together

Some practitioners can maintain a reasonable degree of concentration while investigating experience directly.

For them, samatha and vipassanā can be coordinated throughout the training.

Periods of concentrated meditation support the investigation of mental processes. The understanding developed through investigation helps the practitioner recognize and abandon distractions. Both practices deepen through continued cultivation.

For the Practitioner to be Fully Established in Their Higher Self / Soul-Spirit

They need to study the Dhamma intensively first, experience persistent agitation associated with spiritual inquiry and Gautama’s Dhamma.

They may be preoccupied with questions about liberation, repeatedly compare teachings, or become frustrated by their inability to resolve every uncertainty.

For them, instruction emphasizes the cultivation of inward stability, the reduction of unnecessary conceptual activity during meditation, and the development of samādhi.

Study and discussion remain available at appropriate times, but the practitioner learns to devote meditation periods to the actual training of the citta.

These approaches are not rigid categories into which every practitioner must permanently fit. A practitioner may move between them as training develops. The appropriate balance can change according to the practitioner's experience, concentration, understanding, and difficulties.

The purpose of individualized instruction is to support progress without losing sight of the common objective.

12. What to Expect During a Meditation Retreat

A meditation retreat offers an opportunity to experience a more concentrated form of training than is usually possible amid ordinary responsibilities.

The precise schedule and intensity of practice may vary according to the length of the retreat, the experience of the participants, and the guidance provided by the instructor. Nevertheless, the training can be organized around several complementary activities.

Meditation instruction introduces the relevant method, explains its purpose, and establishes a clear basis for practice. Participants learn how to approach their meditation object, recognize common obstacles, and adjust their practice appropriately.

Formal meditation provides sustained periods for developing samatha, vipassanā, or a coordinated combination of the two. Repeated practice allows participants to recognize habitual patterns of distraction and develop greater continuity of attention.

Dhamma instruction explains the principles underlying the training. Participants study the relationship between ethical discipline, concentration, vipassanā, renunciation, and liberation from worldly bondage.

Contemplation and reflection allow participants to examine how desire, aversion, and ignorance influence their lives. The purpose is not to become absorbed in abstract thinking but to develop an understanding that supports the practical work of meditation.

Periods of silence and simplicity reduce unnecessary stimulation and create opportunities for inward stability. By temporarily setting aside ordinary distractions, participants can observe their habits of attention and their dependence on external activity more clearly.

Teacher guidance helps participants understand their experiences without drawing premature conclusions. Meditation can involve unfamiliar sensations, changes in attention, periods of calm, and difficulties with restlessness. These experiences should be approached carefully and interpreted in relation to the purpose and method of practice.

A retreat is therefore not simply a period of sitting quietly. It is a structured opportunity to integrate ethical conduct, mental cultivation, contemplation, and instruction.

13. A Progressive Path: From Ethical Discipline to Liberation

Although AN 4.170 describes four approaches to Arahantship, a practical training program must also consider how practitioners prepare for sustained meditation.

For this reason, our training places the four approaches within the broader progression of the liberation path.

Stage One: Establishing Ethical Discipline

The practitioner begins by reducing conduct that reinforces worldly craving, aversion, and confusion.

Ethical discipline establishes a foundation of sense restraint and spiritual responsibility. It also helps reduce the remorse and agitation that can arise from harmful conduct.

For those undertaking more intensive renunciant training, discipline becomes progressively more comprehensive.

Stage Two: Simplifying Life and Cultivating Renunciation

The practitioner examines the habitual pursuit of sensory gratification, possessions, entertainment, recognition, and other worldly concerns.

The purpose is not to reject the world through hostility. It is to understand the role that worldly attachment plays in maintaining worldly bondage and to create the conditions for sustained spiritual cultivation.

A simpler life can provide more time and energy for meditation.

Stage Three: Developing Samatha

The practitioner establishes a regular meditation practice and develops the ability to remain with a chosen object.

Attention becomes more stable, distraction is increasingly recognized, and the mind develops the capacity for sustained concentration.

The degree of concentration required and the appropriate methods depend on the practitioner and the training undertaken.

Stage Four: Developing Vipassanā

The practitioner investigates the processes of experience and the movements of attraction, aversion, and ignorance.

The aim is to develop direct understanding of the conditions that sustain worldly bondage and to cultivate the vipassanā necessary for liberation from worldly bondage.

Stage Five: Coordinating Samatha and Vipassanā

As practice matures, samatha and vipassanā support one another.

The practitioner learns to cultivate concentration without becoming attached to it and to investigate experience without allowing investigation to degenerate into restlessness.

The training becomes increasingly integrated.

Stage Six: Deepening Samādhi and the Inward Establishment of the Citta

The practitioner continues to cultivate mental unification and inward stability.

For those following the fourth approach described in AN 4.170, particular importance is given to the transition from Dhamma-related agitation to the inward establishment of the citta into the Higher Self / Soul-Spirit.

Stage Seven: The Arising and Cultivation of the Liberating Path

The four approaches converge upon the central objective described by the sutta: the arising, development, and cultivation of the path through which the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies eliminated.

This final objective cannot be reduced to a prescribed number of meditation sessions or a fixed period of retreat.

A retreat can establish conditions for practice, deepen understanding, and help a practitioner overcome obstacles. The completion of the path requires the actual realization of liberation.

The progression outlined here is a practical training framework developed from the sutta's principles. It should not be mistaken for a claim that AN 4.170 itself prescribes these seven stages in this exact order.

14. Why the Monastic Path Is Central to Arahanism

Arahanism places Arahantship at the centre of its spiritual objective.

The training is therefore oriented toward a fundamental reorganization of life around worldly renunciation, meditation, and liberation from worldly bondage.

In our understanding, the full monastic life provides the most comprehensive institutional and practical framework for undertaking this work. The discipline of a bhikkhu or bhikkhunī establishes a way of life in which ethical conduct, renunciation, sense restraint, study, meditation, and the cultivation of vipassanā can be integrated into a single commitment.

This does not mean that every person attending a meditation retreat must immediately undertake ordination. A retreat can serve as an introduction to the path, an opportunity to deepen an existing practice, or a setting in which a practitioner examines the possibility of a more comprehensive commitment.

Participants may arrive with different levels of experience and different capacities for renunciation. The appropriate starting point will vary.

Nevertheless, the direction of the training remains clear.

For those who aspire to the complete renunciant path, a retreat can be an important step toward understanding the discipline, responsibilities, and practical demands of monastic life.

For those already undertaking renunciant training, it can provide an opportunity to strengthen concentration, deepen vipassanā, and renew their commitment to liberation from worldly bondage.

Our aim is to cultivate a training environment in which the path to Arahantship can be studied seriously and practiced systematically.

15. The Ultimate Objective: Beyond Temporary Peace

Meditation can produce many benefits.

It can reduce agitation, improve concentration, support emotional balance, and help practitioners respond more wisely to difficult circumstances. These benefits are meaningful, but they do not exhaust the purpose of the liberation path.

Arahanism directs attention toward a more fundamental question: Can the underlying causes of worldly bondage be completely eradicated?

A person may learn to manage anger without eradicating the underlying tendency toward aversion. One may learn to control sensual desire without eliminating the deeper inclination toward attachment. One may develop profound concentration without overcoming the ignorance that maintains worldly bondage.

The training must therefore continue beyond the acquisition of useful psychological skills. Samatha and vipassanā needed to be developed to understand experience and the processes that maintain worldly attachment.

Samādhi establishes the mind in unification.

Sīla provides the ethical foundation and progressive withdrawal, while renunciation creates the conditions for sustained spiritual cultivation.

Together, these dimensions support the development of the path leading to Arahantship.

The goal is not to become dependent upon a particular meditative experience, nor to accumulate spiritual achievements while leaving the underlying causes of worldly bondage intact.

The goal is liberation from worldly bondage.

The Venerable Ānanda's teaching in AN 4.170 reminds us that the decisive work is the development of the path through which the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies eliminated.

This is the standard toward which our training is directed.

16. Begin the Training

The path leading to Arahantship requires more than curiosity about spiritual matters. It requires sustained practice, ethical discipline, sense restraint, patience, and a willingness to examine the deepest habits through which the mind remains attached to worldly existence.

A meditation retreat offers an opportunity to begin or deepen this work within a structured environment.

Participants are introduced to the principles of samatha and vipassanā, learn to cultivate mental stability, investigate the movements of craving and aversion, and develop a clearer understanding of the relationship between meditation and liberation.

Those with previous meditation experience can use the retreat to strengthen their practice and examine obstacles that may have limited their progress. Those who are new to meditation can establish a foundation for continued training.

For practitioners considering the monastic path, the retreat also provides an opportunity to learn about the role of ethical discipline, simplicity, renunciation, and sustained meditation in the life of a renunciant.

Progress should be approached with patience and discernment. Unusual experiences, temporary happiness, and periods of concentration should not be mistaken for final realization. The practitioner must continue to cultivate the path and examine whether the underlying tendencies that sustain worldly bondage are genuinely being weakened and abandoned.

Our invitation is to approach the training with sincerity and a clear understanding of its purpose.

The purpose of meditation is not merely to make life within the world more comfortable. It is to cultivate the path leading beyond worldly bondage.

Through ethical discipline, sense restraint, samatha, vipassanā, we undertake the training directed toward the ultimate objective of Arahanism: Arahantship.

The Arahanist Order of Canada offers meditation training for those who wish to understand and practice the liberation path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

title: AN 4.170 Yuganaddha Sutta Part 2
content:
The Four Paths Leading to Arahantship  (catuhi maggehi arahatta-patti)

AN 4.170 Yuganaddha Sutta: In Conjunction

Bāhiya Sutta (Udāna 1.10) is the most famous example in the entire Pāḷi Canon of the 4th path described in the Yuganaddha Sutta (AN 4.170)—where a practitioner whose mind is stirred/agitated suddenly turns completely inward (ajjhattameva), aligns with the higher self / soul-spirit (adhi-attā), and attains immediate Arahantship. Here is how the Bāhiya Sutta connects directly to this dimensional breakthrough and liberation:

1. The Agitation and Immediate Turning Within

Bāhiya Dārucīriya was desperately seeking true liberation. After traveling across India without rest, he rushed up to the Buddha in Savatthī while the Buddha was walking for alms. Bāhiya repeatedly begged for instruction on the spot.

His mind was intensely urgent—a prime example of dhammaddhacca (spiritual urgency/restlessness regarding the Dhamma).

The Buddha gave him the concise instruction on sense-perception: "Diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṁ bhavissati, sute sutamattaṁ bhavissati, mute mutamattaṁ bhavissati, viññāte viññātamattaṁ bhavissati..."

"In what is seen, there will be merely the seen; in the heard, merely the heard; in the sensed, merely the sensed; in the cognized, merely the cognized..."

2. Disentangling the Higher-Dimensional Spirit from Lower Aggregates

The core of the Buddha's teaching to Bāhiya is the absolute separation between lower-dimensional, worldly phenomena and the true, guarded soul-spirit: "Tato tvaṁ, Bāhiya, na tena. Yato tvaṁ, Bāhiya, na tena, tato tvaṁ, Bāhiya, na tattha. Yato tvaṁ, Bāhiya, na tattha, tato tvaṁ, Bāhiya, nevīdha na huraṁ na ubhayantare. Esevanto dukkhassā’ti."

"When, Bāhiya, for you there is merely the seen in the seen, merely the heard in the heard... then, Bāhiya, you are not 'by that' (na tena). When you are not 'by that' (na tena), you are not 'in that' (na tattha). When you are not 'in that' (na tattha), then you are neither here, in this current life/realm (na idha), nor next, in the next existence or hereafter (na huraṁ), nor in between the two (na ubhayantare). Just this is the end (anto) of dukkha."

The Dimensional Shift:

  • The Worldly Aggregates (Anattā): The sights, sounds, thoughts, and sensory processes belong to this physical world (loka). They are transient, subject to cause and effect, and are not our soul-spirit, nor part of our soul-spirit, nor belonging to our soul-spirit.
  • Not 'In That' (na tattha)/ Not 'By That' (na tena): Bāhiya is instructed to immediately stop identifying his true spirit (attā) with these lower-dimensional sensory inputs.
  • Neither Here, Nor Next (Nevīdha na huraṁ): The purified Citta drops all spatial/dimensional location within the physical or mental universe. It is no longer bound "here" (in this current life/realm) or "next" (in the next existence or hereafter, next reincarnation).

3. Immediate Realization of Arahantship

Upon hearing this brief instruction, Bāhiya’s mind was instantly freed from all taints right on the spot without remaining clinging (anupādāya āsavehi cittaṁ vimucci). He attained complete Arahantship in a moment.

Because he completely severed attachment to the lower-dimensional aggregates, when he was killed shortly after by a cow with a young calf, his final physical body dissolved.

The Buddha then uttered the solemn solemnity (udāna) regarding Bāhiya's ultimate transcendence: "Yattha āpo ca pathavī, tejo vāyo na gādhati... Tadaññāāya munino, monena brāhmaṇo; Rūpā rūpā ca muccati, dukkhā muccati sabbaso."

"Where water (āpo), earth (pathavī), fire (tejo), and air (vāyo) find no footing (na gādhati)... Having fully known this (tadaññāya) for himself, the muni, the true Brāhmaṇa through pure inner awareness (monena); From form (rūpa) and the formless (arūpa) he is completely freed (muccati); from dukkha he is freed in every way (sabbaso).”

mona is ñāṇa: higher direct knowledge, paññā: wisdom, and vijjā: transcendent vision.

Munino: For the muni who has quieted the restless lower mind.

Monena: Through pure inner awareness / silent sagehood—not merely because he stopped talking, but because his Citta turned completely inward (ajjhattameva), disengaged from the four elements (āpo, pathavī, tejo, vāyo), and stood firm in its unconditioned core.

Rūpā Arūpā Ca Muccati "Freed from Form and the Formless": The Arahant's Citta drops all clinging to both physical/material planes (rūpa-loka) and subtle non-material planes (arūpa-loka).

This verse highlights the final threshold of an Arahant - Exiting the Universe:

  1. Transcending the Four Elements: Physical manifestations and material aggregates (anattā) are built entirely of the four elements (pathavī, āpo, tejo, vāyo). When the Buddha states that these elements find no footing (na gādhati), it signifies that the unconditioned core of Citta has completely disengaged from material density.
  2. Beyond Form and Formless: By transcending both rūpa (dense 3D material worlds) and arūpa (subtle higher worlds), the Arahant is no longer bound to any realm within the law of death and rebirth (saṁsāra).

Summary Connection

The Bāhiya Sutta is the ultimate real-world demonstration of collapsing the distance between lower sensory distraction and inner alignment with the higher self / soul-spirit (ajjhatta) to realize total liberation.

Why This Instruction Leads Directly to Arahantship

"In the seen, there shall be merely the seen; in the heard, there shall be merely the heard; in the sensed, there shall be merely the sensed; in the cognized, there shall be merely the cognized..."

This brief formula is the absolute core mechanism of liberation. It strips away the entire psychological mechanism that creates ego-clinging and worldly bondage:

  1. Severing the Conceptual Overlay: Normally, when sensory contact occurs, the uninstructed mind immediately projects lower-dimensional narratives onto it: "I am seeing this, this is mine, I like this, I hate this." That extra step creates the delusion of a localized ego interacting with external objects.
  2. Stopping at Raw Perception: By keeping perception strictly as "merely the seen" (diṭṭhamattaṁ), the process stops before identification or craving can ignite. The physical and mental aggregates (rūpa, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhārā, viññāṇa) are recognized as transient phenomena belonging strictly to this physical world (loka) and operating under cause and effect—they are non-self (anattā).
  3. The Immediate Consequence (The Passage Following the Formula): The Buddha immediately follows this by explaining what happens when you stop identifying with sensory aggregates:

"When for you there is merely the seen in the seen... then you are not 'by that' (na tena). When you are not 'by that', you are not 'in that' (na tattha). When you are not 'in that', then you are neither here, nor next, nor in between the two (nevīdha na huraṁ na ubhayantare). Just this is the end of dukkha."

How This Relates to the Higher Self / Soul-Spirit (Adhi-Attā)

When understood in a structural, multidimensional framework, this instruction is the precise key that frees the higher self (adhi-attā) from lower-dimensional entanglement:

[ Lower 3D Realm / Aggregates (Anattā) ]            [ Inward Core / Unconditioned (Adhi-Attā) ]

Sights, Sounds, Thoughts, Sensations   <===|===> Pure, Guarded Citta

("Merely the seen, merely the heard")      |        ("Not 'in that', not bound 'here or next")

                                        CUT HERE

  • Disentangling the Spirit from the Lower Aggregates: The lower-dimensional aggregates (the 5 khandhas) are the raw sensory streams—the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, sense-generated consciousness. They are not our Adhi-Attā, nor part of our Adhi-Attā, nor belonging to our Adhi-Attā.
  • Refusing Lower-Dimensional Identification: As long as awareness believes "I am this body, I am this thought, I am this feeling," the spirit/soul is trapped "in that" (tattha) dense, 3D lower plane.
  • Standing Firm in the Inner Axis (Ajjhattameva): By reducing sensory inputs to mere phenomena (mattaṁ), awareness disengages from external objects (bahiddhā). The core awareness retreats completely inward into its own elevated, uncorrupted higher self/ soul-spirit (adhi-attā).
  • Complete Transcendence: Once the citta is no longer "in that" (the lower sensory stream), it is freed from location "here or next." It is guarded (rakkhitatto), isolated from lower-dimensional worldly defilements (rāga, dosa, moha), and completely ready to pass through the final threshold into the Nibbāna-Dhātu.

By cutting off lower-dimensional identification in a single moment, Bāhiya’s awareness detached from all worldly aggregates, aligned instantly with its deepest internal axis (ajjhattameva), and achieved immediate Arahantship.

Commentary: Ajjhatta in Jain Tradition

In Jain literature, both the term adhyātma (Prakrit: ajjhattha) and the title Arhat / Arihant (Prakrit: Arahanta) occupy a central position. Examining how Jainism treats these concepts reveals profound structural parallels—as well as important doctrinal differences.

1. Adhyātma in Jain Literature: The Internal Science of the Soul

In Jainism, adhyātma (adhi + ātman) literally means "pertaining to the ultimate inner Soul/Self (jīva or ātman)". It forms an entire branch of Jain philosophy and mysticism known as Adhyātma-śāstra (the discipline of inward realization of Higher Self/Soul).

A. The Core Meaning: Turning Inward Away from Bahir-ātman

Jain texts explicitly divide the human experience into three progressive stages of the self (most famously in Ācārya Kundakunda's Samayasāra and Śubhacandra's Jñānārṇava), division of the soul into Bahir-ātman, Antar-ātman, and Param-ātman is systematically laid out in Acharya Pujyapada’s Samādhitantra (5th century CE) and elaborated in Acharya Yogindu’s Paramātmaprakāśa (6th century CE) and Śubhacandra’s Jñānārṇava (11th century CE).

Acharya Pujyapada, Samādhitantra (Verse 4): Bahir-antaḥ paraś-ca iti tridhā-ātmā sarva-dehiṣu, Bahir-ātmā śarīrādau jātātma-bhrāntir, Āntaraḥ citta-doṣātma-vibhrāntiḥ, Paramātmeti kīrtyate.

In all embodied beings (sarva-dehiṣu), the self (ātmā) is threefold (tridhā): external (bahir), internal (antaḥ), and supreme (paraś-ca iti). The external self (bahir-ātmā) is the misconception of selfhood (jātātma-bhrāntir) regarding the physical body and external objects (śarīrādau). The internal self (āntaraḥ) is [the state free from] the delusion of selfhood (ātma-vibhrāntiḥ) regarding mental defilements (citta-doṣa); [the third] is proclaimed as the supreme self (paramātmeti kīrtyate).

Acharya Pujyapada, Samādhitantra (Verse 7): Bahir-ātmā samūḍhātmā, Kalevaram ahetukam swam eva abhimanyeta, Swa-para-avedakaḥ.

The external self (bahir-ātmā) is a deeply deluded self (samūḍhātmā). Through illusion (bhrāntyā), lacking knowledge (avedakaḥ) of what belong to oneself (swa) and external/foreign (para), it falsely considers (abhimanyeta) the transient (Ahetukam) physical body (kalevaram) to be verily (eva) its own self (swam).

Ācārya Kundakunda, Samayasāra (Gāthā 186): aham edam udo cedi ya ajjhavasāṇaṁ karei jo jīvo | so parabhāvaṁ ṇecchai ṇiyattade so a aṇṇāṇā ||

Which soul (jo jīvo) makes the mental delusion (ajjhavasāṇaṁ karei) that 'I am this, this is mine' (aham edam udo cedi ya)... That soul does not desire foreign modifications (so parabhāvaṁ ṇecchai), and that one turns away (so a ṇiyattade) from ignorance (aṇṇāṇā).

Ācārya Yogindu Deva, Paramātmaprakāśa (Gāthā 11): ṇimmala-ṇāṇa-sahāu jiu kamma-malehiṁ vimukku | so paramappā ṇicchaeṇa jo samāhihiṁ ṭhiu ||

The soul (jiu) whose inherent nature is spotless, pure direct knowledge (ṇimmala-ṇāṇa-sahāu), completely freed from karmic stains (kamma-malehiṁ vimukku)... Which stands firm in Samādhi (jo samāhihiṁ ṭhiu), that one, in absolute reality (so ṇicchaeṇa), is the supreme ātma (paramappā).

Ācārya Yogindu Deva, Yogasāra (Verse 1): jiu ṇimmalu ṇāṇa-sahāu jiu kamma-malehiṁ vimukku | appi-chahi jo maṇu dharai so bohiya paramappā ||

The soul (jiu) whose inherent nature is spotless, pure direct knowledge (ṇimmalu ṇāṇa-sahāu jiu), and completely freed from karmic stains (kamma-malehiṁ vimukku)... Whosoever holds their mind (jo maṇu dharai) in desireless contemplation of that Self / Soul ātma (appi-chahi), that awakened one knows the supreme ātma (so bohiya paramappā).

B. Major Jain Texts Dedicated to Adhyātma

Ācārya Haribhadra Sūri, Yogabindu (Verse 31): adhyātmaṁ bhāvanā dhyānaṁ samatā vṛttisaṁkṣayaḥ | mokṣeṇa yojanādyogo eṣa śreṣṭho yathottaram ||

The Higher Self / Soul (adhyātmaṁ), worldly manifestation / becoming (bhāvanā), Jhana meditation (dhyānaṁ), equanimity (samatā), and the complete destruction of mental fluctuations (vṛtti-saṁkṣayaḥ)— From joining (yojanāt) with liberation (mokṣeṇa), this (eṣa) is yoga (yogaḥ); each successive stage is superior (śreṣṭho yathottaram) to the preceding one.

  • Upādhyāya Yaśovijaya (17th century CE): Authored the famous Adhyātmasāra ("The Essence of Adhyātma"), where adhyātma is defined as the internal purification of the mind (manaḥśuddhi) and direct experience (anubhava) of the pure self.

Mahāpadhyāya Yaśovijaya Gaṇi, Adhyātmasāra (1.1–4): ātmānam adhikṛtyaiṣā pravṛttir adhyātmam ucyate | manaḥśuddhyādikā sā ca jñeyā samyag-vimuktaye || ragādimatamattyāgaḥ śuddhir mana ity ucyate | sā caiva svātmano bhāvaḥ śuddha-saṁvittilakṣaṇaḥ || cittair viśuddhair manaso virago, virāgataḥ syād anubhūtir ātmanaḥ | tato bhavet kevala-bodha-lakṣmiḥ, sa caiva mokṣaḥ sa sukhaṁ tad eva || anubhavasi yadātvam ātmānaṁ svatantraṁ, parama-pada-samīsthaṁ śuddha-bodha-svarūpam | tada iha sakala-duḥkhaiḥ mucyase saṁsārāt, labhase ca nija-mūlaṁ śāśvataṁ brahma-dhāma ||

This (eṣā) directed activity (pravṛttir) having taken the Soul / ātmā (ātmānam) as its supreme subject (adhikṛtya) is declared as the Higher Self / Soul (adhyātmam ucyate). And (ca) that (sā), having mind-purification as its primary quality (manaḥ-śuddhy-ādikā), must be understood (jñeyā) for complete, right liberation (samyag-vimuktaye).

The complete abandonment of the intoxicated conviction of attachment and related defilements (rāgādi-mata-māt-tyāgaḥ) is declared as the purification of the mind (śuddhir manasa iti ucyate). And that [purification] is verily (sā caiva) the intrinsic state of one's own Self / Soul (svātmano bhāvaḥ), defined by pure, direct consciousness (śuddha-saṁvitti-lakṣaṇaḥ).

Through fully purified minds (cittair viśuddhair), detachment of the mind (manaso virāgo) [occurs]; From detachment (virāgataḥ), the direct experience (anubhūtir) of the Soul (ātmanaḥ) arises (syād). From that (tato), the splendor (lakṣmiḥ) of omniscience knowledge (kevala-bodha) arises (bhavet); and that verily is liberation (sa caiva mokṣaḥ), that precisely is ultimate bliss (sa sukhaṁ tad eva).

When (yadā) you (tvam) directly experience (anubhavasi) the Soul (ātmānaṁ) as self-dependent (svatantraṁ), situated at the supreme state (parama-pada-samīsthaṁ), whose intrinsic form is pure direct knowledge (śuddha-bodha-svarūpam)... Then (tadā), here (iha), from all sufferings (sakala-duḥkhaiḥ) and from saṁsāra (saṁsārāt) you are released (mucyase), and (ca) you attain (labhase) one's own primordial root (nija-mūlaṁ), the eternal/deathless (śāśvataṁ) brahma-dhāma.

  • Acharya Pujyapada & Yogindu Dev: Works like Samādhitantra and Yogasāra frame adhyātma as the direct contemplation of the uncorrupted soul, severing the bond with karmic particles.

Ācārya Pūjyapāda, Samādhitantra (Verse 14): ātmānam ātmany evābhyasya samyag-jñāna-mayena hi | prāpnoty ātmani samyag-jñānaṁ karmāṇi kṣapayaty api ||

Having repeatedly contemplated (abhyasya) the Soul (ātmānam) in the Soul (ātmani) precisely (eva) through [a mind] consisting of right direct knowledge (samyag-jñāna-mayena), indeed (hi)... One attains (prāpnoti) right direct knowledge (samyag-jñānaṁ) in the Soul (ātmani), and also (api) exhausts / severs (kṣapayati) the karmic particles (karmāṇi).

(Verse 26-27) Pūjyapāda details how contemplating the soul as uncorrupted and distinct from body/karma acts as the cutting tool that severs the karmic bond.

dehāntara-gatenāpi dehe 'smin nātmanā saha | ekatvaṁ bhāvyate 'yuktāiḥ kṣīrodakavat ātmanaḥ || pṛthag-bhāvaṁ tu sañcintya deho 'yaṁ nātmanā saha | dhyāyed ātmānam evāgre karma-bandha-vinirmokṣāya ||

But (tu) having deeply contemplated (sañcintya) the distinct nature (pṛthag-bhāvaṁ)—that this physical body (deho 'yaṁ) is not (na) together with (saha) the Soul (ātmanā)... One should principally meditate (dhyāyed) upon the Soul (ātmānam) alone (eva), for the complete severance (vinirmokṣāya) from the bond of karmic particles (karma-bandha).

Ācārya Yogindu Deva, Yogasāra (Verse 12): kamma-malehiṁ vimukku jiu ṇaü saṁsāre hoi | appa-jhaṇeṇaṁ jo ṭhiu kammaṁ ḍahai so i ||

The soul (jiu) completely freed (vimukku) from karmic stains (kamma-malehiṁ) is not (ṇaü) in saṁsāra (saṁsāre hoi). Which [soul] stands firm (jo ṭhiu) through meditation on the ātman (appa-jhaṇeṇaṁ), that one verily (so i) burns up / severs (ḍahai) karmic matter (kammaṁ).

2. Does Adhyātma Lead to "Arahantship" for Jains?

Yes, directly. In Jainism, establishing oneself in adhyātma (turning inward away from material aggregates) is the exact path that leads to becoming an Arihant (Pāḷi/Prakrit: Arahanta; Sanskrit: Arhat).

However, the Jain definition of an Arihant / Arahant has its own precise technical framework:

A. The Definition of a Jain Arihant

In Jainism, an Arihant (literally translated traditionally as "destroyer of the inner enemies"—namely krodha [anger], māna [pride], māyā [deceit], and lobha [greed]) is a living human being who has attained Kevala Jñāna (omniscience/infinite direct awareness/knowledge).

  • In the sacred Jain Ṇamōkāra Mantra, the very first bow is offered to the Arihants:

Ṇamō Arihantāṇaṁ "I bow to the Liberated Worthy Ones"

  • An Arihant has destroyed the four destructive karmas (ghātiyā karmas) through total internal absorption in ātma.

Ācārya Kundakunda, Niyamasāra (Gāthā 159): jo jhādi paramappāṇiṁ ghādi-kamma-kkhayaṁ kareṁti so hodi | kevali-aṇaṁta-ṇāṇī aṇaṁta-suha-daṁsaṇo jīvo ||

Which soul (jo jīvo) meditates upon (jhādi) the supreme Soul/ātman (paramappāṇiṁ), that one performs (kareṁti) the complete destruction of the destructive karmas (ghādi-kamma-kkhayaṁ)... That soul becomes (so hodi) an omniscient one (kevali), possessing infinite direct knowledge (aṇaṁta-ṇāṇī), infinite bliss, and infinite direct perception (aṇaṁta-suha-daṁsaṇo).

B. The Two Stages of Final Liberation in Jainism

While an Arihant is fully liberated from inner defilements, Jainism distinguishes between two final states:

  1. Arihant / Kevalin (Embodied Liberation): The Arahant remains in a physical body, teaching the path until their remaining non-destructive physical karmas (aghātiyā karmas) exhaust naturally.
  2. Siddha (Disembodied / Ultimate Transcendence): When the physical body dissolves at death, the Arahant sheds the final physical frame and ascends to the Siddhashila (the top of the universe) as a disembodied, pure, eternal soul (Siddha).

title: 8 Precepts Uposatha
content:
Uposatha Eight Precepts

For Upāsaka and Upāsikā Eight Precepts
One Day a WeekThe First Step on the Path to Arahantship

Gahattha Sila Aradhana • Laity Precepts Requesting

Ahaṁ bhante, tisaraṇena saddhim, Pañcama sīlaṁ, dhammaṁ yācāmi, anuggahaṁ katvā sīlaṁ detha me, bhante.

Bhante, may I request the five precepts along with the three refuges. Having shown compassion, please grant me the precepts, Bhante.

Dutiyam'pi, Ahaṁ bhante, tisaraṇena saddhim, Pañcama sīlaṁ, dhammaṁ yācāmi, anuggahaṁ katvā sīlaṁ detha me, bhante.

For the second time, may I request the five precepts along with the three refuges. Having shown compassion, please grant me the precepts, Bhante.

Tatiyam'pi, Ahaṁ bhante, tisaraṇena saddhim, Pañcama sīlaṁ, dhammaṁ yācāmi, anuggahaṁ katvā sīlaṁ detha me, bhante.

For the third time, may I request the five precepts along with the three refuges. Having shown compassion, please grant me the precepts, Bhante.

[Bhante] Yam ahaṁ vadāmi, taṁ vadehi (vadetha) 

Whatever I say, you (all) repeat after me.

[Student] Āma Bhante. 

Yes, Bhante.

Tisarana - Taking Three Refuges

Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhasa (X3)

Homage to the Blessed One, the Supreme Arahant, the Rightly and Fully Awakened One!

Buddhaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

Dhammaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

Saṁghaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

I go to the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha as my refuge.

Dutiyampi Buddhaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

Dutiyampi Dhammaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

Dutiyampi Saṁghaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

For the second time, I go to the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha as my refuge.

Tatiyampi Buddhaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

Tatiyampi Dhammaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

Tatiyampi Saṁghaṁ Saranaṁ Gacchāmi.

For the third time, I go to the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha as my refuge.

[Bhante] Tisaraṇa Gamanaṁ Sam-Puṇṇaṁ.

Taking refuge is complete.

[Student] Āma Bhante

Yes, Bhante.

Aṭṭhaṅga Uposatha Sīla • Uposatha Eight Precepts

1. Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi

I undertake the training step to abstain from destroying the life force.

2. Adinnā-dānā veramanī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi

I undertake the training step to abstain from taking what is not given.

3. Abrahma-cariyā veramanī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi

I undertake the training precept to abstain from sexual activity and to maintain celibacy.

4. Musā-vādā veramanī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi

I undertake the training step to abstain from false speech.

5. Surā-meraya-majja-pamā-daṭṭhānā veramanī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi

I undertake the training step to abstain from fermented drink, distilled liquor, and intoxicating substances—the ground of spiritual laxity.

6. Vikāla-bhojanā veramaṇī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi

I undertake the training step to abstain from taking food at improper times.

7. Nacca-gīta-vādita-visūka-dassanā mālā-gandha-vilepana-dhāraṇa-maṇḍana-vibhūsanaṭṭhānā veramaṇī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi

I undertake the training step to abstain from dancing, singing, playing music, and distractive shows and music; and wearing garlands, perfumes, cosmetics, for the purpose of beautification and ornamentation.

8. Uccā-sayana mahā-sayanā veramaṇī, sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi.

I undertake the training step to abstain from high beds and luxurious beds.

[Bhante] Tisaranena saddhim Aṭṭhaṅga Samannāgatam Uposatha sīlaṁ dhammam sādhukam surakkhitam katvā Appamādena sampādethabbam.

Maintaining well the Uposatha Eight Precepts that lead to Samannā together with the Three Refuges, strive on with diligence.

[Student] Āma Bhante.

Yes, bhante

Patthanā & Punnanumodana • Aspirations & Sharing of Merits

Idaṁ me puññam, āsavakkaya vahaṁ hotu,

Idaṃ me silam, nibbānassa paccayo hotu;

Mama puñña-bhāgaṁ, sabbasattānaṁ bhājemi,

Te sabbe me samaṁ, puñña-bhāgaṁ labhantu.

May this merit of mine be conducive to the destruction of the āsavas (defilements). May this virtue of mine be a (supportive) condition for Nibbāna. I share my merits done today with all beings. May all those beings get an equal share of the merits shared by me.

title: 8 Precepts Uposatha Part 2
content:
One Day a Week: The First Step on the Path to Arahantship

The Eight Uposatha Precepts mark the transition from ethical living to spiritual practice. By setting aside one day a week for celibacy, simplicity, and meditation, an ordinary layperson takes the first deliberate step towards renunciation and the liberation taught by Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Every Great Journey Begins with a First Step

You do not need to abandon your family, leave your occupation, or enter a monastery to begin walking the path towards liberation. You can begin where you are, with the life you already have, by setting aside one day a week for spiritual training.

In Arahanism, we recognize a fundamental distinction between living an ethical human life and undertaking the systematic training of a spiritual practitioner.

The Five Precepts establish the foundation of ethical living. They teach us to refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants that undermine restraint. By observing these precepts, we learn to live responsibly, reduce harm, and establish a foundation of wholesome conduct.

This is an important beginning. Yet ethical living and the pursuit of liberation are not identical undertakings.

A person may live an admirable life, maintain good relationships, fulfil social responsibilities, and contribute to the well-being of others while remaining deeply attached to sensual pleasures, possessions, relationships, and the changing circumstances of the world.

The path to Arahantship requires a further step: the deliberate training of the mind to become increasingly independent of these worldly conditions.

The Uposatha Eight Precepts mark the beginning of this transition.

By undertaking them on Uposatha days (about once a week), you temporarily step away from the ordinary patterns of household life and enter a period devoted to sense restraint, meditation, and the cultivation of inner happiness.

The commitment may be small in terms of time, but its direction is profound. You are no longer merely practising how to live ethically within the world. You are beginning to practise how to free the mind from its worldly bondage.

One day a week can become the beginning of a completely different way of life.

From the Five Precepts to the Eight: A Change in Direction

The Five Precepts and the Uposatha Eight Precepts serve different purposes within the progressive training of Sīla.

The Five Precepts establish ethical restraint within ordinary lay life. They protect life, property, relationships, truthfulness, and mental clarity. A person observing them can continue to participate in family life, employment, economic activities, and ordinary social relationships.

The Eight Precepts introduce a more intensive discipline.

The most significant distinction concerns sexual activity. The third of the Five Precepts requires abstention from sexual misconduct, whereas the corresponding precept in the Eight Precepts requires complete abstinence from sexual activity for the duration of the observance. This is the temporary undertaking of brahmacariya, the celibate life of spiritual training.

The remaining precepts further simplify the practitioner's relationship with food, entertainment, adornment, and physical comfort.

Taken together, these disciplines establish a temporary environment of renunciation. They reduce the activities through which the mind habitually seeks gratification and create an opportunity to investigate the relationship between sensual desire, happiness, and worldly attachment.

This is why Arahanism identifies the Eight Precepts as the beginning of yogi training.

Here, yogi is the ancient title for practitioners who deliberately undertakes mental discipline and spiritual cultivation—one who practices yoga to realize union with the higher, divine reality and transcend human limits, a systematic development of the mind. By returning to ancient Arahanist training, we as Arahanists today step directly back into this original, time-tested tradition.

For someone who has never undertaken such training, this is a significant change.

Instead of allowing every day to follow the familiar rhythm of work, consumption, entertainment, and sensual gratification, the practitioner reserves a day for a different purpose.

For that day, spiritual development takes priority.

Why One Day a Week Matters

Modern life encourages continuous participation in the external world. We work to obtain material security, eat for nourishment and enjoyment, seek entertainment to relieve boredom, and maintain relationships that provide companionship and affection. Many of these activities are entirely ordinary, and ethical household life has its rightful place.

The difficulty arises when the mind becomes so accustomed to these sources of satisfaction that it cannot easily remain content without them.

When does the mind experience happiness without entertainment? Can it remain peaceful without seeking another sensory pleasure? Can it experience joy without depending upon the approval of others, the possession of desirable things, or the fulfilment of every passing desire?

These are not merely philosophical questions. They are questions that can be investigated through direct practice.

The Eight Uposatha Precepts create the conditions for this investigation.

By observing them for one day, you voluntarily interrupt familiar habits. You abstain from sexual activity, refrain from entertainment and adornment, eat according to the prescribed discipline, and avoid luxurious beds and seats. You simplify your activities and dedicate more time to meditation, contemplation, and the cultivation of wholesome mental states.

You begin to discover how the mind responds when its usual sources of stimulation are temporarily withdrawn.

At first, the absence of familiar pleasures may make you more aware of your habitual desires. You may notice how frequently the mind anticipates its next enjoyment or seeks something external whenever it becomes restless.

Rather than immediately satisfying these impulses, you learn to observe them, exercise restraint, and redirect attention towards spiritual cultivation.

Gradually, you have an opportunity to discover another possibility: the mind can develop gladness, joy, and contentment through cultivation itself.

The purpose of the weekly observance is not simply to give up worldly pleasures for a day. It is to learn how to cultivate happiness without depending so heavily upon them.

One day of restraint becomes one day of discovery. Repeated over weeks and months, that discovery can begin to change your understanding of happiness and the direction of your life.

The Eight Precepts: A Practical Introduction to Renunciation

The Eight Precepts are not arbitrary restrictions. Within Arahanist training, each contributes to the gradual reduction of worldly dependence upon sensual gratification and the establishment of conditions favourable to meditation. It also draws the mind away from worldly law of survival.

1. Refraining from Killing – Non-harming and kindness

The practitioner undertakes to refrain from taking life.

This precept cultivates respect for living beings and establishes a foundation of non-harming. It also encourages the practitioner to examine hostility, carelessness, and the impulses that lead to harmful conduct.

A mind committed to non-harming is better positioned to develop samadhi and goodwill.

2. Refraining from Stealing - fear and insecurity, the belief that one must acquire and possess more in order to feel safe

The practitioner undertakes to refrain from taking what has not been given.

This discipline develops honesty, restraint, and contentment. It challenges the assumption that satisfaction must be obtained by acquiring whatever one desires.

Beneath the desire to take what belongs to others, there may be a deeper sense of insecurity: the fear of not having enough, the need to accumulate material resources to guarantee one's future, or the belief that possessing more will provide greater safety and protection against uncertainty. When the mind is governed by such fears, it may continually seek additional possessions and material security, never feeling that it has enough.

The practice of this precept therefore goes beyond respecting the property of others. It invites the practitioner to examine the fear and craving that drive the pursuit of possession. True security cannot be established simply by accumulating more of what belongs to the world, because material conditions are themselves subject to change. Through ethical restraint and the cultivation of contentment, the practitioner gradually learns to loosen the connection between happiness and possession, developing greater inner independence from the demands of material security.

3. Refraining from Sexual Activity: Brahmacariya

This precept marks the most decisive difference between the Five Precepts and the Eight Precepts.

For the duration of the observance, the practitioner undertakes complete abstinence from sexual activity. This is a temporary commitment to brahmacariya, introducing the discipline of celibacy that becomes central to sustained renunciation.

Sexual desire can be a powerful influence upon human attention, intention, relationships, and the pursuit of pleasure. Human body is saturated with sexual hormones. By voluntarily suspending sexual activity, the practitioner creates an opportunity to observe sensual desire without continually acting upon it.

The purpose is not hostility towards the body or contempt for human relationships. It is the development of freedom from habitual dependence upon the innate human design for sexual and sensual gratification.

Within the Arahanist framework, this discipline begins the deliberate loosening of the mind's attachment to the sexual and sensual sphere, kāma-dhātu.

A day of celibacy is therefore more than a temporary prohibition. It is an introduction to a different relationship with desire.

4. Refraining from False Speech

The practitioner undertakes to refrain from lying.

Truthfulness establishes integrity between intention, speech, and conduct. It also encourages greater awareness of the impulses behind speech, including the desire to gain approval, avoid responsibility, or manipulate circumstances.

When speech becomes more restrained and truthful, the mind has fewer reasons to become entangled in deception and its consequences.

5. Refraining from Intoxicants

The practitioner undertakes to abstain from intoxicants that lead to zeallessness (pamāda).

Mental clarity is essential to meditation and insight. Intoxicants that impair judgement and restraint work against the purpose of this training.

By maintaining clarity, the practitioner supports the development of concentration, self-observation, and disciplined conduct.

6. Refraining from Eating After Midday

The practitioner undertakes to abstain from eating after midday, according to the traditional discipline.

This precept simplifies the daily relationship with food. Instead of eating whenever pleasure, habit, or appetite suggests, the practitioner follows a defined boundary.

Food remains necessary for sustaining the body, but its role becomes more deliberate. The practitioner learns to distinguish nourishment from the repeated pursuit of taste and gratification.

This discipline also serves a deeper purpose: the deliberate reduction of happiness derived from external sources. Eating is not only a means of sustaining the body; it is also a familiar source of sensory pleasure and emotional satisfaction. By abstaining from food after midday, the practitioner temporarily relinquishes this recurring source of enjoyment and learns to remain content without continually satisfying the desire for taste and gratification.

Beneath the habitual pursuit of food for pleasure may lie a deeper dependence upon external experiences to relieve boredom, soothe discomfort, or produce a feeling of satisfaction. When the mind repeatedly seeks happiness through eating, it becomes accustomed to looking outward whenever it wants to feel better. The practitioner uses this discipline to recognize and gradually loosen that dependence.

Rather than seeking further gratification through food, the practitioner can redirect attention towards meditation and the cultivation of pāmojja (gladness), pīti (spiritual joy), and sukha (inner happiness and well-being). Through the development of Samādhi, the practitioner begins to discover the possibility of happiness arising from mental cultivation rather than from continually satisfying bodily desires.

The resulting simplicity can also support alertness and leave more time for meditation. The purpose is not to reject food or deny the body's legitimate needs, but to reduce dependence upon eating as a source of pleasure and to cultivate a mind that can experience contentment without continually seeking gratification from the external world.

7. Refraining from Entertainment and Adornment

The practitioner undertakes to refrain from dancing, singing, playing music instruments, distractive shows and music, and wearing garlands, perfumes, cosmetics, for the purpose of beautification and ornamentation.

Ordinary life provides many opportunities to stimulate the senses. Entertainment occupies attention, while adornment can reinforce the desire to enhance one's appearance and receive admiration.

During Uposatha observance, the practitioner deliberately steps away from these activities.

The aim is not to condemn music, art, or beauty in every circumstance. It is to discover what happens when the mind no longer relies upon sensory stimulation for its regular supply of enjoyment.

By reducing these distractions, the practitioner makes room for silence, contemplation, and the development of inner gladness.

8. Refraining from High and Luxurious Beds

The practitioner undertakes to refrain from high and luxurious beds.

This discipline encourages simplicity and reduces the pursuit of bodily luxury. The practitioner learns to be content with reasonable comfort rather than making increasingly refined comfort a condition of well-being.

The precept also expresses a broader principle: spiritual training becomes more effective when daily life is organized around what supports cultivation rather than what continually gratifies preference.

Together, these eight disciplines create a day in which sense restraint, simplicity, and spiritual development take priority.

title: 8 Precepts Uposatha Part 3
content:
One Day a Week: The First Step on the Path to Arahantship

Discovering Inner Happiness: Pāmojja, Pīti, and Sukha

A common misunderstanding of renunciation is that it consists primarily of giving things up.

If a practitioner abandons familiar pleasures but develops no alternative source of well-being, the experience may seem like nothing more than deprivation. Such an approach overlooks an essential dimension of the Arahanist path: the cultivation of inner happiness.

Human beings naturally seek happiness and avoid distress. The question is not simply whether we should abandon pleasure, but whether our happiness must remain dependent upon external conditions or not.

Sensual enjoyment depends upon circumstances. Food must be available, entertainment must be encountered, desirable objects must be obtained, and relationships must unfold according to conditions that cannot always be controlled.

Even when these experiences are pleasant, they change. Their availability is uncertain, and the satisfaction they provide does not necessarily bring an end to craving.

The Eight Precepts invite the practitioner to investigate another source of well-being: happiness arising through sense restraint, mental cultivation, and the development of concentration.

In the Buddhist vocabulary adopted by Arahanism, several important terms describe aspects of this process.

Pāmojja is gladness or mental delight. It can arise when the mind recognizes the value of wholesome conduct and experiences the lightness associated with living in accordance with one's spiritual commitment.

Pīti is rapture or spiritual joy. It can arise as the mind becomes increasingly engaged in meditation and less occupied with its usual distractions.

Sukha is happiness, ease, or well-being. In meditative development, it can accompany the settling and unification of the mind.

These qualities are not identical, but they help illuminate the positive dimension of spiritual discipline. Sense restraint can establish conditions in which wholesome joy becomes possible, and that joy can support further cultivation.

The practitioner therefore does not simply endure a day without familiar pleasures. They learn to use that day to develop the mind.

When the Eight Precepts are observed together with meditation, contemplation, and the cultivation of wholesome mental states, the practitioner can begin to experience the satisfaction of a simpler and more inwardly directed life.

This is a crucial preparation for deeper renunciation.

One Day of Samatha and Vipassanā

The objective is not to eliminate happiness, but to loosen dependence upon worldly gratification while developing the inner conditions for deeper and more stable well-being.

Uposatha observance becomes especially meaningful when the Eight Precepts are combined with systematic meditation.

Arahanist training emphasizes the complementary development of samatha and vipassanā: the cultivation of tranquillity and concentration, and the development of insight into the nature of worldly experience.

Samatha practice trains the mind to become calmer, more stable, and more unified. Rather than allowing attention to follow every desire, memory, worry, or sensory distraction, the practitioner learns to remain steadily with a chosen meditation subject.

Depending upon the method being practised, this may involve mindfulness of breathing or another suitable meditation object.

As attention becomes more stable, the practitioner has an opportunity to experience a mind less scattered by habitual stimulation. This stability supports the development of inner gladness, joy, and well-being, and prepares the mind for deeper concentration.

Vipassanā complements this development by investigating experience with wisdom. The practitioner learns to observe arising and passing phenomena, recognize their conditioned nature, and understand the limitations of relying upon them for lasting satisfaction.

The two forms of training serve different but complementary functions. Tranquillity develops stability; insight develops understanding. A settled mind provides a stronger basis for investigation, while insight helps prevent concentration and pleasant meditative experiences from becoming ends in themselves.

During an Uposatha day, the practitioner can devote time to both.

The day need not be complicated. It can include observance of the Eight Precepts, periods of sitting meditation, walking meditation, quiet contemplation, study of the Dhamma, and appropriate rest.

The important point is that these activities are no longer incidental to the day. They become its central purpose.

From Part-Time Practitioner to Full-Time Training

Instead of filling every available moment with external activity, the practitioner creates the conditions to understand the mind directly.

Repeated regularly, this practice can help establish a more disciplined relationship with attention, desire, and happiness.

The weekly observance of the Eight Precepts is designed to make the beginning of yogi training accessible to people who continue to live as householders.

You may have family responsibilities, employment, financial obligations, and other commitments that prevent you from undertaking full-time spiritual practice. These circumstances do not prevent you from beginning.

Choose an Uposatha day, or another suitable day dedicated to spiritual practice, and observe the Eight Precepts sincerely. Arrange your activities so that meditation and contemplation receive your attention. Reduce unnecessary stimulation, simplify your meals, and allow the day to become an opportunity for inward development.

The Five Precepts — Ethical Layperson

Then repeat the practice.

The Eight Uposatha Precepts — Part-Time Yogi

Over time, you may discover that one day a week is no longer sufficient for the depth of training you wish to undertake. You may begin to extend the Eight Precepts to additional days or adopt a more sustained discipline, according to your circumstances and readiness.

The Eight Precepts Observed Daily — Full-Time Yogi

Within the Arahanist framework, the progressive structure of Sīla can be understood as follows:

The Ten Precepts — Novice Renunciation

The Pātimokkha — Full Monastic Renunciation

The practitioner establishes wholesome conduct while continuing to participate in ordinary household life.

The practitioner begins systematic spiritual training by undertaking temporary celibacy, greater sense restraint, simplicity, and dedicated meditation, often one day a week.

A Small Commitment with a Greater Purpose

The practitioner extends this discipline into daily life, establishing a sustained commitment to brahmacariya and mental cultivation while remaining a layperson.

Through pabbajjā, the practitioner enters novice renunciation as a sāmaṇera or sāmaṇerī, undertaking a more comprehensive discipline and a life separated from ordinary household and economic responsibilities.

Through upasampadā, a qualified candidate enters full monastic ordination as a bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, undertaking the applicable monastic discipline.

These stages represent a progressive deepening of commitment. Each requires greater restraint and reorganizes more of the practitioner's life around the pursuit of liberation.

The Uposatha Eight Precepts occupy a particularly important position because they provide the first practical experience of this progression. They allow a person to test and develop a renunciant orientation before making a more comprehensive commitment.

The purpose is not to rush through the stages. It is to begin sincerely, understand what the training requires, and allow experience to clarify one's aspiration.

Begin Your Uposatha Practice

One day a week may appear insignificant beside the demands of ordinary life. Yet a regular spiritual discipline can gradually change the way a person understands time, happiness, desire, and freedom.

Each observance provides an opportunity to step away from familiar habits and examine them. Each period of meditation provides an opportunity to develop the mind. Each deliberate act of restraint strengthens the capacity to live according to a chosen purpose rather than every passing impulse.

Over time, the practitioner may begin to recognize that the external world, with all its pleasures and opportunities, cannot provide an unchanging foundation for happiness.

This recognition is not a reason to become bitter towards the world. It is an invitation to investigate the nature of worldly attachment and to discover whether a different kind of freedom is possible.

The Eight Precepts offer a practical beginning.

You do not have to resolve every question about renunciation before taking the first step. You can begin by observing one day, developing mindfulness, practising meditation, and examining the effects of restraint upon your own mind.

Let the practice itself teach you.

If you find that the discipline supports greater clarity, contentment, and spiritual purpose, continue. If your aspiration deepens, gradually extend your commitment. Allow your understanding to develop alongside your practice.

The path to Arahantship is not completed in a single day. Nevertheless, a single day can mark the beginning of a life directed towards that goal.

Arahanism invites lay practitioners to begin with the Uposatha Eight Precepts as an introduction to systematic spiritual training.

Set aside one day a week. Undertake the precepts with sincerity. Refrain from sexual activity, simplify your relationship with food and bodily comfort, abstain from entertainment and adornment, and devote time to meditation and contemplation.

Throughout the day, observe your mind. Notice its desires, its restlessness, and its dependence upon familiar pleasures. Develop tranquillity through meditation and investigate experience through insight. Cultivate wholesome gladness and learn to appreciate the simplicity of a day devoted to spiritual practice.

You need not begin perfectly. You need to begin with a clear intention and a willingness to train.

The Five Precepts establish the foundation of ethical human life. The Uposatha Eight Precepts take the next step: the beginning of the yogi's path.

One day a week, you step back from ordinary sensual life and turn towards inner cultivation. One day a week, you begin to train not merely to live well within the world, but to understand the possibility of liberation from worldly attachment.

This is the significance of Uposatha in Arahanism.

It is a small beginning, but it points towards a much greater destination: the progressive development of Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, culminating in the complete liberation of an Arahant.

Begin with one day. Practise sincerely. Let the first step lead you towards the Deathless.

title: 10 Precepts
content:
Ordination Guidelines & Protocol

Sāmaṇera / Sāmaṇerī Novice Ordination

Arahanist Order of Canada

Introduction

Pabbajjā marks the beginning of formal monastic life. Through this ordination, a candidate leaves the ordinary household way of life and undertakes the discipline of a novice renunciant.

The purpose of Pabbajjā extends beyond wearing the robes or adopting a new religious identity. It is a commitment to a life directed toward liberation from worldly bondage: abandoning unnecessary worldly concerns, cultivating virtue, developing concentration, investigating the nature of worldly existence, and following the path leading toward Arahantship.

The Sāmaṇera or Sāmaṇerī undertakes the Three Refuges and the Ten Training Precepts, places themselves under the guidance of a preceptor and teacher, and begins systematic training in monastic conduct, Dhamma, and meditation.

The ordination ceremony should therefore be conducted with dignity, composure, and a clear understanding of its spiritual significance. Every stage—from the candidate's initial preparation to the final instructions—should help establish the foundation for a life of renunciation.

These guidelines establish a consistent ceremonial sequence for novice ordination within the Arahanist Order of Canada. They are intended to guide candidates, preceptors, assisting monastics, and those responsible for preparing the ordination gathering.

Pabbajjā: Restoring the Meaning of Renunciation

Arahanism officially translates the Pāli term Pabbajjā (Sanskrit: Pravrajyā) as Renunciation, rejecting the conventional English rendering "going forth" as inadequate to communicate the full religious significance of this decisive spiritual undertaking.

Pabbajjā marks the renunciation of household existence and the beginning of a life devoted to spiritual purification and liberation. It signifies leaving behind domestic life, worldly attachments, and ordinary household responsibilities to undertake the disciplined renunciant path. Although "going forth" reflects the term's literal etymological expression, it describes departure without adequately conveying the profound commitment to renunciation that defines the practice.

This terminological restoration forms part of Arahanism's wider critique of traditional commentarial interpretations and modern academic scholarship, whose translations and interpretive frameworks have, in Arahanism's assessment, contributed to obscuring the centrality of renunciation in Gautama's liberation teaching. The reduction of liberation to psychological well-being, emotional management, or freedom from negative mental states further diminishes the original objective: liberation from worldly bondage through the complete eradication of rāga, dosa, and moha.

Within Arahanist Training, Pabbajjā — Renunciation marks the decisive transition from household life into the renunciant discipline. It is the threshold of a spiritual quest directed towards the purification of citta, the cessation of the conditions sustaining renewed existence, and the attainment of Arahantship.

The official Arahanist rendering is therefore unequivocal: Pabbajjā means Renunciation. This is a declaration of terminological restoration in service of the liberation teaching of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Read the Full article
Restoring the True Meaning of Pabbajjā

Part I. Preparation for Ordination

1. Understanding the Commitment

Before requesting Pabbajjā, a candidate should receive instruction concerning the purpose and responsibilities of novice life.

The candidate should understand that renunciation involves more than changing clothing or residing in a monastery. It requires a sincere willingness to simplify one's life, observe the Ten Training Precepts, accept guidance, and devote oneself to spiritual development.

The candidate should be prepared to undertake:

  • The Three Refuges as the foundation of spiritual commitment.
  • The Ten Training Precepts governing novice conduct.
  • Training under the guidance of a preceptor and teacher.
  • The study of Dhamma and the practice of meditation.
  • A life of simplicity, sense restraint, contentment, and disciplined conduct.
  • The gradual development of the qualities necessary for progress toward Arahantship.

The preceptor should ensure that the candidate has a reasonable understanding of these commitments before the ordination date is confirmed.

2. Personal Responsibilities and Readiness

Before ordination, the candidate should review and settle responsibilities that may conflict with monastic life.

These may include:

  • Family and dependent-care responsibilities.
  • Employment, business, and financial commitments.
  • Outstanding debts, legal proceedings, or other unresolved obligations.
  • Ownership or management of property, investments, and possessions.
  • Necessary consent or authorization, including parental or guardian consent where applicable.
  • Health considerations that may affect the candidate's ability to participate in and sustain monastic training.

The candidate should discuss relevant circumstances honestly with the preceptor. The purpose of this preparation is to ensure that the decision to renounce is responsible, informed, and compatible with the candidate's circumstances and the applicable requirements.

Any eligibility restrictions or required permissions should be reviewed before the ceremony. Where the candidate's circumstances require additional consideration, the preceptor should resolve the matter before confirming the ordination.

3. Confirmation of the Ordination

Once the candidate has been accepted for training and the necessary preparations have been completed, the candidate and preceptor should agree upon the date, place, and arrangements for the ceremony.

The preceptor should confirm:

  1. The candidate's readiness for novice life.
  2. The availability of the preceptor and any assisting monastics.
  3. The preparation of the robes, alms bowl, and other necessary requisites.
  4. The arrangement of the ordination space.
  5. The availability of the Pāli recitations and ceremonial instructions.
  6. The arrangements for the candidate's immediate training following ordination.

The ceremony should take place in a clean, quiet, and suitably prepared setting. The atmosphere should support reverence, concentration, and reflection.

4. Required Requisites

The following items should be prepared before the ceremony:

  • A complete set of novice robes.
  • An alms bowl.
  • A suitable tray or arrangement for offerings.
  • White clothing for the candidate before ordination.
  • A clean and appropriate space for the ceremony.
  • A printed or otherwise accessible copy of the Pāli recitations.
  • Any additional requisites considered necessary by the preceptor.

The assisting monastics should check that the robes and other requisites are ready before the candidate enters.

5. Preparation of the Candidate

On the day of ordination, the candidate should have the head and beard shaved, as appropriate to the tradition and circumstances, and change into clean white clothing.

White clothing represents the candidate's condition before taking on the robes of renunciation. The candidate should approach the ceremony with humility and a sincere intention to begin a disciplined spiritual life.

The candidate should carry the prepared set of robes on the forearms, with the hands joined in a gesture of respect when appropriate.

Before entering the gathering, the candidate should be reminded of the ceremonial sequence and the importance of following the preceptor's instructions attentively.

Part II. The Pabbajjā Ceremony

6. Entrance and Initial Homage

The candidate enters the gathering carrying the robes and approaches the preceptor.

The candidate places the robes to the left and the offering tray to the right, or follows the arrangement directed by the preceptor. The candidate then presents the offerings to the preceptor and pays homage three times using the five-point prostration, with the forehead, two forearms, and two knees touching the floor.

After paying homage, the candidate remains kneeling, takes the robes onto the forearms again, and joins the hands respectfully in preparation for requesting Pabbajjā.

The preceptor should allow sufficient time for the candidate to settle physically and mentally before beginning the recitations.

7. Request for Pabbajjā Ordination

The candidate requests ordination three times.

Candidate:

Okāsa, ahaṃ, bhante, pabbajjaṃ yācāmi.

Permit me, Bhante. I request Pabbajjā ordination.

Dutiyam'pi, ahaṃ, bhante, pabbajjaṃ yācāmi.

For the second time, Bhante, I request Pabbajjā ordination.

Tatiyam'pi, ahaṃ, bhante, pabbajjaṃ yācāmi.

For the third time, Bhante, I request Pabbajjā ordination.

The candidate then makes the principal request for renunciation, repeated three times.

Candidate:

Sabba-dukkha-nissaraṇa-nibbāna-sacchi-karaṇatthāya, etaṃ kāsāvaṃ datvā pabbājetha maṃ, bhante, anukampaṃ upādāya.

For the release from all dukkha and for the purpose of directly realizing Nibbāna, please give me these saffron robes and ordain me, Bhante, out of compassion.

Second request:

Dutiyam'pi, sabba-dukkha-nissaraṇa-nibbāna-sacchi-karaṇatthāya, etaṃ kāsāvaṃ datvā pabbājetha maṃ, bhante, anukampaṃ upādāya.

For the second time, for the release from all dukkha and for the purpose of directly realizing Nibbāna, please give me these saffron robes and ordain me, Bhante, out of compassion.

Third request:

Tatiyam'pi, sabba-dukkha-nissaraṇa-nibbāna-sacchi-karaṇatthāya, etaṃ kāsāvaṃ datvā pabbājetha maṃ, bhante, anukampaṃ upādāya.

For the third time, for the release from all dukkha and for the purpose of directly realizing Nibbāna, please give me these saffron robes and ordain me, Bhante, out of compassion.

After the requests, the candidate places the robes before the preceptor as directed.

8. Instruction in the Three Refuges and the Purpose of Renunciation

The preceptor explains the significance of the Three Refuges and the responsibilities of novice life. The candidate should be reminded that the robes symbolize a commitment to renunciation and spiritual training.

The preceptor should explain that Pabbajjā begins a course of disciplined practice. Its purpose is to establish the conditions for the cultivation of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, leading toward the eradication of defilements and the realization of liberation.

The preceptor then introduces the Taca Pañcaka Kammaṭṭhāna, the meditation on five bodily constituents traditionally taught at ordination.

The Taca Pañcaka Kammaṭṭhāna

The candidate repeats each word after the preceptor, first in the forward order and then in reverse order.

Forward order: Kesā - Head hair. Lomā - Body hair. Nakhā - Nails. Dantā - Teeth. Taco - Skin.  

Reverse order: Taco - Skin. Dantā - Teeth. Nakhā - Nails. Lomā - Body hair. Kesā - Head hair.

The preceptor should explain the purpose of this contemplation in an accessible manner, introducing the examination of the body as a foundation for disenchantment with physical appearance and the development of insight.

The candidate should repeat the words attentively and learn to recollect them as part of subsequent training.

9. Receiving the Robes

After teaching the contemplation, the preceptor removes the appropriate shoulder cloth (aṃsa) from the robe set and places it over the candidate's head, covering the left shoulder according to the local ceremonial custom.

The preceptor returns the remaining robes and explains how they are to be worn.

The candidate receives the robes respectfully, keeps the hands joined where appropriate, and withdraws from the ceremonial area according to the preceptor's directions. If required by the established custom of the gathering, the candidate backs away on the knees before standing and proceeding to the place designated for changing.

An assisting monastic accompanies the candidate and provides help with putting on the robes.

10. Reflection on the Use of the Robes

While putting on the robes, the candidate recites the reflection on the proper use of monastic clothing.

Paccavekkhaṇa: Reflection on the Robes

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevāmi, yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāya, uṇhassa paṭighātāya, ḍaṃsa-makasa-vātātapa-siriṃsapa-samphassānaṃ paṭighātāya, yāvadeva hirikopīna-paṭicchādanatthaṃ.

Reflecting wisely, I use the robes only to protect myself from cold and heat, from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping creatures, and for the purpose of covering the parts of the body that should be concealed.

This reflection establishes the proper attitude toward the robes. They are requisites for a life of renunciation, not ornaments for personal display. The novice should learn to use them with gratitude, restraint, and understanding.

After dressing, the candidate returns to the gathering, pays homage to the Saṅgha as directed, and approaches the preceptor to request the Three Refuges and Ten Training Precepts.
