Human civilization suddenly appears extraordinarily fragile.

Individual existence becomes almost infinitesimal against cosmic vastness.

Actor William Shatner famously described his brief journey beyond Earth's atmosphere not as joyful enlightenment but as an encounter with overwhelming grief and existential emptiness.

Rather than discovering comforting transcendence, he confronted the stark contrast between Earth's vibrant biosphere and the immense lifeless darkness surrounding it.

The emotional impact deeply unsettled him.

These contrasting responses illustrate an important psychological principle.

Expanded perception does not automatically produce comfort.

Sometimes greater awareness reveals beauty.

Sometimes it reveals vulnerability.

Sometimes it reveals both simultaneously.

Consciousness Beyond Evolutionary Design

One interpretation emerging from both astronaut testimony and consciousness research proposes that the human brain evolved primarily for terrestrial survival rather than comprehensive perception.

Natural selection favors efficiency.

Organisms need not perceive every aspect of reality.

They need only perceive enough to survive and reproduce.

Consequently, consciousness may function much like a reducing valve.

Rather than opening perception completely, it selectively filters overwhelming quantities of information into a manageable stream relevant for everyday existence.

Spaceflight temporarily disrupts many of those filtering mechanisms.

Gravity disappears.

Environmental familiarity dissolves.

The sensory hierarchy reorganizes itself.

The brain adapts accordingly.

Some researchers interpret the resulting experiences as purely neurobiological consequences of unusual environmental conditions.

Others suggest that removing terrestrial constraints allows consciousness to register aspects of reality ordinarily filtered from awareness.

The evidence remains inconclusive.

The question, however, remains deeply fascinating.

The Alien Obelisk as an Artificial Overview Effect

Viewed through this lens, the alien obelisk in Disclosure Day may be understood not merely as a communication device but as an artificial catalyst for expanded consciousness.

Rather than physically transporting its user into space, the obelisk temporarily restructures the nervous system in ways analogous to radical sensory reorganization.

Ordinary cognitive boundaries dissolve.

New informational channels become accessible.

Neural architecture reorganizes itself.

The difference, of course, is that Noah Scanlon weaponizes this expanded access.

Instead of encouraging broader perception, he exploits direct neurological connection for authoritarian control.

The same mechanism capable of expanding consciousness becomes an instrument for suppressing autonomy.

This inversion represents one of the film's central warnings.

Technological advances affecting consciousness will not automatically liberate humanity.

Like every previous technological revolution, they will amplify the intentions of those who possess them.

A New Frontier of Human Evolution

Ultimately, the relationship between spaceflight and consciousness invites us to reconsider one of the oldest assumptions in neuroscience—that ordinary waking awareness represents the complete range of human perception.

History suggests otherwise.

Meditative traditions have long reported expanded states of awareness.

Astronauts have described transformative cognitive experiences.

Cold War researchers investigated anomalous perception.

Modern neuroscience increasingly recognizes the remarkable plasticity of the human brain under novel environmental conditions.

Disclosure Day synthesizes these diverse threads into a single proposition.

Perhaps higher perception is not foreign to humanity.

Perhaps it has always existed as latent potential, hidden beneath the immense sensory demands of ordinary terrestrial life.

If that is true, then the next great frontier of exploration may not lie solely among distant stars.

It may lie within consciousness itself.

Space exploration would therefore become more than a journey across physical distance. It would become an experiment in human perception—a gradual discovery of how consciousness behaves when removed from the sensory architecture under which it evolved. In this context, the alien obelisk is not simply an advanced extraterrestrial machine. It symbolizes the possibility that consciousness, once liberated from its ordinary biological constraints, may perceive reality in ways that challenge our deepest assumptions about the nature of mind, perception, and human potential.

8. Observer Consciousness, the TPJ, and the Reduction-Valve Theory

If Disclosure Day asks how technology might eventually interface with human consciousness, it also raises a deeper and more fundamental question that has occupied philosophers, neuroscientists, and contemplative traditions for centuries:

What is consciousness in the first place?

Is consciousness merely the electrical activity produced by billions of interconnected neurons?

Or is the brain better understood as an interface—a biological system that organizes, filters, and expresses a deeper field of awareness?

The psychic interrogation of Jane Blankenship never explicitly answers this question. Instead, Spielberg constructs the entire sequence around a fascinating possibility: consciousness itself remains remarkably stable even while the brain's motor systems are externally manipulated.

Throughout the interrogation, Jane continues thinking.

She continues feeling.

She continues making moral judgments.

She continues resisting.

What changes is not consciousness itself.

What changes is the neurological machinery through which consciousness expresses itself physically.

This distinction leads naturally into one of the most intriguing intersections between modern neuroscience, astronaut psychology, and theories of expanded human perception: the relationship between observer consciousness, the temporoparietal junction, and what philosopher Aldous Huxley famously described as the "reduction-valve" theory of the brain.

The Emergence of the Observer

One of the defining characteristics of Jane's experience is the gradual separation between awareness and bodily action.

She no longer identifies completely with her movements.

Instead, she begins witnessing them.

Her body reaches.

Her body walks.

Her body acts.

Yet internally she remains distinct from those actions.

She watches herself becoming an unwilling participant inside her own nervous system.

This transformation from participant to observer represents one of the oldest descriptions of altered consciousness found across philosophical traditions.

Ordinary consciousness is immersive.

We become absorbed in thoughts.

We become absorbed in emotions.

We become absorbed in bodily sensations.

There is little distinction between awareness and experience.

Under extraordinary circumstances, however, this relationship can change dramatically.

Awareness begins observing experience rather than becoming completely identified with it.

Instead of saying,

"I am moving,"

one begins experiencing,

"I am watching movement occur."

This subtle but profound shift lies at the center of Jane's psychic resistance.

Although Scanlon succeeds in commandeering her motor system, he never fully captures the observing awareness witnessing the occupation.

The observer remains free even while the body is constrained.

The Temporoparietal Junction and the Sense of Self

Modern neuroscience has identified one brain region particularly relevant to this discussion: the temporoparietal junction (TPJ).

Located where the temporal and parietal lobes converge, the TPJ plays a central role in integrating sensory information into a coherent experience of embodied selfhood.

It continuously combines signals from vision, hearing, touch, proprioception, and the vestibular system.

From this enormous flow of information, the brain constructs one extraordinarily convincing illusion:

"This body is me."

Under ordinary circumstances, this integration operates seamlessly.

The boundaries between self and environment remain remarkably stable.

You know where your body begins.

You know where the surrounding world ends.

Your conscious awareness appears firmly localized behind your eyes.

Yet neuroscience has repeatedly demonstrated that this localization is surprisingly flexible.

Electrical stimulation of the TPJ has, in some experimental settings, been associated with reports resembling out-of-body experiences.

Disruptions involving vestibular integration, sensory conflict, or neurological injury can alter one's sense of bodily ownership.

Individuals may temporarily experience themselves as observing the body from an unusual perspective.

Others report feeling strangely detached from ordinary physical identity.

Importantly, these observations do not establish that consciousness literally leaves the body.

They demonstrate something equally significant.

Our ordinary experience of self-location depends upon ongoing neural integration.

The sense of "being here" is actively constructed by the brain.

Jane Blankenship and the Neurological Observer

Viewed through this framework, Jane's experience becomes particularly fascinating.

The alien obelisk appears to interfere primarily with descending motor pathways rather than with the neural architecture supporting conscious awareness.

Consequently, the integration ordinarily binding intention to movement begins to fracture.

Her body continues acting.

Her awareness ceases identifying completely with those actions.

Instead, she becomes an observer.

From a cinematic perspective, Spielberg repeatedly reinforces this transformation through careful visual composition.

Close-up shots linger on Jane's eyes.

The audience rarely experiences the scene from Scanlon's perspective.

Instead, viewers remain psychologically aligned with Jane's witnessing consciousness.

Her body becomes almost another character within the scene.

Something observed.

Something no longer entirely identical with the observing mind.

This distinction explains why the sequence feels so psychologically disturbing.

The horror lies not merely in bodily control.

It lies in the forced separation between observer and participant.

The Reduction-Valve Theory

Long before modern neuroscience developed sophisticated brain imaging technologies, philosopher Aldous Huxley proposed an influential hypothesis regarding consciousness.

Rather than viewing the brain primarily as a producer of consciousness, Huxley suggested that it might function as a reducing valve.

According to this idea, reality contains vastly more information (multidimensional) than human beings can process consciously.

The nervous system therefore performs an essential filtering function.

Instead of revealing everything,

it excludes almost everything.

Only information directly relevant to biological survival reaches ordinary awareness.

From this perspective, the brain resembles a selective gatekeeper rather than a generator.

Consciousness may be inherently broader than ordinary waking experience suggests.

The brain simply narrows it into a manageable stream.

Although Huxley's theory remains philosophical rather than scientifically established, it has continued influencing discussions within psychology, neuroscience, contemplative studies, and consciousness research.

Remarkably, Disclosure Day appears to adopt a fictional model strikingly compatible with this perspective.

The Alien Obelisk as a Reduction-Valve Override

The screenplay repeatedly suggests that the human brain already possesses dormant neural pathways capable of extraordinary perception.

The limitation is biological.

Humans evolved without the necessary neurological infrastructure to broadcast or receive information across non-local distances.

The alien obelisk does not manufacture consciousness.

It temporarily bypasses ordinary biological restrictions.

It widens the aperture.

It increases bandwidth.

It exposes neural processes normally inaccessible to conscious awareness.

In effect, the obelisk functions as a technological override for the brain's ordinary filtering mechanisms.

Instead of processing only local sensory information, the nervous system suddenly gains access to entirely new streams of data.

Unfortunately, Noah Scanlon weaponizes this expanded access.

Rather than allowing Jane to explore broader awareness, he occupies the newly opened channel.

The very mechanism capable of expanding perception becomes an instrument of domination.

From Participant to Witness

Throughout human history, contemplative traditions have repeatedly emphasized the importance of cultivating observer consciousness.

Meditative disciplines often encourage practitioners to witness thoughts without attachment.

Witness emotions without identification.

Observe bodily sensations without immediately reacting.

Whether interpreted spiritually or psychologically, the objective remains remarkably consistent.

Move from participant...

to witness.

Interestingly, Jane undergoes precisely this transformation—but involuntarily.

Her ordinary identification with bodily movement collapses under technological pressure.

The observer emerges not through meditation but through neurological crisis.

Yet once established, that observer becomes the foundation of resistance.

She no longer mistakes externally imposed movements for authentic expressions of herself.

This distinction preserves her psychological integrity.

She refuses internally to identify with actions she never truly chose.

The Observer Sensation in Spaceflight

This same separation between observer and participant appears repeatedly in reports from astronauts returning from long-duration space missions.

Many describe living life "a half-step outside themselves."

Ordinary activities seem strangely automatic.

Walking.

Opening doors.

Holding objects.

The body performs familiar tasks while consciousness temporarily occupies a more detached perspective.

From a neurological standpoint, this phenomenon likely reflects the brain's ongoing recalibration following prolonged exposure to microgravity.

The body schema requires reconstruction.

Sensorimotor integration must be rebuilt.

Awareness temporarily assumes a more observational role while the nervous system relearns terrestrial movement.

Whether interpreted purely neurologically or more philosophically, the experience illustrates an important principle.

Observer consciousness appears naturally under conditions in which ordinary bodily integration becomes unstable.

The Expansion of Perception

Some researchers have suggested that when the brain devotes fewer computational resources to maintaining ordinary bodily orientation, additional perceptual capacity may become available.

Reports from astronauts, sensory deprivation studies, contemplative practitioners, and certain altered states frequently describe remarkably similar themes.

Enhanced pattern recognition.

Expanded spatial awareness.

Greater psychological detachment.

A diminished sense of rigid personal boundaries.

Whether these experiences represent purely internal neurophysiological phenomena or access to broader informational structures remains debatable.

Disclosure Day deliberately leaves this ambiguity intact.

The film neither confirms nor denies extraordinary interpretations.

Instead, it invites viewers to ask whether human perception may ordinarily operate under far narrower conditions than consciousness itself permits.

The Brain as Receiver Rather Than Generator

The reduction-valve theory naturally leads toward another provocative possibility.

Suppose the brain functions less like a computer generating consciousness and more like a receiver organizing it.

Modern technology already provides useful analogies.

A radio does not create broadcasts.

It receives them.

A television does not manufacture transmitted signals.

It decodes them.

Damage the receiver...

and reception changes.

The broadcast may remain unchanged.

Applied to consciousness, this analogy suggests that neurological changes may alter how awareness is expressed without necessarily explaining consciousness itself.

Although contemporary neuroscience generally interprets mental activity as emerging from brain function, the "receiver" hypothesis continues attracting philosophical interest because it offers an alternative framework for understanding extraordinary conscious experiences.

Disclosure Day appears to adopt a fictional variation of this model.

The alien obelisk neither creates Jane's consciousness nor replaces it.

Instead, it establishes a second communication pathway into the existing receiver.

The nervous system begins decoding two streams simultaneously.

One originates internally.

The other arrives externally.

Conflict becomes inevitable.

The Final Sanctuary

Ultimately, the concept of observer consciousness explains why Jane never truly loses herself despite Scanlon's overwhelming technological advantage.

Her body becomes occupied.

Her movements become manipulated.

Her nervous system becomes contested territory.

Yet the witnessing awareness observing these events remains psychologically coherent.

This observer preserves memory.

It preserves conscience.

It preserves moral identity.

Most importantly, it preserves the possibility of resistance.

Even when every outward action appears controlled, the observer refuses surrender.

It continues witnessing.

It continues evaluating.

It continues searching for a pathway toward liberation.

In this respect, Disclosure Day presents a remarkably hopeful vision beneath its technological dystopia. The film suggests that consciousness possesses a depth exceeding the mechanisms through which it ordinarily expresses itself. Technology may gain extraordinary access to the nervous system. It may influence perception, movement, and behavior. Yet there remains interior dimensions of awareness that cannot be reduced simply to electrical circuitry.

Whether one interprets this observer as a product of sophisticated neural integration, an emergent property of complex cognition, or something that transcends current scientific explanation, its narrative function remains unmistakable.

It is the final sanctuary of human freedom.

And as long as that witnessing consciousness endures, no technology—however advanced—can achieve complete dominion over the human mind.

9. Disclosure Day as a Modern Allegory of Consciousness, Freedom, and Technological Power

At first glance, Disclosure Day appears to belong comfortably within the tradition of extraterrestrial conspiracy thrillers. It contains crashed UFOs, classified military programs, powerful defense corporations, government secrecy, and recovered alien technology. These elements naturally invite comparisons with decades of science-fiction cinema concerned with offworld civilizations and deep state conspiracies.

Yet to understand Disclosure Day merely as another alien invasion narrative is to overlook its deeper achievement.

The extraterrestrials are not the true subject of the film.

Neither is Roswell.

Nor secret government laboratories.

Nor advanced technology itself.

The true subject of Disclosure Day is human consciousness.

The alien obelisk is simply the narrative instrument through which Spielberg explores one of the oldest philosophical questions in human history:

What makes a human being truly free?

The answer offered by the film is striking.

Freedom is not ultimately political.

It is not primarily technological.

Nor is it merely physical.

Freedom begins with the sovereignty of consciousness.

Everything else follows from that foundation.

A Story About the Mind Rather Than Aliens

Throughout cinematic history, extraterrestrials have frequently served as metaphors.

Sometimes they symbolize fear of invasion.

Sometimes they represent technological superiority.

Sometimes they embody humanity's encounter with the unknown.

In Disclosure Day, however, the extraterrestrial presence functions differently.

The aliens remain largely in the background.

Their recovered technology occupies center stage.

The true conflict emerges not between humanity and an alien civilization but between competing visions of what consciousness should become.

Noah Scanlon sees consciousness as infrastructure.

Something to be mapped.

Controlled.

Weaponized.

Commercialized.

Integrated into systems of surveillance and military power.

Jane Blankenship, by contrast, represents the opposite principle.

For her, consciousness is not property.

It is personhood itself.

This ideological conflict transforms the film from science fiction into philosophical allegory.

The Obelisk as a Symbol Rather Than a Machine

Although the screenplay presents the alien obelisk as advanced extraterrestrial technology, its symbolic function extends far beyond speculative engineering.

The obelisk represents every technological breakthrough that fundamentally alters the relationship between human beings and their own minds.

Historically, humanity has repeatedly developed technologies that transformed civilization.

Writing externalized memory.

The printing press democratized knowledge.

Electricity extended productivity.

Radio expanded communication.

Television reshaped culture.

The internet interconnected billions of minds.

Artificial intelligence increasingly participates in cognition itself.

Each technological revolution changed not only what people could do but how they thought.

Disclosure Day imagines the logical continuation of that historical trajectory.

What happens when technology no longer mediates communication between people...

but enters consciousness directly?

The obelisk therefore symbolizes the next evolutionary threshold.

The moment technology ceases being external.

The moment it becomes neurological.

The Last Frontier of Privacy

Modern society has witnessed an extraordinary erosion of privacy.

Our movements are tracked.

Our purchases analyzed.

Our communications archived.

Our online behavior continuously monitored.

Algorithms increasingly predict preferences before individuals consciously recognize them themselves.

Yet despite these developments, one sanctuary has largely remained intact.

The interior life of the mind.

One may choose whether to speak.

One may conceal thoughts.

One may refuse confession.

One may preserve silence.

Disclosure Day imagines the disappearance of that final sanctuary.

When Scanlon establishes direct neural access to Jane's consciousness, privacy reaches its absolute endpoint.

The invasion is no longer informational.

It is existential.

Her memories.

Her intentions.

Her motor functions.

Her decision-making.

All become accessible to external authority.

This represents the ultimate form of surveillance.

Not watching behavior.

Watching consciousness itself.

Technology and Moral Neutrality

One of Spielberg's most important observations throughout the film is that technology itself remains morally neutral.

The alien obelisk possesses extraordinary capabilities.

It can establish direct neural communication.

It can expand perception.

It can synchronize nervous systems.

None of these functions are inherently evil.

What determines their ethical significance is the intention guiding their use.

This principle echoes every major technological revolution in human history.

Nuclear physics produced electrical power.

It also produced atomic weapons.

Artificial intelligence can accelerate medical research.

It can also automate surveillance.

Genetic engineering may eliminate inherited disease.

It may also enable unprecedented forms of biological control.

Technology amplifies intention.

It rarely determines it.

The true danger therefore lies not within machinery but within the moral character of those directing it.

Noah Scanlon is terrifying not because he possesses advanced technology.

He is terrifying because he views consciousness itself as an instrument of power.

Consciousness as the Final Human Right

Perhaps the deepest philosophical implication of Disclosure Day is that consciousness itself may ultimately become humanity's most fundamental right.

Traditional political philosophy emphasizes freedom of speech.

Freedom of religion.

Freedom of assembly.

Freedom of movement.

These liberties all presuppose something deeper.

The freedom to think.

Without independent thought, every other freedom gradually becomes symbolic.

Speech becomes repetition.

Belief becomes programming.

Choice becomes simulation.

The film therefore shifts the discussion from civil liberties to cognitive liberty.

Who owns your thoughts?

Who governs intention?

Who authorizes access to consciousness?

These questions remain largely theoretical today.

They may not remain theoretical forever.

Artificial Intelligence and the Next Technological Revolution

Although Disclosure Day focuses upon extraterrestrial technology, its underlying concerns increasingly resonate within contemporary discussions surrounding artificial intelligence, neurotechnology, and brain-computer interfaces.

Modern neural engineering already enables direct communication between brains and machines.

Artificial intelligence increasingly interprets human intention.

Machine learning systems model personality, emotion, attention, and decision-making with growing sophistication.

No existing technology remotely resembles the alien obelisk.

Yet the trajectory deserves thoughtful reflection.

Humanity has entered an era in which technology is moving steadily inward.

From external tools...

to wearable devices...

to implanted interfaces...

to neural decoding.

Each step narrows the distance between computation and consciousness.

The film asks a timely question.

As this boundary disappears,

what ethical principles will remain non-negotiable?

The Battle Between Power and Value

Throughout this analysis, a recurring distinction has emerged.

Two fundamentally different relationships to consciousness.

The first understands consciousness primarily as power.

Power to command.

Power to predict.

Power to manipulate.

Power to optimize.

Power to dominate.

The second understands consciousness as value.

The capacity for truth.

Compassion.

Freedom.

Moral responsibility.

Self-reflection.

Human dignity.

These two visions define the conflict between Noah Scanlon and Jane Blankenship.

Scanlon seeks mastery.

Jane seeks integrity.

His objective is control.

Her objective is authenticity.

This opposition extends far beyond individual characters.

It reflects one of civilization's oldest ethical tensions.

Whether power exists to serve humanity...

or humanity exists to serve power.

Freedom Begins Within

Jane's victory over Scanlon ultimately carries significance far beyond physical survival.

She defeats him because she refuses to surrender the distinction between imposed action and authentic intention.

Even while externally controlled,

she internally remains free.

This insight recalls one of the oldest observations within philosophy.

External freedom can be taken.

Internal freedom requires consent.

Empires throughout history have imprisoned bodies.

Much more rarely have they conquered conscience.

Disclosure Day modernizes this ancient insight for the age of neurotechnology.

The battlefield has moved inward.

The contest no longer concerns merely physical territory.

It concerns cognitive territory.

Who occupies the mind?

Who defines reality?

Who determines identity?

Jane answers these questions not through superior force but through unwavering preservation of interior autonomy.

Consciousness and the Future of Civilization

The historical programs examined throughout this essay—Project MKUltra, Project Stargate, Soviet psychotronics, astronaut consciousness research, and modern neuroscience—all point toward an emerging realization.

Humanity increasingly recognizes consciousness as the next great frontier of scientific inquiry.

This development offers extraordinary possibilities.

Treatments for neurological disease.

Restoration of lost communication.

Enhanced education.

Expanded creativity.

New forms of collaboration.

Yet every expansion of capability simultaneously expands responsibility.

The more directly technology interfaces with consciousness,

the greater the ethical obligations governing its use.

The alien obelisk therefore represents not simply futuristic hardware but a warning.

Technological advancement without corresponding moral development creates unprecedented risks.

The future will not be determined solely by what humanity invents.

It will be determined by the wisdom—or the lack of wisdom—with which those inventions are employed.

The Ultimate Disclosure

The title Disclosure Day carries an important double meaning.

Within the narrative, it refers to the revelation of extraterrestrial existence and decades of governmental secrecy.

Yet at a deeper philosophical level, another disclosure occurs.

The film gradually reveals something about humanity itself.

It discloses that consciousness cannot be understood merely as information.

Nor merely as biology.

Nor merely as electrical activity.

Consciousness is the foundation from which freedom, morality, identity, responsibility, and civilization emerge.

The alien technology exposes this truth by threatening it.

Only when consciousness becomes vulnerable do we fully appreciate its value.

In this sense, the real disclosure is not the existence of extraterrestrials.

It is the recognition that the future of civilization may depend less upon mastering advanced technologies than upon understanding the nature of consciousness itself.

Beyond Science Fiction

Great science fiction has never been primarily about the future.

It has always been about the present.

The distant worlds imagined by visionary filmmakers are mirrors reflecting contemporary hopes, fears, and ethical dilemmas.

Disclosure Day belongs firmly within that tradition.

Its alien obelisk is not simply a fictional artifact recovered from Roswell.

It is a metaphor for every technology that challenges the boundary between human freedom and technological capability.

Its psychic interrogation is not merely an action sequence.

It is a dramatization of humanity's oldest struggle—the preservation of inner freedom against forces seeking external domination.

Its battle is not ultimately between humans and extraterrestrials.

It is between two competing futures.

One future regards consciousness as data to be harvested, predicted, engineered, and controlled.

The other recognizes consciousness as the irreducible foundation of human dignity, moral responsibility, creativity, and freedom.

That choice does not belong to science fiction alone.

As neuroscience, artificial intelligence, neuroengineering, and brain-computer interfaces continue to advance, it is becoming one of the defining ethical questions of the twenty-first century.

In that respect, Disclosure Day functions as far more than entertainment. It is a modern allegory reminding us that every civilization is ultimately judged not by the sophistication of its technologies, but by whether those technologies deepen human freedom or diminish it. The greatest disclosure awaiting humanity may therefore not concern visitors from another world. It may be the realization that the most important frontier has always been the one within—the mystery of consciousness itself, and the enduring responsibility to ensure that every technological advance serves the liberation of the human mind rather than its subjugation.

10. Conclusion

Across Disclosure Day, the narrative gradually reveals itself to be less about extraterrestrial contact and more about a systematic interrogation of what it means to be a conscious, self-determining human being under conditions of extreme technological intrusion. The alien obelisk, the neural synchronization protocols, and the psychic coercion enacted by Noah Scanlon are not isolated speculative inventions; they function as a unified conceptual architecture through which the film examines the fragility and resilience of human consciousness.

At its core, the film proposes a central thesis: the human mind is both the target and the boundary of all power. Every technological extension of influence—whether cultural, media and entertainment, chemical, psychological, electromagnetic, or neural—ultimately converges upon the same frontier: the capacity of consciousness to remain internally autonomous even when externally constrained.

Jane Blankenship’s experience crystallizes this tension with particular clarity. Her struggle is not simply physical resistance against forced motor control, but a layered confrontation between imposed agency and preserved interior awareness. Even when her body becomes an instrument of external command, her consciousness remains capable of observation, evaluation, and refusal. This distinction between enacted behavior and witnessing awareness becomes the decisive factor in her survival.

The film’s broader historical and conceptual framework reinforces this point by weaving together multiple trajectories of twentieth- and twenty-first-century inquiry: MKUltra’s attempts at behavioral dismantling, Project Stargate’s investigations into anomalous perception, Soviet psychotronic engineering, astronaut experiences of perceptual dislocation, and contemporary developments in neurotechnology. Each of these domains reflects a persistent civilizational question—whether consciousness can be measured, modified, extended, or controlled through technological means.

Yet Disclosure Day does not resolve this question in favor of technological determinism. Instead, it repeatedly returns to a more structurally cautious insight: control over external systems does not guarantee control over consciousness itself. Even when the body is overridden, the observing awareness persists. Even when perception is altered, the capacity for internal recognition remains. Even when neural pathways are manipulated, the distinction between imposed action and self-authored intention does not fully collapse.

This is the quiet but decisive boundary the film protects.

At the same time, Disclosure Day refuses to romanticize consciousness as invulnerable or abstractly inviolable. The obelisk’s interface demonstrates that the nervous system is indeed permeable to external influence, and that technological systems—if sufficiently advanced—may gain unprecedented access to cognition, perception, and motor control. The film therefore occupies a critical middle position: neither naive optimism nor absolute dystopian fatalism, but a recognition that consciousness is both deeply embodied and fundamentally irreducible to simple mechanical governance.

This tension defines the ethical gravity of the narrative.

If consciousness can be accessed, it can be influenced.

If it can be influenced, it can be exploited.

And if it can be exploited, then the central challenge of future civilization will not merely be technological innovation, but the establishment of safeguards for cognitive sovereignty.

In this sense, Disclosure Day operates as a warning structure rather than a predictive claim. It suggests that the most significant frontier of technological development is no longer external space, industrial capacity, or even computational power, but the interior domain of subjective awareness itself. The closer technology moves toward direct neural interfacing, the more urgent becomes the question of how autonomy, identity, and moral agency are preserved within that interface.

Jane’s final condition at the end of the psychic sequence—wounded, disoriented, but internally intact—encapsulates the film’s immediate answer. Survival is not defined by the absence of harm, nor by the restoration of bodily control alone. It is defined by the persistence of an inner witnessing capacity that cannot be fully appropriated by external systems.

That persistence makes resistance possible.

That resistance preserves personal freedom.

Yet from the perspective of Gautama the Supreme Arahant, this freedom remains only a relative freedom.

One may successfully resist psychological manipulation.

One may escape political oppression.

One may overcome technological domination.

One may preserve cognitive autonomy against external control.

These are all meaningful victories.

But they do not resolve the deepest condition of existence.

The world itself remains governed by laws far greater than any government, corporation, or advanced technology. Every civilization, regardless of its scientific achievements, continues to exist within the universal processes of competition, conflict, decay, aging, illness, and death. Whether humanity develops artificial intelligence, neural interfaces, extraterrestrial communication, or direct brain-to-brain technology, none of these innovations alters the fundamental structure of conditioned existence.

Technology may expand human capability.

It cannot abolish mortality.

Science may prolong life.

It cannot eliminate aging.

Political systems may defend civil liberty.

They cannot free beings from birth and death.

Even the most advanced civilization imaginable remains subject to the same cosmic laws governing all conditioned existence.

From this perspective, the deepest question raised by Disclosure Day extends beyond technological ethics.

It becomes an existential question.

What constitutes ultimate freedom?

According to Gautama the Supreme Arahant, ultimate freedom is not found in gaining greater mastery over the world, but in completely transcending the world. The goal is not merely to protect consciousness from manipulation within conditioned existence, but to free consciousness entirely from the domain governed by craving, attachment, conflict, aging, and death.

This is why the path taught by Gautama the Supreme Arahant ultimately points beyond every worldly system. Political freedom remains within the world. Scientific progress remains within the world. Technological advancement remains within the world. Even extraordinary expansions of perception remain within the world if they continue to operate inside conditioned existence.

True liberation lies elsewhere.

It lies in the complete cessation of bondage to the conditioned cosmos.

It lies in the ultimate existence of the Deathless realm of Nibbāna.

There, consciousness is no longer threatened by external domination because it has gone beyond the entire world system in which domination exists. There is no competition because there is no such law for survival. There is no conflict because the conditions giving rise to conflict have ceased. There is no aging because such conditioned formation has ended. There is no death because the Deathless realm is beyond birth and dissolution.

Seen from this wider perspective, Disclosure Day becomes more than a cautionary tale about emerging neurotechnology. It becomes an allegory of the human condition itself. Noah Scanlon's psychic domination represents only one manifestation of a much larger reality: all beings living within the conditioned world are subject to forces that continually shape, constrain, and condition their existence.

The film asks whether the mind can remain free under technological domination.

Gautama the Supreme Arahant asks a still deeper question:

Can consciousness become completely free from the entire conditioned world?

The first question concerns political and technological liberty.

The second concerns ultimate liberation and freedom.

The distinction is profound.

One seeks freedom within the world.

The other seeks freedom from the world.

Thus, the final "disclosure" is not merely a revelation about alien intelligence.

Nor is it simply a warning about future technologies.

It is a recognition about ourselves.

The human mind is not simply another system to be optimized.

It is the very condition through which all systems are understood.

Yet according to Gautama the Supreme Arahant, even the most refined consciousness within the conditioned world is not the final destination. The highest freedom is realized only when consciousness completely transcends the world of becoming and enters the Deathless realm of Nibbāna, where ultimate peace, ultimate security, and ultimate freedom are the exact properties of it very existence.

Viewed in this light, Disclosure Day becomes both a compelling science-fiction thriller and a philosophical meditation. It reminds us that the struggle to preserve the integrity of consciousness is indispensable. But it also points toward a larger truth: preserving the freedom of the mind within the world is only the beginning. The highest aspiration is to follow the path that leads beyond the world itself, to the Deathless realm, where no technology, no empire, no biological process, and no cosmic law of aging and death can ever reach again.

title: Summary Commentary for the Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 2): Gautama Buddha and the Ancient Path (Purāṇa-magga / Purāṇa-mārga) to Liberation
content:
Summary Commentary: Gautama Buddha and the Ancient Path (Purāṇa-magga / Purāṇa-mārga) to Liberation

1). Gautama Buddha as the Restorer of the Ancient Path, Not an Academic Revolutionist

Modern Western academia frequently depicts Gautama Buddha as a radical revolutionist who invented an entirely novel religious system ex nihilo. However, textual evidence across both the epic Vedic tradition (such as the Bhagavad Gītā) and the early canonical discourses reveals that Gautama Buddha did not invent these spiritual constructs. Gautama Buddha himself bears the title of Vedagū, the Master of Veda.

In the Nagara Sutta (SN 12.65), Gautama Buddha explicitly clarifies his role using the metaphor of an ancient city: he states that he did not construct a new road, but rather rediscovered an "ancient path" (purāṇa-magga [Pāḷi] / purāṇa-mārga [Sanskrit]), an ancient road trod by the Rightly and Fully Awakened Ones (Sammā-sam-buddhas) of past ages. Gautama Buddha inherited the foundational Brahma tradition, restored and elevated it, organized its core tenets into a systematic training framework, and revitalized it to bring back its true historic glory for his assembly of bhikkhus [Pāḷi] / bhikṣus [Sanskrit] and bhikkhunīs [Pāḷi] / bhikṣunīs [Sanskrit].

2). The Pre-Existing Terminology in the Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 2)

The occurrence of core terminology throughout Chapter 2 confirms that these concepts belonged to the shared cultural and spiritual heritage of ancient India long before (thousands of years) later sectarian divisions arose:

  • Brahma-nirvāṇa (brahma-nibbanā [Pāḷi] / brahma-nirvāṇam [Sanskrit]): Mentioned explicitly in Verse 2.72. The final liberation realized by extinguishing the unwholesome roots (rāga, dosa, moha) is directly called brahma-nirvāṇa—Brahma’s Nibbana.
  • Mental Defilements: The fundamental root causes of worldly bondage—rāga [Pāḷi/Sanskrit] (attachment/lust; BG 2.56, 2.64), dosa [Pāḷi] / dveṣa [Sanskrit] (fear/anger; BG 2.64), and moha [Pāḷi/Sanskrit] (ignorance/delusion; BG 2.52, 2.72)—are systematically identified as the drivers of unwholesome karma lead to involuntary reincarnation.
  • The Internal Spirit / Self: attā [Pāḷi] / ātmā [Sanskrit] is addressed as the internal mind/spirit that must be anchored away from external sensory objects (ora) and directed toward the transcendent Other Shore (pāra). Unlike today’s academia’s relentless distortion to Gautama Buddha’s teachings, he never denied the existence of attā / ātmā, it is this essence of human existence to enter the realm of Nibbana, not its annihilation.
  • The Renunciate Order: The concept of the alms-seeking renunciate—bhikkhu [Pāḷi] / bhikṣu [Sanskrit]—was already an established social and spiritual norm within the ancient India (Bharata) civilization, which Arjuna himself references when contemplating a life of renunciant over worldly slaughter (bhikṣām in BG 2.5).

3). Brahma-Nirvāṇa and Gautama’s Nibbāna Through the Five Pure Abode Brahma Heavens

Gautama Buddha’s teaching on Nibbāna [Pāḷi] / Nirvāṇa [Sanskrit] is inextricably linked to Brahma. The ultimate threshold of liberation is achieved by going through the five Pure Brahma Abodes (Suddhāvāsa [Pāḷi] / Śuddhāvāsa [Sanskrit])—the highest Brahma heavens in this world/galaxy located within the fourth jhāna realm (catuttha jhāna [Pāḷi] / caturtha dhyāna [Sanskrit]):

  1. Avihā [Pāḷi] / Avṛhā [Sanskrit] (The Durable Realm)
  2. Atappā [Pāḷi] / Atapā [Sanskrit] (The Serene Realm)
  3. Sudassā [Pāḷi] / Sudṛśā [Sanskrit] (The Beautiful Vision Realm)
  4. Sudassī [Pāḷi] / Sudarśī [Sanskrit] (The Clear-Sighted Realm)
  5. Akaniṭṭhā [Pāḷi] / Akaniṣṭha [Sanskrit] (The Highest Realm)

These five Brahma realms serve as the ultimate stepping stone within this saṁsāric world. Upon reaching total mental purification through Brahmacariya, the practitioner ascends and exit this world through these Brahma heavenly kingdoms.

4. De-Mystifying the Attributes of Ātman: Dimensional Immunity vs. Eternal Dogma (BG 2.18)

Traditional translations routinely inflate terms like nitya, anāśin, and aprameya into vague, sweeping metaphysical dogma ("eternal," "indestructible," "immeasurable"). Within the operational context of Chapter 2, these terms do not signify that the embodied entity (śarīrin / dehin / ātman / soul / spirit) is eternal or indestructible at all. Rather, they only suggest its concrete dimensional immunity over the physical body (deha):

  • Nitya (Continuously Lasting, not "Eternal"): Derived from ni- ("inward," "dwelling within") + -tya ("belonging to"). It literally means "inwardly abiding." Rather than denoting an unconditioned, timeless state outside saṁsāra, nitya signifies uninterrupted continuity across time—the internal entity remains present and continuously lasts through physical realm changes while the physical body crumbles.
  • Anāśin (Physically Non-Perishing, not generic "Indestructible"): Derived from a- ("non-") + nāśin (from naś, "to perish / dissolve"). It specifically addresses Arjuna's battlefield fear of physical weapons (śastrāṇi). The internal entity is immune to lower-dimensional physical trauma, weapon impact, or bodily dissolution.
  • Aprameya (Physically Immeasurable, not "Mystically Incomprehensible"): Derived from a- + pra- + meya (from mā, "to measure"). While a physical body can be measured, weighed, or bounded by empirical instruments (pramāṇa), the higher-dimensional internal entity cannot be gauged by physical metrics or sensory organs.

These terms confirm that the internal mind/spirit (attā / ātmā) easily survives physical death and physical realm changes. Because physical death cannot destroy it, involuntary reincarnation (bhava) remains a continuous trap until the unwholesome roots of rāga, dosa / dveṣa, and moha are completely eradicated.

5. Dual Terminology Glossary (Pāḷi / Sanskrit Equivalents in Chapter 2)

This commentary is excerpted from my forthcoming book, Bhagavad-Gītā: A Theravāda Buddhist Reading. This work presents a systematic structural breakdown of the text, featuring original Sanskrit verses, precise word-by-word literal translations, and rigorous analytical commentary grounded directly in the original teachings of Gautama Buddha.

Why Read the Bhagavad-Gītā Through Theravāda Buddhism?

Modern scholarship frequently presents Hinduism and Buddhism as two separate religious systems whose histories diverged from the moment of Gautama Buddha's awakening. Such a presentation is useful for describing later institutional developments, yet it can obscure an older and deeper reality. Before they became distinct religious traditions, they belonged to the same civilizational world.

Ancient India was not merely a collection of competing doctrines. It was a shared intellectual and spiritual landscape. Its people inherited common stories, symbols, heroes, ethical ideals, cosmological visions, and philosophical questions. The search for liberation, the reality of karma, the cycle of rebirth, the practice of meditation, the existence of higher realms, and the pursuit of ultimate truth formed the common vocabulary of that civilization.

Among the greatest expressions of this shared inheritance stands the Bhagavad-Gītā.

Whether preserved through oral recitation, dramatic performance, temple reliefs, family instruction, or the education of Brahmanical lineages, the story of the Mahābhārata permeated ancient Indian culture. Long before manuscripts became widespread, these narratives lived in memory. Every generation encountered them in one form or another. Like the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata was not simply literature; it was part of the cultural atmosphere in which ancient Indians understood themselves and the world.

Siddhattha Sakya of the Gautama lineage grew up within this same civilizational environment.

Although the historical Gautama Buddha never quotes the Bhagavad-Gītā, it would be mistaken to imagine that he emerged from a cultural vacuum. The philosophical questions addressed in the Gītā - the nature of duty, the problem of suffering, the struggle between worldly responsibility and renunciation, the cultivation of inner discipline, and the search for liberation - were precisely the questions that occupied the spiritual life of ancient India. They formed part of the collective consciousness from which Gautama Buddha himself emerged.

Reading the Bhagavad-Gītā, therefore, is not merely reading a Hindu scripture. It is entering the psychological world of ancient India. It provides access to the collective memory, symbolic representation, and philosophical vocabulary that shaped generations of seekers, including the generation to which Gautama Buddha belonged.

This does not imply that Gautama Buddha accepted every conclusion found within the Gītā. Nor does it suggest that the two traditions are identical. On many fundamental questions they differ profoundly. The Gītā ultimately directs the seeker toward participation in a divine lineage centered upon devotion to the Lineage God, whose Avatar became Kṛṣṇa, whereas the Buddha directs the practitioner toward liberation through individual effort with the help of His Dhamma (“Atta-dīpā viharatha, atta-saraṇā, anañña-saraṇā; dhamma-dīpā, dhamma-saraṇā, anañña-saraṇā. Dwell with your Soul/Atman as your island, your Soul/Atman as your refuge, there is no other refuges; My Dhamma as your island, my Dhamma as your refuge, there is no other refuges”). Their paths diverge in important respects.

Reading the Sanskrit Before Reading the Tradition

This study is also motivated by another concern. Many of the Bhagavad-Gītā's most influential doctrines are not simply inherited from the Sanskrit text itself, but through centuries of later theological interpretation. Over time, certain Sanskrit terms acquired meanings that gradually became accepted as unquestioned orthodoxy, even when those meanings are broader or more absolute than the immediate context of the verses requires.

One of the most significant examples is the doctrine of Ātman.

In many traditional commentaries, Ātman is presented as absolutely eternal, absolutely indestructible, absolutely immutable, and identical with the ultimate metaphysical reality. These conclusions have profoundly shaped the history of Indian philosophy, especially within the various schools of Vedānta. Yet an important question remains: Does the Bhagavad-Gītā itself always make such absolute claims?

This book argues that, in many passages, it does not.

Rather than beginning with later philosophical systems, I return first to the original Sanskrit. I examine the etymology of key words, their grammatical construction, and, most importantly, their immediate literary context. When Kṛṣṇa describes the embodied being (Dehin, Śarīrin, Ātman) as nitya, avināśi, anāśin, or avyaya, these words are often translated as "eternal," "indestructible," or "imperishable" in an absolute metaphysical sense. Yet within the context of the battlefield dialogue, Kṛṣṇa is addressing Arjuna's fear of physical death. The immediate issue is not whether the embodied being possesses absolute, unconditioned existence, but whether it can be destroyed by physical weapons or perish when the body dies.

Read in this context, these terms naturally convey a more limited and precise meaning. They affirm that the embodied being survives bodily death and cannot be destroyed by physical force. They do not necessarily establish that it is absolutely eternal, unconditioned, or beyond every form of change. The distinction is subtle but significant. Something may endure beyond the destruction of the physical body without thereby possessing the same absolute permanence traditionally reserved for ultimate reality.

This distinction also opens a fruitful dialogue with the Theravāda tradition. The Pāli Canon likewise distinguishes between the destruction of the physical body and the continuation of rebirth within saṃsāra. Surviving death is not identical with liberation. Continued existence within the cycle of becoming, however long it may endure, remains conditioned existence. From a Theravāda perspective, true security lies not merely in surviving physical death, but in transcending the entire cycle of birth and rebirth through the realization of Nibbāna.

Accordingly, this commentary seeks to distinguish carefully between what the Sanskrit text explicitly states and what later philosophical traditions infer from it. This is not an attempt to diminish the profound contributions of Vedānta or other Hindu schools. Rather, it is an invitation to read the Bhagavad-Gītā afresh—to allow its own language, context, and internal logic to speak before later doctrinal systems are imposed upon it.

Only after listening carefully to the voice of the text itself can we fairly compare it with the teachings preserved in the Theravāda Nikāyas. Such a comparison, grounded in careful philology rather than inherited assumptions, allows both traditions to illuminate one another with greater precision and greater mutual respect.

Yet meaningful comparison requires first recognizing their common cultural foundation.

A civilization often explores the same existential questions through multiple voices. The Bhagavad-Gītā represents one such voice. The Theravāda Nikāyas preserve another. Both arise from the same ancient Indian search for the meaning of existence, the reality of suffering, and the possibility of ultimate freedom.

This book therefore approaches the Bhagavad-Gītā neither as an object of criticism nor as a text to be harmonized artificially with Buddhism. Instead, it asks a different question:

How does the Bhagavad-Gītā appear when read through the perspective of Theravāda Buddhism?

Such a reading allows the two traditions to illuminate one another. The Gītā reveals the philosophical atmosphere of ancient India, while the teachings of Gautama Buddha provide a distinctive lens through which many of its themes may be reconsidered. Similarities become clearer, differences become more precise, and the intellectual achievement of both traditions becomes more fully appreciated.

The Shared Vocabulary and the Systematized Training

When we compare the technical terminology found within the Bhagavad-Gītā with the Pāli Nikāyas, a revealing historical pattern emerges. On one hand, both traditions inhabit the exact same linguistic world. Core operational terms—such as Dukkha, Samādhi, Jhāna (Dhyāna), Virāga, Taṇhā (Tṛṣṇā), Brahmacariya, and even Brahma-nirvāṇa—form a shared civilizational vocabulary. Gautama Buddha did not invent these terms out of whole cloth, nor did he enter a cultural void. He inherited the ancient Indian Brahma tradition, operating directly within a worldview that sought liberation from the cycles of saṃsāra through internal purification and moral restraint.

On the other hand, analyzing the terms that are absent from the Gītā exposes the specific nature of the Buddha’s genius. While the Gītā organizes reality through broad cosmological frameworks—such as Prakṛti, Puruṣa, the Guṇas, and the broad category of the Field (Kṣetra)—the Pāli Canon introduces a far more rigorous, analytical taxonomy. In place of grand cosmic categories, Gautama Buddha mapped human experience into direct, empirical units: the Five Aggregates (Khandhas), the Twelve Sense Media (Āyatanas), and the Twelve-Linked Chain of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda).

Where the surrounding culture offered general contemplative advice, Gautama Buddha systematized an exact, step-by-step path of training (Anupubbaniyyāma). He organized moral conduct (Sīla), concentration (Samādhi), and wisdom (Paññā) into a precise methodology to analyze how mental phenomena arise and pass away.

This perspective also helps us understand Gautama Buddha himself. He was not an isolated religious revolutionary standing outside Indian civilization. He was one of its greatest sons. Formed within its intellectual world, conversant with its spiritual vocabulary, and recognized in the Pāli Canon as a vedagū— one who has fully mastered sacred knowledge of Veda— he carried the contemplative quest of ancient India in a direction uniquely his own.

To read the Bhagavad-Gītā alongside the teachings preserved in the Pāli Canon is therefore not merely an exercise in comparative religion. It is an exploration of two of the most profound expressions of the spiritual genius of ancient India. By entering the world of the Gītā, we come closer to understanding the civilizational landscape that shaped Gautama Buddha. By reading it through the lens of Theravāda Buddhism, we gain a fresh perspective on both traditions and on the enduring human search for liberation.

Appendix: Comprehensive Dual Terminology Glossary (Pāḷi / Sanskrit Equivalents in the Bhagavad Gītā)

Key Pāḷi Operational Terms Absent from the Bhagavad Gītā

Arahant / Arhat

The Pāḷi term Arahant (Sanskrit: Arhat, meaning "Worthy One" or "Purified One") does not explicitly appear in the Bhagavad Gītā. While the concept of a fully liberated being who has completely eradicated rāga, dosa, and moha is central to both traditions, the Gītā uses its own specific Sanskrit terminology to describe an individual who has attained ultimate freedom.

Equivalent Terms in the Bhagavad Gītā

Etymology: The Root √arh

The word stems from the Proto-Indo-Iranian root *ar- or *arh-, which carried the fundamental meaning of "to be worthy," "to deserve," "to have value," or "to be fit/capable."

1). Vedic and Pre-Buddhist Indian Usage

Before it became a technical term for a fully purified being who has completely eradicated rāga, dosa, and moha, arhat was a secular and religious honorific in Vedic literature.

  • In the Ṛgveda: The word appears as an adjective applied to deities like Agni, Indra, and Rudra to signify their cosmic worthiness and majesty (e.g., calling Agni arhat—"the worthy one" who deserves the sacrificial offering).
  • In Early Ascetic Traditions: Non-Vedic śramaṇa traditions (such as Jainism) used Arhat or Arihant (meaning "conqueror of internal enemies") to describe perfected spiritual teachers long before its systematic adoption in early Pāḷi texts.

2). The Iranian Connection: Avestan and Old Persian

While Arhat itself is a South Asian development, its cognates appear in ancient Iranian texts written in Avestan (Zoroastrian scriptures) and Old Persian:

  • Avestan Arəja-: In the Zoroastrian Avesta, words derived from arəg- mean "value" or "precious." A person of noble spiritual worth held arəja.
  • Persian Arda-: The Old Persian term Arda or Arta (cognate to Sanskrit Ṛta and related conceptually to spiritual worthiness) merged the ideas of truth, holiness, and high status.

Because Old Persian and Vedic Sanskrit were closely related sister languages, their vocabularies shared dozens of cognates related to ritual, nobility, and spiritual duty.

3). Key Verses in Ṛgveda with Arhat

(1). Ṛgveda 2.33.10 – Applied to Rudra (The Worthy Lord)

arhan bibharṣi sāyakāni dhanvārhan niṣkaṃ yajataṃ viśvarūpam

arhan nidaṃ dayāse viśvam abhvaṃ na vā ojīyo rudra tvad asti

"O Worthy One, you carry the bow and arrows! O Worthy One, you wear the holy, multi-form necklace! O Worthy One, you protect this entire vast realm! Indeed, O Rudra, there is none mightier than you."

Here the sage Gritsamada addresses Rudra as the supreme "worthy one" who holds the bow and arrows, possessing absolute divine majesty.

(2). Ṛgveda 1.63.7 – Applied to Indra (The Deserving Conqueror)

ya eka id dhavyaś carṣaṇīnām indraṃ taṃ gobhir arkair arhantaṃ vardhayanti

"He who alone is to be invoked with offerings among all people—him, Indra, the Worthy One, they exalt with songs and sacred hymns."

Here, Indra is declared arhat—deserving and worthy of praise and oblations because of his power to shatter strongholds and establish order.

(3). Ṛgveda 1.127.6 – Applied to Agni (The Worthy Sacrificer)

sa hi śardho na mārutaṃ tuviṣvaṇir arnāṃsīva pra rinati yudhā gan

sa dvibarhā amartyaḥ sa hotā havyavāhaḥ sa arhān

"He indeed is doubly exalted, immortal; he is the invoking priest, the bearer of offerings, he is the Worthy One."

Agni (the sacrificial fire) is termed arhat because he acts as the clean, purified messenger who carries offerings directly to the high realms.

(4). Ṛgveda 1.170.5 – Applied to the Worthy Assembly / Priests (Arhantaḥ)

kim an no arthaṃ yad arātir āṃ asmabhyaṃ śaṃsam arhantaḥ

"Why then hinder our purpose? Overcome the hostility and bestow blessings upon us, O Worthy Ones (arhantaḥ)!"

Here, the plural form arhantaḥ ("the worthy ones") is used by Agastya to describe the noble, deserving sacrificers/gods working in harmony.

(5). Ṛgveda 10.63.4 – Applied to the Viśvedevas (All the Worthy Gods)

nṛcakṣaso ye divyāny āṃ yayur devāso adbhir manuṣo yajatrāḥ

te asmabhyam śarma bahulaṃ ni yacchantv arhanto devā avasā sacantām

"Those gods who watch over men, holy and heavenly, may they grant us abundant shelter! May those Worthy Gods (arhantaḥ devāḥ) accompany us with their protection!"

In this late Rigvedic hymn, the collective gods (Viśvedevas) are described as arhat—deserving of worship.

(6). Ṛgveda 10.99.7 – Applied to the Worthy Supreme Commander

sa nṛṣṭubho nāvam adhād bṛhadbhiḥ sa rodhasī ahar dasyuhābhiḥ

sa usriyā arhato nir dadāti gṛṇāno aṅgirobhir ṛkvabhiḥ

"Acclaimed by the human crew and commanders (nṛṣṭubhaḥ), He deployed using massive power/thrusters (adhāt bṛhadbhiḥ) the massive sky-vessel (nāvam) into position. Utilizing his anti-hostile strike weaponry(Dasyuhābhiḥ), He breached the atmospheric boundaries between Earth and space (rodhasī ahat). Guided by the Aṅgiras engineering staff via acoustic signal arrays (Aṅgirobhiḥ ṛkvabhiḥ), the Worthy One (arhataḥ) discharged directed energy beams outward(Usriyāḥ nir dadāti)."

Here, Indra is addressed as arhat in his role as the Supreme Commander / High Officer in the space vessel came to Earth.
