title: Voices of Liberation (on Amazon now)
content:
Now available on Amazon

Theragāthā & Therīgāthā: Verses of the Elder Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs on the Path to the Realm of Nibbāna
Volume I

What if one of the most fundamental teachings of modern Buddhism has misunderstood the very word on which it is built?

Voices of Liberation is a direct and uncompromising challenge to the modern interpretation of anattā as “there is no self” or “there is no soul,” —and, more fundamentally, to the assumption that because the five aggregates are not attā, a human being is nothing more than the five aggregates and therefore has no Soul beyond them.

The question is not merely philosophical.

If the earliest disciples of Gautama the Supreme Arahant actually completed the path to liberation, then their own words should tell us what they practiced, what they abandoned, and what they attained.

And that is precisely where this book begins.

The Theragāthā and Therīgāthā preserve the voices of Elder Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs who entered the holy life, renounced household existence, trained their minds, cultivated samādhi, developed higher seeing, became disenchanted with worldly existence, developed dispassion, relinquished attachment, and declared liberation.

Yet where, in these voices of accomplished practitioners, is the supposed practice of repeatedly meditating upon “there is no self”?

This book confronts that question directly.

The Anattā-Lakkhaṇa Sutta is examined in detail, beginning with the distinction between anattā and lakkhaṇa. The five aggregates are identified as anattā—not attā. But the statement that the aggregates are not attā is not logically identical to the philosophical proposition that attā does not exist.

That distinction is the foundation of this book's challenge.

The body is not attā. Feeling is not attā. Perception is not attā. Mental formations are not attā. Sense-based consciousness is not attā.

But saying that these are not attā is not the same statement as saying that there is no attā.

The difference is enormous.

When anattā is transformed from a teaching concerning the five aggregates into a doctrine that denies the existence of Self or Soul-Spirit altogether, and then that denial is made into a central object of meditation, the direction of the liberation path is fundamentally altered. This book argues that such a transformation deserves to be confronted rather than simply inherited.

This is why this book was written.

It is not another summary of Buddhist philosophy.

It is not a modern mindfulness manual.

It is not an attempt to make Gautama's Dhamma fit contemporary psychology, secularism, academic consensus, or later philosophical systems.

It is an attempt to recover the liberation teaching of Gautama the Supreme Arahant by returning to the testimony of the practitioners who followed him.

The Theragāthā and Therīgāthā are therefore approached not merely as ancient poetry or historical literature, but as testimony from yogis who actually undertook the renunciate path. Their verses speak repeatedly of renunciation, solitude, discipline, meditation, overcoming sensuality, abandoning attachment, purification, liberation, and the realization of arahantship.

Alongside the verses is an extensive, practice-oriented commentary examining their Pāli terminology, doctrinal implications, philosophical assumptions, and soteriological direction.

The result is a substantial contribution to the contemporary discussion of Gautama's original liberation teaching.

At the center of the book is a radically different understanding of the destination of the path.

The elders were not merely seeking to become psychologically healthier people within the world. They were not practicing merely to manage stress or improve their relationship with ordinary existence.

They were seeking vimutti—liberation.

Liberation from loka.

Liberation from worldly bondage.

Liberation from conditioned existence.

Liberation toward the Deathless Realm of Nibbāna.

The path presented throughout this volume can be summarized as:

Renunciation → Sīla → Samādhi → Paññā → Nibbidā → Virāga → Vimutti → Nibbāna.

This is the direction the author believes must be recovered.

The book therefore confronts not only the distortion of anattā, but the larger transformation of Gautama's Dhamma into a teaching for living more comfortably within the world. When renunciation becomes “simplicity,” samādhi becomes “relaxation,” liberation becomes “freedom from stress,” and Nibbāna becomes merely a metaphor for psychological peace, the language may remain Buddhist—but the destination has changed.

Voices of Liberation refuses to allow that change to pass without examination.

Its central principle is simple:

Interpretation must not be allowed to erase the testimony of the practitioners themselves.

Bhante Mudita approaches these ancient verses not only as a scholar but as a practicing bhikkhu whose years of monastic training at Pa-Auk Forest Monastery and Meditation Center in Myanmar, samādhi practice, Pāli study, and life within the Saṅgha provide the practical foundation for his reading. The book deliberately approaches the verses through the perspective of yogi practice rather than intellectual analysis alone.

This Volume I brings together the Theragāthā of the Elder Bhikkhus and the Therīgāthā of the Elder Bhikkhunīs, accompanied by detailed commentary intended to recover the direction, meaning, and ultimate destination of Gautama's liberation path.

This book is for readers who are willing to question inherited assumptions.

For those who want to examine anattā for themselves.

For those who believe the Pāli Canon deserves to be read more carefully.

For serious practitioners of renunciation and samādhi.

For scholars willing to reconsider established interpretations.

And for anyone who wants to ask the most important question of all:

What did the people who actually completed Gautama's path say about liberation?

The ancient voices have survived.

Now they must be heard.

Not as objects of modern interpretation.
Not as evidence to be forced into a predetermined doctrine.
But as the voices of practitioners who walked the path, attained liberation, and left their testimony behind.

Voices of Liberation is an invitation—and a challenge—to return to those voices and reconsider what Gautama the Supreme Arahant actually taught about the path from worldly bondage to the Deathless Realm of Nibbāna.

I am writing this book because I believe that something fundamental has been lost in the way the Dhamma of Gautama the Supreme Arahant is understood and practiced today.

Voices of Liberation: Theragāthā & Therīgāthā: Verses of the Elder Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs on the Path to the Realm of Nibbāna is an attempt to return directly to the voices of those who followed Gautama the Supreme Arahant, entered the holy life (brahmacāriya), practiced his teaching (dhamma), and became Arahants themselves who were ready to exit the universe to enter the deathless realm of Nibbāna.

This book is therefore not primarily an academic study of ancient Buddhist literature. It is not an attempt to fit the words of the elders into theories developed many centuries after them. Nor is it an attempt to reconcile Gautama’s original liberation teaching with whatever forms Buddhism has subsequently taken.

The purpose is much simpler and, at the same time, much more serious:

What did the earliest disciples of Gautama the Supreme Arahant actually practice, and what did they say they attained?

I believe this question has become increasingly important because Buddhism today is moving further and further away from its original purpose.

For more than two thousand years, the Dhamma has passed through different cultures, languages, philosophical systems, religious institutions, and interpretive traditions. In that long process, teachings have been added, transformed, reinterpreted, simplified, and sometimes fundamentally misunderstood. What began as a direct path of liberation from the world has, in many places, become something very different.

Buddhism today is increasingly being presented as philosophy, psychology, mindfulness, secular ethics, stress reduction, self-development, or a method for becoming more comfortable or competitive within ordinary worldly life.

These things may have their own value. But they are not the liberation teaching of Gautama the Supreme Arahant.

Gautama did not leave the household life, establish the bhikkhu-saṅgha, teach renunciation, develop samādhi, teach higher seeing, and direct his disciples toward complete liberation merely so that human beings could become somewhat calmer or psychologically healthier while remaining fully invested in the world.

His Dhamma was a teaching of liberation from the world and enter the realm of Nibbāna (Nibbāna-dhātu). The destination was outside of the universe where the universal law of decay and death does not apply.

The task was to cut all bondages with the world and become disenchanted with the world (nibbida), relinquish worldly passion (viraga), and liberated from the world (vimutti), and enter the Deathless realm of Nibbāna.

That is the Dhamma that I believe must be recovered.

True Dhamma Is Not a Teaching of Secularization

One of the great dangers facing Buddhism today is secularization.

As Buddhism enters the modern world, teachings that once pointed beyond ordinary existence are increasingly translated into concepts that remain entirely within ordinary existence.

Renunciation becomes "simplicity." Samādhi becomes "calm or relaxation." Mindfulness becomes "present-moment awareness." Wisdom becomes "psychological insight." Liberation becomes "freedom from stress." Nibbāna becomes a metaphor for psychological peace. The Deathless becomes a symbolic description of a state of mind.

In this process, the language may remain Buddhist, but the destination has changed. A teaching intended to lead beyond loka is transformed into a teaching for living better within loka. That is not a small change.

It changes the entire direction of the path.

If the problem is understood merely as psychological discomfort, then psychological improvement becomes the solution.

If the problem is understood as attachment to worldly existence, then relinquishment becomes necessary.

If the problem is understood as repeated conditioned existence subject to arising and passing away, then the practitioner must seek release from that condition.

And if Nibbāna is the Deathless, then liberation cannot simply mean becoming happier within the realm of death and decay.

This distinction is fundamental to the reading offered in this book.

The Question of Anattā

One of the clearest examples of this transformation concerns anattā.

In contemporary Buddhism, anattā—usually translated as "no-self" or "non-self"—has become one of the most prominent teachings and, in many circles, one of the highest practices.

The standard explanation is familiar. "This is not my self." "This I am not." "This does not belong to me."

The practitioner is encouraged to examine the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness and repeatedly recognize that none of them is self.

This interpretation has become so dominant that it is often treated as though it were the central method by which liberation is accomplished.

It appears in meditation instructions, books, courses, lectures, modern Buddhist psychology, and increasingly in explanations produced by artificial-intelligence systems trained on the modern Buddhist consensus.

But there is a question that deserves to be asked before this interpretation is accepted as the original practice of Gautama Buddha:

Did Gautama Buddha’s early disciples actually practice in this way?

The answer is NO!

The Theragāthā and Therīgāthā preserve the voices of elder bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs who entered the Buddha's path and described their own practice and realization.

They speak about leaving the household life.

They speak about renunciation.

They speak about abandoning sensuality.

They speak about overcoming attachment.

They speak about meditation.

They speak about seeing.

They speak about dispassion.

They speak about release.

They speak about freedom.

They speak about deathlessness.

They speak about crossing over.

They speak about escape from the world.

They speak about the end of bondage.

And they speak as people who have attained something.

Yet when these verses are read through the modern assumption that anattā—understood as the denial of self—is itself the supreme practice, something remarkable becomes visible:

No elder bhikkhus and bhikkhunis actually practiced ANATTĀ! They did not even mention this word. Why? Why has a concept of ANATTĀ that no one practiced at the Buddha’s time become a central practice for today’s practitioners? What has happened?

Their voices only describe a path of renunciation, concentration, higher seeing, disenchantment, dispassion, relinquishment, and release.

This deserves serious consideration.

If the people who actually completed Gautama Buddha's path do NOT describe their liberation practices in the language in which modern Buddhism teaches such as anattā, then we must ask how and why anattā became transformed into one of the dominant practices of Buddhism today.

That historical and doctrinal development cannot simply be assumed away. It must be examined.

Listen to the Voices

That is why I have chosen the title Voices of Liberation. The title is deliberate.

Voices means that the elders themselves are allowed to speak. These are not merely statements about Buddhism written by later interpreters. They are the words attributed to men and women who entered the Buddha's dispensation, undertook the holy life, practiced the path, and declared their practices and attainment.

Liberation means that we must listen to these voices according to the destination they themselves describe. They were not practicing merely to improve their worldly personalities. They were not seeking merely a healthier relationship with life. They were not attempting simply to become mindful human beings.

They were seeking vimutti—release. Release from what? From loka – the world. From the bondages to the world. From attachment to worldly phenomena. From the bondage of worldly-conditioned existence.

And toward what? Toward a real Deathless and Blissful Permanent existence.

The Realm of Nibbāna

The subtitle of this book uses the expression "Realm of Nibbāna." The word "realm" renders the Pāli dhātu. It should not be understood as requiring a particular conception of physical space, geography, or material location as we are perceiving using our senses.

The important distinction is ontological and soteriological. Nibbāna does not belong to loka – the world we are living in and familiar with. It is not another loka-conditioned region within the universe under the universal law of decay and dissolution. It is not simply another existential state produced by causes and conditions of this universe. It is not subject to the universal law governing all existence in this universe, that is characterized by arising and passing away under the universal law of death. Whatever belongs to world-conditioned existence is subject to decay and death.

Nibbāna is the Deathless. Therefore, when the elders speak of deathlessness, release, escape, crossing over, going beyond, peace, permanence, freedom, and final liberation, these expressions deserve to be taken seriously. They should not automatically be reduced to metaphors for psychological well-being. They point toward the very purpose of Gautama Buddha's liberation teaching.

Whether the Deathless is described in terms of a realm, dimension, mode of existence, reality beyond the universe, or by another conceptual framework, the essential point remains:

Nibbāna-dhātu does not belong to loka. It is beyond the jurisdiction of loka-conditioned arising and passing away. It is beyond the realm governed by universal law of decay and death. That is why the attainment of Nibbāna-dhātu is liberation from the loka.

They Were Going Somewhere

A major difference between the reading presented in this book and many modern interpretations of Buddhism concerns the direction of the path.

Modern Buddhism often places enormous emphasis upon changing one's relationship with the present world.

The Buddha's disciples, however, repeatedly speak of going beyond. This is not merely a change in attitude. It is a movement of liberation.

They came from the world. They entered Gautama Buddha's path. They confronted the conditions of worldly existence. They renounced. They practiced. They developed samādhi. They saw. They became disenchanted with the world. They developed dispassion. They relinquished attachment. They became liberated from the world. And they reached the Deathless. This is the movement that I believe must be restored to the center of Buddhist understanding.

From the world → renunciation → practice → higher seeing → disenchantment → dispassion →  liberation → the Deathless.

The Theragāthā and Therīgāthā become profoundly different when read from this perspective. They are not merely collections of ancient poems. They are not merely autobiographical religious literature. They are not simply historical documents illustrating what some early Buddhists happened to believe.

They are voices of practitioners who speak about the path from bondage to liberation. Their words should therefore be read as testimony.

Recovering the Original Direction

I do not claim that every question concerning the early Buddhist texts is simple. Nor do I claim that every verse can be understood without interpretation. But I do insist upon one basic principle:

Interpretation must not be allowed to erase the testimony of the practitioners themselves.

When later interpretations conflict with the plain direction of the elders' own descriptions of practice and realization, we should not automatically force the elders to conform to those later interpretations. We should stop and reconsider.

The purpose of this book is therefore not to create another philosophical system. It is to ask the reader to listen. Listen to the bhikkhus. Listen to the bhikkhunīs. Listen to those who renounced. Listen to those who practiced. Listen to those who saw. Listen to those who became disenchanted. Listen to those who let go. Listen to those who declared liberation. And above all, listen to what they say about where the path leads.

If we genuinely want to know the Dhamma of Gautama the Supreme Arahant, then we must be willing to follow the path all the way to its destination. He taught how to go beyond the world. He taught liberation from bondage to worldly-conditioned existence. He pointed toward Nibbāna-dhātu, the Deathless realm.

And the elders who followed him left their voices behind so that we could hear what that path was like. Those voices deserve to be heard again.

That is why I wrote this book.

This is Voices of Liberation.

title: Blue Valentine and the Future of Human Relationships
content:
What happens when an institution designed for social stability is asked to carry the entire emotional weight of modern human life?

Derek Cianfrance’s Blue Valentine (2010), starring Ryan Gosling as Dean and Michelle Williams as Cindy, is one of the most unsettling films about romantic love precisely because it refuses to give us a simple villain.

The film does not portray the collapse of a marriage as the consequence of one spectacular betrayal. Instead, it shows something much more ordinary—and therefore much more frightening: the gradual transformation of two people who once loved each other deeply.

Dean and Cindy do not simply stop loving each other overnight. Their relationship changes.

And that is the film's deepest insight.

Human emotions are not static possessions. Love, attachment, attraction, admiration, resentment, loyalty, and desire can all change as people themselves change. A relationship that once felt natural can eventually become constraining. Qualities that initially attracted two people can later become precisely the qualities that separate them.

When Love Changes Its Meaning

The film moves between two periods of Dean and Cindy's lives.

In the past, Dean is a charming high-school dropout who falls in love with Cindy, an ambitious pre-med student. Their circumstances are complicated by Cindy's pregnancy from a previous relationship. Dean nevertheless chooses to raise the child as his own, and the two marry.

Their early relationship contains something profoundly human: idealism.

Dean is attracted to Cindy's ambition. Cindy is attracted to Dean's devotion and uncomplicated affection. Each appears to offer the other something missing from their own life.

But several years later, those same qualities have changed meaning.

Dean's devotion, once experienced as romantic, begins to feel suffocating. Cindy's ambition, once admired, becomes associated with emotional distance and dissatisfaction.

The people have not necessarily become completely different people. Rather, the meaning of their characteristics has changed within a changing relationship.

This is one of the film's most painful observations.

The person we once loved does not necessarily disappear. Sometimes the person remains, but the relationship through which we experienced that person no longer exists.

The Mechanics of Heartbreak

Blue Valentine is therefore less a story about betrayal than about erosion.

Resentment accumulates.

Communication becomes increasingly difficult.

Expectations diverge.

Physical and emotional intimacy weaken.

Small disappointments acquire historical weight.

Eventually, the relationship becomes burdened by everything that was never adequately resolved.

This is why the film feels so different from a conventional romantic tragedy. There is no single moment that explains everything.

The marriage deteriorates through thousands of ordinary moments.

A relationship can therefore fail without anyone consciously deciding to destroy it.

Two people can sincerely want things to work and nevertheless discover that they are moving in different directions.

This raises a larger question:

Can an institution designed to create permanence adequately accommodate human beings whose identities, priorities, desires, and aspirations continually change?

Marriage: From Social Institution to Emotional Ideal

Marriage did not historically emerge primarily as a mechanism for maximizing romantic fulfillment.

Across many societies, marriage served economic, familial, reproductive, inheritance, property, labor, political, and social functions. The precise structure varied enormously across cultures and periods, but the institution generally had purposes extending far beyond personal romance.

Modern marriage, however, has accumulated an extraordinary number of expectations.

A spouse may simultaneously be expected to be:

  • a romantic partner,
  • a sexual partner,
  • a best friend,
  • a co-parent,
  • a financial partner,
  • a household manager,
  • an emotional support system,
  • an intellectual companion,
  • a source of personal affirmation,
  • and a lifelong companion.

The modern individual may therefore enter marriage expecting one relationship to satisfy an enormous range of psychological, social, domestic, and emotional needs.

That represents a profound historical transformation.

The question is not whether marriage is "good" or "bad." The more interesting question is whether one relationship structure should be expected to satisfy every major human need for an entire lifetime.

That is the structural question Blue Valentine quietly raises.

The Problem of Permanence

The traditional ideal of lifelong marriage assumes a remarkable degree of continuity.

But human beings do not remain psychologically static for fifty or sixty years.

A person's ambitions at twenty-five may be radically different at forty-five.

Their economic circumstances change.

Their interests change.

Their understanding of themselves changes.

Their spiritual aspirations may change.

Their relationship to sexuality may change.

Their priorities concerning children, career, location, family, and community may change.

Yet the traditional model often treats the relationship as a permanent structure within which all these changes must occur.

This can create a peculiar contradiction.

We recognize that individuals change continuously, yet we construct intimate institutions around the assumption of enduring identity.

The result can be an increasing tension between permanence of commitment and impermanence of human experience.

Beyond the Marriage-or-Divorce Binary

If marriage is not the only possible structure for organizing adult life, what might replace or supplement it?

The answer does not have to be a single alternative.

The future may instead involve a plurality of relationship structures designed for different purposes.

1. Term-Based Partnerships

One possibility is a partnership entered into for a defined period, perhaps five or ten years, followed by an intentional review.

At the end of the period, partners could:

  • renew the agreement,
  • renegotiate its terms,
  • restructure their domestic arrangements,
  • or separate amicably.

The important principle would be renewed consent rather than assumed permanence.

Instead of asking, "How do we remain together because we promised to do so indefinitely?" the partners would periodically ask, "Do we still consciously choose this relationship?"

Such a structure would not eliminate heartbreak or conflict. No contract can do that.

But it could make relationship continuation an active decision rather than simply the default consequence of inertia.

2. Modular Relationships

Another possibility is to stop assuming that every function of adult life must be bundled into one relationship.

Parenting, companionship, housing, finances, romance, and sexuality could theoretically be organized through different agreements.

A parenting partnership, for example, could focus specifically on raising children and providing financial and emotional stability.

A domestic partnership could focus on shared housing, economic cooperation, and companionship.

A romantic relationship could exist without requiring shared property, cohabitation, or joint financial obligations.

The central principle would be functional differentiation.

Instead of asking one institution to perform every function, society could develop multiple forms of cooperation appropriate to different human needs.

3. Networks Instead of Dyads

Traditional marriage concentrates enormous responsibility into a two-person unit.

Two adults are expected to provide each other with companionship, childcare, emotional support, economic cooperation, household labor, sexual intimacy, and care during illness and old age.

That is an extraordinary concentration of responsibility.

An alternative is to distribute some of those responsibilities across wider networks.

Intentional co-living communities, extended households, cooperative housing, shared childcare arrangements, and networks of friends could provide forms of social resilience that do not depend entirely upon the stability of one romantic relationship.

A child, for example, could have several deeply invested adults in their wider community rather than depending entirely upon two parents for every form of support.

This does not mean eliminating the family.

It means expanding the definition of family beyond the romantic couple.

4. Civil Rights Without Romantic Status

There is also a legal question.

Why should important civil rights automatically depend upon being someone's spouse?

Medical decision-making, inheritance, property rights, taxation, caregiving authority, and other legal arrangements can theoretically be structured around designated relationships rather than marital status.

A person might designate a sibling, friend, caregiver, collaborator, or romantic partner as their primary legal beneficiary or decision-maker.

This would separate civil recognition from romantic recognition.

Marriage could then become one relationship choice among several rather than the legal gateway through which adults organize their entire lives.

From Institutional Obligation to Intentionality

These possibilities share one underlying principle:

intentionality.

Traditional institutions often rely upon default assumptions.

You marry.

You remain together.

You share a household.

You raise children.

You combine finances.

You grow old together.

The emerging alternative is more explicit:

What are we actually agreeing to?

What responsibilities do we share?

For how long?

What happens if our circumstances change?

Which functions belong to this relationship, and which belong elsewhere?

What happens when our paths diverge?

These questions may sound less romantic than "forever."

But they may also be more honest.

The future of relationships may not be about eliminating commitment. It may be about making commitment more conscious.

The Other Possibility: Choosing Celibacy

There is another response to the instability of romantic and domestic structures that is rarely discussed in contemporary society with sufficient seriousness: celibacy.

Celibacy is often interpreted as the absence of something—a relationship, sexuality, marriage, family life.

From a spiritual perspective, however, it can represent something entirely different.

It can be a deliberate redirection of human energy.

For someone committed to liberation, the central question is not necessarily:

"How can I build the most satisfying domestic life?"

It may instead be:

"How can I devote the greatest possible proportion of my life to transformation, purification, meditation, wisdom, and liberation?"

That is a fundamentally different orientation.

A Historically Unusual Opportunity

For much of human history, living independently was difficult.

Food production required labor.

Household work required substantial physical effort.

Economic survival was deeply connected to family structures.

Social identity was strongly associated with marriage and kinship.

Religious renunciation therefore often required an institutional framework.

The monastery provided food, shelter, community, discipline, education, and a social environment in which a person could dedicate life to spiritual practice.

The modern world has changed many of those conditions.

A person can now survive without establishing a traditional household.

Food can be purchased rather than produced.

Information can be accessed instantly.

Texts once available only in specialized libraries can be obtained digitally.

Meditation instructions, philosophical works, languages, lectures, and communities can be accessed across geographical boundaries.

This creates a historically unusual possibility:

an individual can organize a substantial portion of life around inner transformation without necessarily depending upon marriage or a traditional household for survival.

Celibacy as Deliberate Energy Allocation

From this perspective, celibacy is not merely sexual abstinence.

It is a question of allocation.

Time is limited.

Attention is limited.

Emotional energy is limited.

Mental energy is limited.

Human life is limited.

Every major commitment therefore consumes a portion of these finite resources.

Marriage and family can be profoundly meaningful for those who choose them. But they also involve responsibilities that naturally demand substantial time and attention.

A person who chooses celibacy for spiritual purposes makes a different allocation.

Instead of concentrating life around domestic consolidation, the person may concentrate it around meditation, study, ethical purification, solitude, service, and liberation.

This is not necessarily an escape from life.

It can be a deliberate redefinition of what constitutes a meaningful life.

The New Challenge: Distraction Without Boundaries

Yet the modern world creates a strange paradox.

It has made independent living easier while making sustained concentration harder.

The traditional renunciant had to physically leave many worldly environments.

The contemporary individual can carry the world into the room through a small electronic device.

Entertainment, advertising, social media, sexual imagery, news, arguments, commercial persuasion, and endless novelty can enter private space continuously.

The problem is therefore no longer merely physical proximity to worldly stimulation.

It is permanent accessibility.

A person can be physically alone while psychologically surrounded by thousands of voices.

This makes deliberate boundaries increasingly important for anyone pursuing serious contemplative practice.

Solitude Is Not Just Isolation

There is also an important distinction between solitude and isolation.

Isolation is the absence of human connection.

Solitude is the intentional creation of space in which consciousness can become quiet enough to observe itself.

A celibate practitioner therefore cannot simply remove relationships and assume that spiritual development will automatically follow.

A disciplined life still requires friendship, guidance, community, ethical responsibility, and meaningful human connection.

The objective is not to completely become disconnected from humanity.

It is to become less enslaved by compulsive attachment.

A Different Measure of Freedom

This leads back to Blue Valentine.

The film asks what happens when two human beings enter a permanent institution while continuing to change internally.

A spiritual path asks a different question:

What happens when a human being deliberately reduces unnecessary entanglement in order to devote life to transformation?

These are not equivalent questions.

The first concerns how human beings organize intimate life.

The second concerns what human beings ultimately want from life itself.

And that distinction matters.

If the highest aspiration of a person is domestic happiness, then marriage or another partnership structure may be entirely appropriate.

If the highest aspiration is the cultivation of wisdom, liberation, and transcendence of worldly existence, then a radically different life structure may become appropriate.

The Future May Be Plural

Perhaps the future does not require one universal model.

Marriage may continue.

Long-term partnerships may continue.

Co-parenting arrangements may develop.

Communal living may expand.

Friendship networks may assume greater legal and social significance.

People may experiment with more flexible forms of companionship.

And some individuals will choose celibacy and dedicate themselves to spiritual practice.

The important development is not that one structure replaces another.

It is that human beings gain greater freedom to consciously choose the structure appropriate to their actual aims.

The mistake is assuming that every human being wants the same destination and therefore requires the same vehicle.

From "Forever" to "For What?"

Perhaps the deepest lesson of Blue Valentine is not that love fails.

It is that love exists within time.

People change.

Relationships change.

Circumstances change.

Desires change.

And institutions designed around permanence must continually confront the impermanence of the people inside them.

The mature question may therefore be less:

"How can we guarantee that this relationship lasts forever?"

and more:

"What are we building together, why are we building it, and does it still serve the lives we are actually living?"

That question can apply to marriage, partnership, community, friendship, and even the solitary life.

For those who choose the path of celibacy and spiritual liberation, the question becomes still more fundamental:

If human life is temporary, what is worthy of giving one's limited time and energy to?

The modern world has unexpectedly created conditions in which a person can ask that question with greater freedom than many previous generations possessed.

The challenge is no longer simply whether one can escape worldly structures.

The challenge is whether one can use freedom wisely.

And perhaps that is the real opportunity of the present age: not the abolition of marriage, not the abolition of romance, and not the rejection of human connection, but the emergence of a society in which adults can consciously distinguish between love, companionship, parenting, economic cooperation, domestic life, sexuality, friendship, and spiritual liberation rather than assuming that all of them must be contained within one institution.

The future of human relationships may therefore be less about finding the perfect permanent arrangement and more about learning how to build relationships—and lives—that are consciously aligned with what human beings actually seek.

title: VOLUME II of BHAGAVAD-GĪTĀ is Available
content:
on Amazon

What if reading the Bhagavad-Gītā is not merely an encounter with an ancient religious text, but a journey into the subconscious spiritual world of ancient India?

This Volume II continues Bhante Mudita’s comparative examination of the Gītā through the liberation teaching of Gautama the Supreme Arahant. It asks a more uncomfortable question: What does the Gītā reveal about the religious doctrines, aspirations, fears, promises, and competing claims that surrounded the human search for liberation in ancient India?

At the heart of the Gītā stands Kṛṣṇa, who offers Arjuna a remarkable solution to his crisis. Arjuna is caught between worldly duty and his inclination of renunciation. Rather than abandoning the battlefield, he is taught Karma-Yoga: remain in the world, perform one's duty, relinquish attachment to its fruits, remember Kṛṣṇa, and ultimately attain the divine.

But is this really the same liberation pursued by the ancient renunciates?

Volume II examines this question verse by verse through the vocabulary of the Sanskrit text and the liberation framework preserved in Theravāda Pali Canon. It investigates saṁnyāsa, Karma-Yoga, Sāṅkhya, samādhi, Brahmacariya, Ātmā, nirvāṇa, Brahma, bhakti, the guṇas, divine union, cosmic existence, and versions of liberation.

A central discovery of this reading is the tension between two radically different destinations. One path demands complete renunciation of worldly existence and seeks an ultimate exit from saṃsāra. The other permits the practitioner to remain within society, perform worldly duties, and seek freedom through inner detachment and devotion.

The book therefore asks a fundamental question:

Are these really two paths to the same destination?

Again and again, the Gītā makes extraordinary claims: that action and renunciation lead to the same goal; that Karma-Yoga may be superior to complete renunciation; that the practitioner can act without being bound; that devotion to Kṛṣṇa leads to the supreme destination; and that what is called nirvāṇa can ultimately be understood in relation to Kṛṣṇa.

Bhante Mudita examines these claims critically and compares them with the radically renunciant path of Gautama. From this perspective, the difference is not merely philosophical. It concerns the destination itself.

Does liberation mean remaining within the cosmic order while becoming inwardly detached? Does it mean union with or absorption into a divine source? Or does genuine liberation require complete transcendence of the world and entry into Nibbāna-Dhātu, the Deathless realm?

This comparison also casts new light on Gautama’s own life.

Gautama was born into the very civilization represented by the Gītā and its surrounding traditions. He inherited a world already filled with gods, sacrifices, spiritual teachers, promises of heaven, theories of immortality, yogic disciplines, claims concerning the soul-spirit, and competing declarations about the ultimate destination of human existence.

Yet Gautama did not simply accept these claims.

He left the life of a prince.

He became a renunciate.

He endured years of extraordinarily difficult spiritual practices in the forest.

He pursued samādhi and liberation wisdom.

And, rather than accepting liberation on the authority of a deity or tradition, he personally sought to discover what was true.

This makes the comparison with Kṛṣṇa especially important. Was Gautama’s great quest itself a response to an ancient religious world already crowded with competing promises of immortality and liberation?

Perhaps the Gītā allows us to see more clearly the intellectual and spiritual environment from which Gautama emerged—and therefore to appreciate more deeply why he undertook his own independent search.

This book does not ask the reader to accept its conclusions merely because they come from a Buddhist monk. It asks the reader to examine the Sanskrit, compare the doctrines, follow the logic of the competing paths, and decide independently.

The question is ultimately simple but profound:

When different teachers promise liberation, immortality, heaven, divine union, or the Deathless, how do we determine which promise is true?

Read the Gītā carefully.

Read Gautama carefully.

Then decide for yourself.

This is not merely a commentary on the Bhagavad-Gītā. It is an invitation to enter the spiritual mind of ancient India—and to reconsider one of the most important questions ever asked by the Indian renunciate tradition:

What does it actually mean to be liberated?

Prologue: From the Renunciate Path to Karma-Yoga

The first volume of Bhagavad-Gītā: A Theravāda Buddhist Reading began with a simple but fundamental question: What does the Bhagavad-Gītā reveal when it is read through the liberation teaching of Gautama the Supreme Arahant, rather than through later sectarian assumptions about either Hinduism or Buddhism?

Volume I established that the Bhagavad-Gītā cannot be understood adequately by isolating it from the ancient Indian civilization in which it arose. The Gītā belongs to the vast spiritual, philosophical, social, and cultural world of ancient Bharata—a world in which questions concerning karma, rebirth, dharma, meditation, renunciation, higher realms, the nature of the human being, and liberation were already deeply established. The Mahābhārata itself was not merely a literary composition but part of the cultural atmosphere through which generations of Indians understood themselves and the world. Gautama the Supreme Arahant emerged from this same civilization and inherited this ancient spiritual vocabulary.

Chapter 1: The Historical and Social World of the Bhagavad-Gītā

Chapter 1 therefore examined the historical background and social context of the Bhagavad-Gītā. The battlefield of Kurukṣetra is not an isolated philosophical stage. It represents an ancient society structured around family, kingship, social duty, lineage, warfare, sacrifice, Brahmanical authority, and the obligations of the various social classes.

The crisis of Arjuna is consequently much deeper than the personal fear of a warrior standing before battle. His crisis is the collision between two powerful demands: the demand of worldly duty and the desire to renounce worldly life. Arjuna sees his relatives, teachers, elders, and friends standing on the opposite side of the battlefield. He begins to question whether victory, kingdom, pleasure, and even life itself have any value when they must be purchased through the destruction of those to whom he is bound by family and social obligation. This historical and social setting becomes essential for understanding everything that follows.

The Gītā is speaking to a human being who is deeply embedded in society. Arjuna cannot simply abandon his position, his family, his kingdom, and his social obligations without consequences. The problem that emerges throughout the Gītā is therefore not simply, How can a human being become liberated? It is also, How can a human being pursue spiritual freedom while continuing to participate in the world? This tension becomes central moving from Chapter 2 into Chapter 3.

Chapter 2: The Renunciate Path and the Forgotten Significance of Ātmā

Chapter 2 is, in many respects, the most remarkable chapter of the Gītā for a student of Gautama's liberation teaching of renunciants.

When read carefully, Chapter 2 presents an extraordinary concentration of terminology and concepts associated with the ancient Indian renunciate path: Ātmā, Brahma-nirvāṇa, Brahmacariya, bhikkhu/bhikṣu, paññā/prajñā, samādhi, rāga, dosa/dveṣa, moha, the worldly shore, the other shore, renunciation, restraint of the senses, freedom from craving, and liberation from the cycle of birth and death.

More importantly, Chapter 2 describes a path that is remarkably close to, if not the exactly summary from a 200 BC’s view, the renunciate path preserved in the Bhikkhu and Bhikkhuni lineages of Gautama the Supreme Arahant. This is not merely a path of intellectual knowledge. It is not merely a philosophical yoga for contemplative thinkers. It is a path of renunciation.

The practitioner turns away from the worldly objects of attraction, abandons rāga, dosa, and moha, disciplines the senses, cultivates samādhi and paññā, develops disenchantment with the world, allows worldly passion to fade away, and ultimately seeks complete liberation from worldly existence. As Volume I argued, this is fundamentally a path of total renunciation of worldly life and activities for complete liberation from the world.

The sequence is therefore unmistakable: Nibbidā → Virāga → Vimutti. Disenchantment with the world leads to fading away of worldly passion, which leads to complete liberation from worldly existence. The ultimate problem is not simply suffering inside the world. The problem is continued involuntary existence within the world—continued birth, aging, death, and rebirth. The goal is therefore not to become more comfortable within saṃsāra, nor merely to ascend to a higher cosmic state, but to overcome the entire cycle of worldly existence and reach the deathless realm of Nibbāna.

And yet one striking feature of the Gītā must be emphasized. The doctrine of anattā is absent as a teaching from this presentation.

The Gītā does not present anattā as a meditation subject, a practice, a method of liberation, or the central philosophical discovery by which the practitioner is instructed to deny the existence of Ātmā. Instead, the language repeatedly points toward Ātmā as the internal spiritual principle of the human being. Chapter 2 even speaks directly in the language of Ātmā, while the renunciate path is presented as a movement away from the external world toward the transcendent shore.

This absence is significant.

If the doctrine in today’s mainstream academia commonly presented as the defining teaching of Gautama Buddha—“there is no self,” “there is no soul,” and liberation comes through realizing anattā—were truly the central engine of Gautama's original renunciate path, one would expect this teaching to appear naturally within a text that preserves such a detailed summary of the ancient Indian path of renunciation.

But it does not.

What we instead find is a vocabulary of liberation built around renunciation, Brahmacariya, samādhi, paññā, purification, abandonment of rāga, dosa, and moha, nibbidā, virāga, and vimutti.

This raises a profound question that Volume I deliberately places before the reader: Has the later Buddhist emphasis on anattā obscured the actual structure of Gautama's original liberation teaching?

The argument of this work is that it has.

Modern Buddhist interpretation has elevated anattā into a dominant doctrinal principle and, in doing so, has frequently displaced the actual practical structure of Gautama's path. Volume I therefore returns attention to what the earliest renunciants actually practiced: the purification of the human being, the overcoming of worldly bondage, the destruction of rāga, dosa, and moha, and the movement beyond the world toward Nibbāna.

Gautama's teaching was not designed to make the practitioner intellectually comfortable with worldly existence. It was designed to escape it. The ancient path is a path toward the Deathless.

The Historical Significance of Chapter 2

The remarkable similarity between Chapter 2 and the renunciate path of Gautama also raises a historical question.

The Bhagavad-Gītā was incorporated into the larger Mahābhārata literature during a period in which Gautama's renunciate movement had already become a major spiritual force in India. The Gītā's Chapter 2 can therefore be read as preserving, a summary, in another Sanskrit tradition, a substantial body of the ancient renunciate vocabulary and methodology that had become associated with the liberation movement of the śramaṇas.

This is why Chapter 2 is so important.

It allows us to see that the renunciate path was not an invention of a later Buddhist scholastic tradition. The spiritual vocabulary was already part of the ancient Indian world. Gautama did not appear in an intellectual vacuum. He inherited an ancient path, rediscovered its deepest dimensions, purified it, systematized it, and led his bhikkhu and bhikkhuni disciples toward complete liberation from the world to attain the deathless, permanent and joyful existence in another realm names Nibbana. Volume I therefore emphasized Gautama as the restorer of the purāṇa-magga, the ancient path, rather than as a philosopher who invented an entirely new spiritual system.

Chapter 2 consequently stands at the threshold of the entire argument of this book. It shows us the possibility of complete renunciation.

But Chapter 3 asks a different question: What happens when human beings are not prepared to renounce the world?

Chapter 3: Karma-Yoga and the Necessity of Remaining in the World

Chapter 3 introduces the great counter-movement. Arjuna has just heard a teaching that points toward renunciation, spiritual discernment, restraint, samādhi, and liberation. Naturally, he asks why he is then being commanded to perform terrible worldly action. The Gītā's answer is Karma-Yoga.

Human beings have social responsibilities. They have families, kingdoms, occupations, duties, relationships, and obligations. They cannot all simply abandon society, take up the alms bowl, enter the forest, and devote themselves entirely to meditation and liberation. This is the social problem that Karma-Yoga attempts to solve.

The Gītā therefore teaches Arjuna to continue acting while abandoning attachment to the fruits of action. One should perform one's obligatory duty without becoming attached to the results. Action itself need not become a source of bondage if the practitioner acts without personal attachment.

This is the fundamental innovation of Chapter 3. Instead of saying, leave the world, it says, in effect: Remain in the world, perform your duty, but do not become attached to what you do.

This allows the individual to participate in society while attempting to maintain an inward freedom from the results of action. The tension between the two paths is therefore unmistakable. Chapter 2 presents the possibility of complete renunciation and departure from worldly existence. Chapter 3 presents a way for the householder, warrior, ruler, and socially obligated person to continue living and acting within the world while attempting to free himself from karmic attachment.

The Gītā thus creates a spiritual accommodation between liberation and worldly responsibility. The practitioner does not necessarily have to abandon action. He can transform action into yoga. He can perform his duty. He can sacrifice the fruits. He can remain inwardly unattached. And through this process, action itself becomes a means of purification. This is the great subject that Volume II will examine more deeply.

Chapter 4: The Fruits of Karma-Yoga and the Question of the Final Destination

Chapter 4 develops the consequences of this teaching. Karma-Yoga is joined with jñāna, renunciation, sacrifice, devotion, and the divine identity of Kṛṣṇa. Action performed without attachment becomes karmically neutral, while knowledge destroys ignorance and enables the practitioner to transcend ordinary bondage.

But here the deepest problem emerges. Where does this path ultimately lead? The Gītā's answer moves toward higher cosmic existence, divine participation, celestial realms, and ultimately union with or re-absorption into the divine source.

This is where the distinction between the Gītā and Gautama's liberation teaching becomes fundamental. There is a profound difference between ascending within the universe and exiting the universe. There is a profound difference between union with the cosmic source and entry into Nibbāna-Dhātu. There is a profound difference between non-duality and Gautama's path of liberation through the destruction of rāga, dosa, and moha.

The so-called transcendence of duality described in the Gītā does not produce the same destination as Gautama's liberation. In the Gītā, the practitioner can remain active within the material field while realizing an unconditioned divine core beyond the changing guṇas. The world becomes something to transcend inwardly while continuing to participate in it.

But this is not the liberation taught by Gautama the Supreme Arahant. Gautama's liberation is not the realization that the individual is ultimately one with the universe. It is not dissolution into the universal source. It is not absorption into the cosmic engine. It is not merely elevation into a higher heaven. It is exit.

The purified Citta leaves behind the entire worldly structure of loka and passes beyond the universe into the deathless realm of Nibbāna-Dhātu. Volume I therefore distinguished sharply between divine re-absorption and true renunciation: the former remains connected to the cosmic structure, while the latter culminates in complete transcendence of it. This distinction is the key to reading the Bhagavad-Gītā through Gautama's Dhamma.

From Volume I to Volume II

Volume I therefore established four fundamental movements.

Chapter 1 placed the Bhagavad-Gītā within its historical, civilizational, and social environment.

Chapter 2 revealed the extraordinary presence of the ancient renunciate path: Ātmā, Brahmacariya, samādhi, paññā, purification, abandonment of rāga, dosa, and moha, nibbidā, virāga, vimutti, and the aspiration toward the deathless.

Chapter 3 introduced Karma-Yoga as the solution to the social problem created by radical renunciation: human beings have worldly duties, and they must continue to act, but they can attempt to free themselves from attachment to the fruits of their actions.

Chapter 4 developed the fruits of this path into a larger theological and cosmological system involving divine knowledge, higher realms, non-duality, divine participation, and ultimately union with the cosmic source.

The crucial question is therefore no longer simply whether the Bhagavad-Gītā contains elements of the ancient Indian liberation path. It clearly does. The more important question is: What happened to that renunciate path when it was placed alongside the demands of worldly duty, social order, divine sovereignty, and cosmic union?

And beyond that lies an even more fundamental question: Does liberation mean leaving the world, or does it mean remaining within the world without attachment?

These are not two descriptions of the same liberation. They are two fundamentally different answers to the human problem. Gautama's path is a path of world-renunciation. Karma-Yoga is a path of worldly engagement without attachment. One seeks to conquer saṃsāra and exit the universe. The other seeks freedom while continuing to participate within the cosmic order. One culminates in Nibbāna-Dhātu, the Deathless realm. The other ultimately directs consciousness toward divine and cosmic realities.

Volume II begins from this threshold.

Having established the historical setting, recovered the renunciate vocabulary, examined the conflict between renunciation and social duty, and exposed the fundamental difference between Nibbāna and cosmic re-absorption, we can now proceed further into the Bhagavad-Gītā and examine what its teachings reveal about Ātmā, karma, renunciation, knowledge, devotion, divine reality, cosmic existence, and liberation.

The purpose is not to force the Gītā to become Buddhism. Nor is it to force Gautama's Dhamma to conform to the Gītā. The purpose is much more direct: to read the Sanskrit carefully, to recover the ancient spiritual vocabulary shared by these traditions, and then to distinguish precisely where their paths converge—and where they finally separate.

Only by making this distinction can we understand what the Bhagavad-Gītā is actually teaching, what Gautama the Supreme Arahant actually taught, and why the difference between remaining within the universe and exiting the universe into the Deathless is the decisive question of liberation.

title: A New Publication
content:
Vandanā Pūjā – Homage and Veneration

More Than a Chanting Book: An Introduction to the Arahanist Order of Canada and the Liberation Path of Gautama

We are pleased to announce the publication of Vandanā Pūjā: Homage and Veneration, a new book by Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera, founding Ācariya of Arahanism and spiritual founder of the Arahanist Order of Canada.

Now available on Amazon, this publication marks an important milestone in the development of the Arahanist Order and its commitment to preserving, practising, and transmitting the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

At first glance, Vandanā Pūjā may appear to be a traditional Buddhist chanting book. It certainly serves that purpose, bringing together important Pāli recitations, devotional practices, protective suttas, and religious ceremonies. However, its scope extends considerably further.

More Than Chanting: From Devotion to Spiritual Practice

It is more than a chanting book. It is an introduction to an entire religious tradition, a framework for spiritual training, and a guide to the renunciant life.

The opening sections contain traditional practices of homage and recollection, including the Three Refuges (Tisarana), recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, and Paritta-Paritāṇa, the protective recitation of sacred discourses.

Readers will also find the Ratana Sutta, Mahā Maṅgala Sutta, Karaṇīya Mettā Sutta, and other traditional Pāli recitations.

The book provides Pāli texts alongside English translations and explanations, allowing practitioners to approach these recitations with greater understanding.

Yet chanting is only one aspect of religious life.

A Progressive Path of Renunciation

The deeper purpose of these practices is to strengthen confidence in the Dhamma, cultivate wholesome qualities, establish ethical discipline, and direct the mind towards spiritual development.

For this reason, the book also explores the Five Precepts (Pañca Sīla) and the Uposatha Eight Precepts (Aṭṭhaṅga Uposatha Sīla), explaining their significance as foundations for progressively deeper renunciation.

  • Five Precepts: The foundation of ethical conduct in daily life.
  • Uposatha Eight Precepts: A more intensive discipline of restraint and spiritual cultivation.
  • Upāsaka / Upāsikā Ordination: A formal commitment to sustained lay renunciant training.
  • Sāmaṇera / Sāmaṇerī Ordination: The beginning of formal novice monastic life.
  • Bhikkhu / Bhikkhunī Upasampadā: Full ordination and the responsibilities of fully ordained monastic life.

Readers are encouraged to move beyond the mere recitation of religious texts and bring their meaning into daily conduct and spiritual practice.

One of the distinctive features of this publication is its presentation of a progressive training system within the Arahanist Order.

Not everyone begins with the same circumstances or degree of commitment. Some begin by undertaking the Five Precepts, while others are prepared to observe the Eight Precepts and devote more time to spiritual cultivation.

The book introduces the different stages of commitment within the Arahanist framework:

Understanding the Monastic Life and Its Discipline

These stages are accompanied by explanations of their respective commitments, responsibilities, and spiritual purposes.

The intention is to establish a meaningful progression through which individuals can deepen their dedication to the Dhamma and, where appropriate, undertake the full renunciant vocation.

The Heart of Arahanism: The Training for Arahantship

Renunciation is not treated simply as an outward religious identity. It is a deliberate reorientation of life towards spiritual cultivation, sense restraint, and liberation from worldly attachment.

Vandanā Pūjā also contains substantial material introducing the principles of monastic formation within the Arahanist Order of Canada.

It discusses the three principal stages of renunciant life: Upāsaka/Upāsikā, Sāmaṇera/Sāmaṇerī, and Bhikkhu/Bhikkhunī.

Particular attention is given to the Theravāda Vinaya, the Pāṭimokkha, the responsibilities of fully ordained monastics, and the importance of the traditional five-year period of dependence upon a qualified teacher following full ordination.

The publication also addresses the full renunciant path for women and the Arahanist Order's commitment to developing opportunities for Bhikkhunī training.

Introducing the Arahanist Order of Canada

These sections provide readers with an introduction to the institutional and disciplinary foundations necessary for sustaining a serious monastic community.

For those considering monastic life, they offer an opportunity to understand the responsibilities and spiritual commitments involved before undertaking such a vocation.

Perhaps the most substantial aspect of the book is its presentation of the Arahanist understanding of the Liberation Path.

Arahanism places Arahantship at the centre of religious life: the complete ending of rāga, dosa, and moha, and liberation from worldly bondage.

The book introduces the relationship between Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā—ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom—and explores how these qualities are developed within a life of renunciation.

A Book for Practitioners, Supporters, and Those Exploring the Renunciant Path

A dedicated section, The Monastic Training for Arahantship, examines the four approaches to the development of Samatha and Vipassanā, the cultivation of Samādhi, the development of insight, the abandonment of fetters and underlying tendencies, and the ultimate purpose of contemplative training.

It also includes the Yuganaddha Sutta (AN 4.170), which presents four approaches leading to Arahantship.

The emphasis throughout is that meditation and spiritual development must be understood within the larger purpose of liberation.

The objective is not simply temporary tranquillity, improved concentration, or a more comfortable experience of ordinary life. The training is directed towards the abandonment of worldly attachment and the supreme liberation taught by Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Another important purpose of this publication is to introduce readers to the religious identity, principles, and long-term vision of the Arahanist Order of Canada.

An Offering to the Dhamma and Future Generations

The book contains a dedicated section explaining the Order's religious purpose, its Theravāda canonical foundation, its understanding of renunciation, and its commitment to developing a living monastic community in Canada.

The Arahanist Order is a Canadian Theravāda lineage dedicated to preserving and practising the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Its work encompasses monastic training, meditation, scriptural study, religious education, publication, and the establishment of communities in which the Dhamma can be studied and practised.

The long-term vision includes local Arahanist viharas, a dedicated monastic training centre, residential meditation facilities, and opportunities for both men and women to undertake serious renunciant training.

The Order also recognises that a living religious tradition requires the participation and support of committed lay practitioners. Their generosity, service, and cooperation help sustain the conditions necessary for monastic life and the transmission of the Dhamma.

In this respect, Vandanā Pūjā serves as an introduction not only to religious practices but also to the wider community and institutional vision that the Arahanist Order seeks to establish.

This publication has been prepared for different audiences.

For those who participate in communal chanting, it provides a practical collection of traditional recitations and devotional practices.

For lay practitioners, it offers guidance on ethical discipline, the Eight Precepts, and progressive spiritual commitment.

For those interested in meditation, it introduces the Arahanist understanding of Samatha, Vipassanā, and the training directed towards Arahantship.

For those considering renunciation, it provides an introduction to the stages of religious commitment, novice ordination, full monastic life, and the responsibilities of the Saṅgha.

For supporters and visitors, it offers a comprehensive introduction to the identity, principles, and aspirations of the Arahanist Order of Canada.

It is therefore a book that can be approached in different ways: used during chanting, consulted when observing the precepts, studied when exploring monastic discipline, or read as an introduction to Arahanism.

Preparing this book has been an undertaking of considerable scope. It brings together traditional Pāli recitations, translations, explanations, religious practices, training principles, ordination guidelines, and the institutional vision of the Arahanist Order.

As expressed in its dedication, this publication is offered to Gautama, the Supreme Arahant; to the Dhamma that guides the renunciant from ethical discipline to concentration, from concentration to wisdom, and from wisdom to liberation; and to the generations of renunciants who have devoted their lives to preserving, practising, and transmitting the path.

The intention is that this book will serve not merely as a collection of words to recite, but as a practical contribution to the preservation and transmission of the Dhamma.

May the chants become occasions for recollection. May the precepts become foundations for conduct. May study lead to practice, and may practice deepen the aspiration to abandon worldly attachment and realise the Deathless.

Vandanā Pūjā: Homage and Veneration is now available on Amazon.

We warmly invite practitioners, supporters, students of the Dhamma, and those interested in the renunciant life to explore this new publication and learn more about the Arahanist Order of Canada.

May the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant, continue to be studied, practised, and transmitted to future generations.

Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera
Founding Ācariya of Arahanism
Spiritual Founder, Arahanist Order of Canada

Arahanism — The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.
