title: Living in Truth: The Courage to Seek What Is Real
content:
Reflections on Verity (2026), the human tendency toward self-deception, and the Arahanist pursuit of truth.

The Irony of Verity

The 2026 film Verity, adapted from Colleen Hoover's novel, leaves a deeply unsettling impression. Its world is entangled in grief, obsession, manipulation, and competing versions of reality. Characters conceal their intentions, protect their interests, and construct narratives that serve their own purposes. As the story unfolds, distinguishing truth from deception becomes increasingly difficult.

The irony begins with the title itself.

Verity means truth: the quality of being true or a fundamental truth. Yet the narrative revolves around a character whose life and manuscript are entangled in ambiguity, deception, and conflicting accounts of reality. The very title invites us to question whether human beings genuinely seek truth or merely invoke it when it serves their interests.

This raises a question far greater than the narrative of a film:

Why is it so difficult for human beings to live in truth?

Why do people manipulate, conceal, distort, and sometimes deceive even themselves? Why does preserving one's own interests so frequently become more important than acknowledging reality?

Perhaps the greatest obstacle to truth is not that truth is inaccessible, but that human beings are often unwilling to accept it when it conflicts with what they desire.

The Reality We Construct

Human beings do not always approach reality with an impartial desire to understand it. More often, they approach it with existing attachments, expectations, fears, and preferences.

When reality agrees with what we want, we readily accept it. When it contradicts us, however, we begin to negotiate with it.

We reinterpret events, justify our decisions, conceal inconvenient information, assign responsibility elsewhere, and construct explanations that protect our self-image. Eventually, we may become so attached to our own interpretations that we mistake them for reality itself.

This is one of the most troubling dimensions of deception: a person may begin by deliberately misleading others and eventually become deceived by their own fabrication.

From an Arahanist perspective, this tendency is rooted in the unpurified citta.

Rāga, dosa, and moha—craving and attachment, fear and aversion, and ignorance and delusion—continually influence how the individual perceives and responds to the world. Craving and attachment resists losing what it desires. Fear and aversion resists accepting what it dislikes. Ignorance and delusion prevents clear comprehension.

Consequently, the mind does not simply observe reality; it attempts to accommodate reality to its own defilements.

A person who cannot accept personal wrongdoing may construct an explanation that makes the wrongdoing appear justified. Someone who fears losing another person's affection may conceal the truth to preserve the relationship. Someone attached to authority may reject any information that challenges their position.

The underlying problem is not merely dishonesty in speech. It is the condition of the mind that produces and sustains dishonesty.

We often do not see reality as it is. We see it through the desires, fears, and attachments we are unwilling to relinquish.

Truth Is Not a Matter of Personal Preference

One of the defining characteristics of contemporary discourse is the tendency to treat personal interpretation as though it were equivalent to truth.

Everyone has opinions, experiences, perspectives, and interpretations. These may differ considerably. But the existence of different perspectives does not mean that reality itself becomes different for each individual.

What happened does not change because we remember it differently. A false statement does not become true because someone sincerely believes it. An action does not become blameless simply because its consequences are inconvenient to acknowledge.

We must distinguish between what is true, what we believe to be true, and what we wish were true.

These are not necessarily the same.

Intellectual honesty therefore requires the willingness to acknowledge uncertainty, admit ignorance, reconsider assumptions, and correct mistaken conclusions. Saying "I do not know" may be more truthful than offering an elaborate explanation. Admitting "I was wrong" may require greater integrity than defending an established position.

Living in truth does not mean possessing complete knowledge. It means refusing to knowingly substitute personal preference for reality.

Truth must remain greater than our attachment to being right.

No One Is Exempt: Not Even Monks

There is an important dimension of this subject that deserves particular attention.

Spirituality and religious life do not automatically protect anyone from self-deception.

A person may wear monastic robes, observe religious ceremonies, possess extensive scriptural knowledge, teach Dhamma, and be recognised as a spiritual authority. Yet none of these things, by themselves, establishes that the person's citta is purified or that their conduct is consistently grounded in truth.

A monk can construct a spiritual identity just as a layperson constructs a worldly identity.

A religious teacher can defend personal interests while speaking about renunciation. A spiritual institution can preserve its reputation at the expense of acknowledging its shortcomings. Someone who teaches others about truth may remain unwilling to examine the distortions within their own mind.

Religious language does not guarantee mental purity. Religious authority does not guarantee wisdom. Ordination does not eliminate the responsibility for individual purification.

Indeed, the spiritual life demands an even greater commitment to honesty because its purpose is the abandonment of defilements, not the construction of a more convincing identity.

One cannot genuinely pursue liberation while continually protecting the very attachments that obstruct it.

This applies equally to every individual, regardless of religious affiliation, intellectual achievement, social position, or spiritual status.

The robes do not make a person truthful. Knowledge does not make a person purified. A spiritual identity is not liberation.

The essential question remains the same: what is happening within one's own citta?

Living in Truth Requires Renunciation

From the Arahanist perspective, truthfulness is inseparable from the pursuit of liberation.

The individual must be willing to relinquish attachment to personal narratives, self-justification, reputation, recognition, and the desire to control how others perceive them.

This is also an aspect of renunciation.

Renunciation is not confined to abandoning material possessions or withdrawing from worldly circumstances. It also involves abandoning the mental attachments through which we continually construct and defend an image of ourselves.

Can we acknowledge wrongdoing without immediately defending ourselves?

Can we accept that another person may disagree with us without becoming hostile?

Can we relinquish an interpretation when we discover that it is mistaken?

Can we admit that our desires have influenced our judgement?

Can we remain honest when dishonesty would be more advantageous?

These are not merely tests of moral character. They reveal the extent to which rāga, dosa, and moha continue to influence the individual.

The purification of citta requires the gradual abandonment of these defilements. Through Sīla, Samādhi, and Paññā, the individual cultivates the discipline, stability, and discernment necessary to understand the mind and overcome its distortions.

Truthfulness is therefore not an isolated virtue. It belongs to the larger process of individual purification.

Have We Lost the Courage to Seek Truth?

Throughout ancient history, we encounter individuals who devoted themselves to investigating existence, questioning established beliefs, and seeking answers to fundamental questions about life and liberation.

For the genuine seeker, truth was not merely an intellectual possession or a convenient opinion. It was something worth pursuing, even when the pursuit demanded the abandonment of familiar beliefs, established positions, and personal attachments.

One cannot help but question whether this spirit has weakened in contemporary society.

We have access to more information than any previous generation, yet information is not the same as wisdom. The ability to communicate opinions is not the same as the willingness to examine them. The accumulation of knowledge does not necessarily produce an honest mind.

People increasingly defend their identities, affiliations, beliefs, and personal narratives. They seek confirmation rather than examination, agreement rather than understanding, and recognition rather than genuine self-knowledge.

The question is not whether we have enough information to discover truth. It is whether we possess the intellectual honesty and mental discipline to accept what we discover.

Are we willing to be wrong?

Are we willing to abandon what we have spent years defending?

Are we willing to discover that the reality we constructed for ourselves was never reality at all?

These questions are especially important for anyone who claims to pursue spiritual development.

A Call to Seek and Live in Truth

Perhaps the greatest challenge is not to demand honesty from the world, but to establish it within ourselves.

We cannot expect others to be truthful while remaining unwilling to examine our own dishonesty. We cannot condemn manipulation while manipulating circumstances for personal advantage. We cannot speak about liberation while remaining attached to the illusions that protect our desires.

The Arahanist path places the responsibility for purification upon the individual. We begin by examining our own citta, establishing Sīla, cultivating Samādhi, and developing Paññā. We learn to recognise the influence of rāga, dosa, and moha and work toward their eradication.

The objective is not to construct a better version of ourselves for others to admire. It is to purify the mind itself.

We do not need to know everything. We do not need to be right about everything. We must, however, remain committed to discovering what is true, acknowledging what is uncertain, and correcting what is mistaken.

Let us recover the courage to question, investigate, and seek truth.

Let us refuse to manipulate reality for personal advantage, deceive others for self-preservation, or deceive ourselves for the comfort of our own desires.

Let us not make truth subordinate to reputation, religious identity, social acceptance, or personal convenience.

Let us seek truth even when it challenges our assumptions. Let us face truth even when it exposes our shortcomings. Let us live in truth even when doing so requires us to relinquish something we wish to preserve.

Seek the Truth. Face the Truth. Speak the Truth. Live in Truth.

Truth is not something to invoke when it benefits us and abandon when it becomes uncomfortable. It is a commitment that must govern our understanding, intentions, and conduct.

For those who genuinely aspire to liberation, this commitment must extend beyond words, beliefs, and religious appearances. It must become part of the purification of the individual citta.

Seek the Truth. Live in Truth. Purify the Mind. Attain Liberation.

title: A Fundamental Question. A Forgotten Spiritual Teaching. A New Chapter in The History of Gautama's Dhamma Dispensation.
content:
What if Gautama, the Supreme Arahant, did not teach the non-existence of Soul-Spirit? What if the ancient renunciants were cultivating, disciplining, elevating, and liberating a spiritual reality whose significance has been obscured by centuries of doctrinal interpretation?

Attā, Citta, and Viññāṇa: Recovering the Soul-Spirit of Gautama’s Liberation Teaching is a landmark Arahanist examination of one of the most consequential questions in the history of Buddhist thought: the nature of Soul-Spirit and its place in the path to liberation.

This work advances a fundamental challenge to the dominant interpretation of Anattā as a universal denial of Soul-Spirit. Drawing upon the Pāḷi Suttas, the testimonies of ancient renunciants, Vedic spiritual knowledge, and the wider Indian renunciant heritage, Bhante Mudita Bhikkhu Thera undertakes a systematic recovery of the spiritual meaning of Attā and its relationship to the true purpose of Gautama's liberation teaching.

THREE FUNDAMENTAL DIMENSIONS OF EXISTENCE

At the heart of this work is the distinction between three dimensions of human existence:

  • Attā (Soul-Spirit): The individual spiritual reality whose liberation from worldly bondage is central to the Arahanist understanding of the path.
  • Citta (Mind-Heart): The sphere of mental and spiritual functioning requiring purification, discipline, and inward establishment.
  • Viññāṇa (Sense-Generated Consciousness): Consciousness arising through sensory experience, distinct from both Citta and Soul-Spirit.

Their relationship provides the foundation for reconsidering the nature of the human being, the purpose of renunciation, and the ultimate attainment of liberation.

RECOVERING THE SPIRITUAL TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENT ELDERS

Through an examination of the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā, the author brings renewed attention to the words of ancient Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs. Their testimonies repeatedly speak of disciplining Attā, elevating it, protecting it, establishing it in Samādhi, and overcoming worldly bondage.

These verses are examined alongside the linguistic and spiritual heritage of Sanskrit Ātmā, Pāḷi Attā, and Prakrit Appā, as well as the wider Indian traditions of spiritual inquiry and renunciation. Particular attention is given to Ajjhatta and its significance for the inward direction of spiritual cultivation.

A FUNDAMENTAL RE-EXAMINATION OF ANATTĀ

Through close examination of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (SN 22.59) and the Cūḷavedalla Sutta (MN 44), this work confronts a central doctrinal question: What exactly did Gautama reject when he declared the five aggregates to be Anattā?

It distinguishes the rejection of the five conditioned aggregates as Attā from the universal denial of Soul-Spirit. It also examines how the translation of Attā as "self", the expansion of Anattā, and subsequent doctrinal developments contributed, in the Arahanist assessment, to the displacement of Soul-Spirit from the understanding of Buddhist liberation.

USHERING IN A NEW ERA OF ARAHANISM

This book marks a significant step in the contemporary articulation and development of Arahanism—the Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.

Its purpose extends beyond challenging inherited interpretations. It seeks to establish a renewed foundation for understanding, practising, and transmitting the liberation teaching through the Sutta and Vinaya, with renunciation and Arahantship restored to their central spiritual importance.

For nearly two millennia, the spiritual significance of Attā has remained obscured within the dominant interpretation of Buddhist doctrine. Arahanism now undertakes the responsibility of bringing this question back to the forefront, recovering the testimonies of the ancient elders, and making their spiritual significance accessible to generations yet to come.

This is a call to re-examine the foundations of Buddhist doctrine, restore the Saddhamma, and renew the pursuit of the Deathless.

The defining question of this work is also its greatest challenge: Is liberation the denial of Soul-Spirit, or the liberation of Soul-Spirit from worldly bondage?

Arahanism — The Liberation Path of Gautama, the Supreme Arahant.
